# Loo-Cast and Vapor: Historical and Repository Evolution

This is the expanded historical companion to [the Vapor ecosystem evidence atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md). It traces the design lineage before Vapor had a visible product/repository identity, the emergence of Vapor as a named system, and the growth and repeated reshaping of its repository family. The detailed Loo-Cast commit register is retained below. For the deeper interpretation of the human and technical through-line, see [Loo-Cast and Vapor: origin, intent, and causal history](loo-cast-vapor-origin-and-intent.md), the [PlantUML timeline source](loo-cast-vapor-mega-timeline.puml), or its [rendered timeline](loo-cast-vapor-mega-timeline.svg).

**Research orientation:** the main chronology remains oldest-to-newest for causal legibility, but it is no longer the starting point for the audit. The active question is now: *what does the latest source snapshot actually mean, how did each of its important seams form, and which other code, documents, proposals, owner decisions, reports, and reversals agree or disagree with it?* Begin with the current-state cross-reference (reviewed October 25–26 and pinned to the October 26 worktree refresh); use this timeline to trace each present boundary backward through the commits and design decisions that formed, revised or abandoned it. Current-state explanation receives the greatest detail; early prototypes are included where they explain a surviving constraint, repeated failure pattern or deliberate reset. A separately labelled appendix at the end groups latest-source audit findings by review date; its notes can discuss older event dates and are not additional chronologically placed commit events.

> **Scope and evidence.** The record is strong from the first reachable `Loo-Cast-Legacy` commit (2022-06-07) and from the first named Vapor repositories (2026-06-30). The owner recalls a 2021 beginning, but the accessible Git history does not prove that date or identify a 2021 repository. No exact “Vapor was named on this day” claim is made: June 30 is the earliest verifiable named-repository/workspace evidence in this audit, not necessarily the moment the name was invented in conversation or privately.

> **Remote-history freshness check (2026-10-25; rechecked 2026-10-26):** connected GitHub reads of the latest commit on default `main` were repeated for all fifteen checked-out repositories on both dates: Loo-Cast; Vapor-Client and its seven product/shared-code submodules; Platform Server and its five independently owned service submodules. Every returned SHA matches its corresponding local checkout on October 26 as well. The latest committed changes among these roots are dated Oct 21–23, with Registry-Server’s latest commit on Sep 15; the local source snapshot and dirty-state inventory were refreshed October 26, not 2022. The October 26 local status is distinct from these public commits: Loo-Cast has a modified Cargo.lock, Vapor-Installer has a modified UI source file, Vapor has two untracked October 24 design documents, and the Client parent reports nested-repository changes for Vapor and Vapor-Installer. These local states were left untouched. This confirms latest default-branch heads for the fifteen checked-out roots, not every remote branch, release, Workshop upload or deployed VPS state.

> **Diagram status (2026-10-25):** the PlantUML source and rendered SVG now include the October 15–19 Workshop/Library lifecycle and October 25 source findings for partial subscription effects, cache-index crash recovery, sequential opaque acquisition, generic artifact staging, the Registry authority gap, distinct GUI process images, and idle-based shared-service lifetime. The diagram is a selected causal map; the text timeline remains the fuller chronology.

> **Diff-review status.** The commit register is chronological coverage, not proof that every changed line has been reviewed. A separate [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md) tracks coverage and records selected hunk-level analysis; the July–October 2024 review now distinguishes renamed request IDs from stored requests, checks entity/actor `save_*` bodies against actual persistence, follows the Rust/Lua operation sketches, and records the unfinished locking hierarchy. Its 2025 supplements examine workflow/action semantics, selection and logging, runtime/module experiments, nested-scale arithmetic, origin rebasing and render/picking ownership; the January–June 2026 Legacy supplements trace the first Rhai/lifetime-erased ECS bridge, the `AccessCell` redesign, the finite Rust signature catalog behind generic script descriptors, April’s reset of USF design authority, May’s experimental math facade/backend split and abandonment, and June’s owner-authority/product-stack correction. Selected Vapor hunks also examine the content kind and pack graph, `Library`→`Crate`, the first wide CLI lifecycle, the October `vapor sdk` command facade and its incomplete dispatch, typed stdout/stderr operation transport, dynamic-Rust-library versus Packagepack-linked examples, the generated-template/build/launch mismatch, target-specific packaging, installed-Packagepack ownership and the broad October shared-service move. The latest cross-check adds the Studio/service/IDE operation-queue split: service reservations reject conflicts, Studio queues those responses locally, and IDE has a separate serialized workspace path. Product/server histories and the remaining cross-repository diffs are still open.

> **Historical depth policy:** early C#/Unity and prototype Rust are mostly rough exploratory work, not a codebase to audit character by character. Those years explain the major attempts, resets, and ideas that survived. Analytical depth rises sharply toward the present: recent Vapor/Loo-Cast decisions, active ownership boundaries, and cross-repository behavior receive the detailed semantic scrutiny because they determine what the ecosystem is now.

## Executive reading

Vapor did not begin as a polished platform architecture and then get distributed into repos. The evidence points to a long-running game/engine project repeatedly encountering the same pressure: gameplay should be separable from reusable machinery; reusable machinery should be modifiable; mods need stable identity and a way to be found, built, distributed, and combined; and development tooling must own more of those steps if the result is to be safe and repeatable. Those pressures predate the word **Vapor** by years.

The lineage has three distinguishable layers:

1. **Loo-Cast as the experimental source of problems (2022–2025):** a Unity game grows data-authoring and modding ambitions, then the project deliberately clears gameplay code to build an engine. The work cycles through custom models, ECS, serialization, scripting, Rust crates and many prototypes. This is where the engine/game and modding problem is repeatedly encountered, but it is not yet Vapor.
2. **Vapor as an explicit ecosystem model (2026):** toolchain control, typed workspace/content identity, sources, Workshop distribution, composition, install/launch and developer workflow are brought into one named system. The first visible named artifacts are created in late June; work quickly separates shared semantics from user-facing products and server facilities.
3. **Repositories as a changing implementation map (June–October 2026):** repos first track experiments and executable/product names; later they are renamed, consolidated, nested under client/server containers, or split by service ownership. The current 21-repository organization snapshot is a historical accumulation, not a single designed-at-once architecture.

The most important interpretive point is that **repository count is not the same thing as semantic complexity**. Some splits represent real isolation (client versus public platform services, or independent service deployment); others record a temporary product label or implementation experiment. The history shows both deliberate boundary design and boundary churn.

## What existed before “Vapor”

### 2021: remembered origin, not yet independently evidenced

The owner places the broader project’s beginning around early-to-mid 2021. The accessible `Loo-Cast-Legacy` GitHub repo was created in June 2022 and its reachable history begins at a Unity project root on June 7, 2022. The repo contains no verifiable parent commit from 2021. This is a boundary of the records examined, not a claim that the project did not exist earlier. A 2021 Unity project archive, Git bundle, old repository URL, dated design notes, or backup could extend this section.

### 2022: a game project develops authorable systems

The first surviving tree is not a platform or engine SDK: it is a Unity/C# game. During 2022, work increasingly moves game data out of one-off behavior and into modular authoring patterns: ScriptableObjects, data modularization, variables and computed variables, interfaces, editor drawers, stats/attributes, persistence experiments, and Steam builds. Gameplay expands into inventory, items/upgrades, stations, missions, targeting, AI and world state.

The July 31 `ca5a77f6` patch tries to make that modularity a general model: it adds Core `Object`/`Component` and `Data`/`RuntimeData` taxonomies, “unique” variants, sample authored objects, runtime sets, and changes the shared lifecycle callback from `Cycle` to `OnPauseableUpdate`. The core classes are empty type labels, while the examples have unset data/runtime properties and no injection path. The migration also leaves movement and experience consumers calling removed parameterless `Initialize()` methods, uses undeclared energy state instead of the new runtime-data object, and gives the experience UI wrapper-style `.Value`/change-event access to plain numeric fields. These are source-level declaration mismatches, not compiler-run claims. The next August change promptly removes the generic Core/Data sample taxonomy and moves toward domain-specific data assets; this makes July a short-lived model experiment rather than the start of a continuously implemented framework. See the exact [July hunk review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#july-2022-the-generic-data-model-and-lifecycle-naming-are-reshaped).

The August data migration shows the cost of declaring abstractions before their lifecycle is closed. [`adb83aa9`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/adb83aa908305ec4012d191e74802244f5c9a232) extends the July generic `Data`/`RuntimeData` framework with health and movement runtime records and modifier objects, but omits the player movement base initializer. About 36 hours later, [`5c9125ab`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/5c9125ab3890f878f6bd972ee6e8175fcb932134) deletes the generic Core `Data`, `Component`, uniqueness and component/object runtime-set specializations, while retaining domain-specific runtime records as ordinary mutable `ScriptableObject` assets. It also restores the player movement initializer, so that specific omission is repaired; the patch still leaves runtime maximum energy unassigned and introduces other Awake/Start-order hazards. The rollback of shared base types is not a move to per-entity runtime ownership: the patch shows no cloning or allocation boundary for those mutable assets. Setup shifts from parent-owned initialization toward separate component `Start` methods. The next day, [`031b8f91`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/031b8f91f26738b8fe1ea467fd0df90ce2c0e236) renames authored `*Reference` fields to `*DataReference` and starts separating them from runtime `Variable` wrappers, but the new constructors fail at their event/setter boundary. The following patches continue changing that value model rather than settling it. The exact hunk review records these source-level defects; none of these historical revisions was built or run for this review.

Persistence enters the same model churn in mid-August. [`3f654f42`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/3f654f42c296605618f3b35101ccac86cde352e5) changes 509 file blobs, including 79 C# paths, 46 JSON snapshots, and code that adds `ISaveable`, `JSONUtil`, and `OnEnable`/`OnDisable` persistence for Attribute, Stat, Coins and Tokens. It stores under `Application.dataPath/Data`, reads user snapshots before `Data/Default`, and throws if neither exists. [`0bf0ba93`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/0bf0ba939d6ccd82937030072bc800bb1b57a74d) then shifts save/load loops onto aggregate `Attributes` and `Stats` assets and removes the shared interface while currency keeps separate self-saving methods. This is a broad, lifecycle-coupled persistence implementation that is promptly reorganized—not a JSON-shape-only patch.

By October, the same boundary problem appears in spatial tooling, movement, AI, and inventory. A “cleanup” renames Universe generation fields while changing noise defaults and removing scene overrides; the new directional movement interface initially receives a Player vector computed as a world-space target near the origin, then the next commit corrects it. A modifier cleanup makes temporary effects easier to name and remove, but still has no timer-start path. The first generic FSM migration leaks Enemy chase updates across pause; its next AI pass moves all state dispatch behind the actor’s pause-gated callbacks and adds a chase-to-roam transition. The targeting helper then moves enemy selection from a known Player reference to raw nearby colliders; a subsequent Ally migration uses the helper only for roaming while leaving its evade query direct. The balance pass gives Allies a return-home state but leaves the analogous Enemy state unregistered, alongside a major station/enemy density rebalance. A later `NewTarget` wrapper adds health and invalidation to raw colliders but installs an event listener on every wrapper without a disposal path; the ensuing bulk integration deletes the old targeting components before all weapon APIs have migrated, and its changed source contains compile-level inconsistencies. Follow-up commits add typed health teams and repair those immediate source mismatches, but rename the wrapper without resolving its unbounded event subscription or the no-target conversion that throws before callers can check for null. A separate station refactor renames PlayerStation to AllyStation across the component and screen, but its first pass leaves the attached health/inventory types under the old name; a follow-up fixes them. The next generation refactor moves three generators behind ScriptableObject data and prefab composition; it initially omits AllyStation from the aggregate's serialized generator list, then adds the reference while deactivating the Ally generator instance. The newly added station-owned AllySpawner tracks actor-level kill events, while health depletion destroys Ally objects through a separate path, so the authored cap can remain exhausted after deaths. At the same time, TagManager renames `Enemy` to `NPC` while enemy prefabs and team/tag utilities still use `Enemy`. A minimap is then added as a camera filtered to layer 21, drawing duplicated marker sprites from entity prefabs into a RenderTexture for a scene RawImage; background renderers also share that layer. A follow-up increases the texture from 512² to 2000² to address icon quality without recorded visual or memory measurements. Background tiling moves from a runtime-created 3×3 renderer array to nine manually referenced scene renderers, then bases wrap thresholds on source sprite bounds while reducing camera orthographic size. On October 21, a shared item setter is changed to normalize containment without updating the old container; its new null path also conflicts with the existing removal operation. These selected diffs show useful abstractions emerging alongside incomplete coordinate, lifecycle, scheduling, target-validity, integration, and ownership contracts.

The October 20–21 upgrade/item commits sharpen the ownership issue. [efd9a11b](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/efd9a11be763b0a4d723ba7a115370f03c191f46) introduces reversible stat-modifier contracts and moves temporary increases ahead of multipliers; [d227708c](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/d227708c303e8c1db1a4dd34097c4f13d06c8f45) converts weapon fields to computed variables but removes constructor-time application of the supplied Stats values, with no new application call shown in that slice. It also wires projectile lifetime to damage multiplier and leaves the cooldown timer configured from the base attack delay. [1668fa79](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/1668fa79b4eaf3f440880b5a6c21b820cc57e0) adds a Player-owned UpgradeSet snapshot copied once in Awake, but no application path. Then [461c62d8](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/461c62d816cc6f08e6cf7fb00707f38a3681432f) advertises null from empty-slot removal while dereferencing the item and attempting to contain null; [1334337e](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/1334337eb69d5c72c321ac500fc9bd4f76b0c198) tries to normalize item ownership but leaves the previous container's slot pointing at the transferred item and still cannot clear a slot. It adds an EnemyStationInventory component without changing the station prefab in that patch. These are patch-level defects and incomplete wiring, not claims about a tested player build; the hunk-by-hunk evidence is in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

This matters as prehistory because it establishes two durable tensions, not because the old systems were carried forward wholesale:

- **Content needs a shape authors can extend.** Data and gameplay are being made more declarative and modular.
- **A game’s runtime and the tools that define it are entangled.** Editor code, data definitions, runtime systems and distribution all live in the same project.

The late-2022 diffs make those tensions concrete. Weapon cooldowns first use a framework timer whose callback runs away from Unity's update thread; the author records AutoFire breaking, then replaces it with a custom MonoBehaviour timer so callbacks return to Unity's frame loop. That fixes the identified thread-affinity seam, but adds a global timer singleton and does not settle disposal or scheduling policy. At almost the same time, `MainManager` acquires new-game creation, scene loading and a large hard-coded generation preset; the subsequent Game/save-slot model adds names and runtime identifiers before its persistence methods are complete. The world-generation work then becomes its own expanding subsystem: chunk hierarchy, per-chunk generation state, raw worker threads, completion queues, profiling and GPU paths. Within weeks, the observer's asynchronous/coroutine machinery is substantially removed, the loading path returns to synchronous per-frame work, and the December 14 `fd6be1b6` patch deletes the attempted persistent-data tree. Thus the surviving lineage is not a steadily completed saveable game: it is a sequence where runtime ownership, durable identity, world generation and frame-budgeted work become recurring architectural questions, while specific 2022 solutions are often abandoned.

November 8–13 revisits item upgrades and exposes a second execution-context boundary. Computed weapon stats are introduced, an UpgradableItem base then applies an owner-provided set on containment, and EnemyStationInventory is eventually attached to the station prefab. But the concrete weapon implementation ignores the passed UpgradeSet and uses its own stored Stats again; item uncontainment has no inverse upgrade removal. System.Timers then calls Unity-facing weapon code asynchronously; the author’s debug instrumentation records manual firing working while AutoFire fails on Unity object access. TimerUtil moves callbacks into MonoBehaviour.Update and station weapons are restored. Five explicit reverts then roll back the earlier October modifier contracts, setter and UpgradeSet snapshots while the newer UpgradableItem hierarchy remains in the November 11 source. So this is not a simple “upgrade system completed” story: one partial design is withdrawn while a distinct, still-incomplete ownership path continues. The exact patch reading is in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

By January 2023 the history explicitly contains a [modding framework](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/d62a53a4e4dcad27f7bd3161b87043fc15848d8e), a [modding plan](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/9d31582be469d746d5a92d615d5d14688c2a0ad1), and [identifier-system work](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/fad054e4a202d691042c2f9f3730f3de38be4852). This is an early ancestor of Vapor’s later content identity/discovery problem, but it is not the same identity model or implementation.

### 2023: “Base Mod” and engine extraction reveal the split problem

In February 2023 the repository is moved into “Base Mod”; the commit itself says the author must weave the threads back together while building the foundation. In April, legacy gameplay code and assets are deliberately wiped to let engine development proceed without the old game interfering. The game is no longer the codebase’s trusted center: the project is trying to extract reusable capability from it.

The next sequence tests several answers: custom entity/data/logic structures, scene and hierarchy systems, then ECS; coordinate and universe representations; chunking and serialization frameworks; management/lifecycle; developer console; and scripting. On August 16, 2023, a command model with reflection-backed descriptors and documentation is drafted, revised, and removed for Lua within hours; the revised model still has empty invocation bodies and a nested-namespace constructor that reaches an uninitialized child map. Lua then moves from a standalone console state toward a manager-owned, attribute/reflection-registered host with `LoadCLRPackage()` enabled. This shows real interest in discoverable commands and host/script composition, but the implementation is short-lived and incomplete; it is not a working ancestor of today’s bounded Rhai model. The broader path repeatedly asks questions later central to Vapor: what is reusable machinery, what is game content, how are modules identified, and how does authored behavior enter a host runtime?

The September chunk-manager sequence makes a similar distinction between an architectural intention and an operational implementation. `437b6b60` adds a worker-based noise-image generator, but the actual observer path still generates or loads chunks synchronously and writes save data beneath `assets/data/saves`. `7e445030` introduces a separate queued worker, but holds shared locks while generating and running callbacks, so callback re-entry can deadlock; duplicate position requests are silently dropped, and the detached worker has no shutdown path. `bf9bc0fa` defines a detailed five-stage state machine and queue/callback machinery, but its worker blocks on the first of five sequential channel receives before reaching any process receiver; it also records unresolved state transitions, lock scope and cancellation in its own TODOs. `e452f605` improves shared ownership and adds transition checks without changing that blocking topology; three spawn branches mistakenly send to the load channel, and the worker still advances states/callbacks without invoking chunk generation or persistence. `37495a30` removes the channels, but its outer worker loop has no wait or sleep and repeatedly logs while idle; it marks work complete without invoking `generate_chunk`, `load_chunk` or `unload_chunk`. The observer’s state matches are empty, and this plugin does not register the added spawn/despawn systems. This is evidence of active design exploration around staged residency and ECS representation—not evidence that a functional asynchronous chunk pipeline was completed. The findings are based on source control flow; no build or runtime trace for these historical revisions was available.

The earliest direct written USF seed located so far is [`e19d4f2c` (September 9)](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/e19d4f2cadf3d537afa18e538a184563acf7f9f2), a 74-line prompt backup. It already links scale-specific phenomenon models, ECS representations, event timing, context dependencies, detail-probability/zone-lookup maps, transitions and chunk-based viewing radius. That makes USF more than a later label for the Rust engine: the scale/detail problem was being articulated in writing while the Unity-to-Rust transition and chunk scheduling were still unsettled. The note is an early concept record, not a finalized specification, and it does not establish that the later Rust, Bevy or current spacetime contracts were already defined.

By October, the work shifts from per-chunk operation state to a cluster residency model and globally encoded chunk IDs. `044eae1f` stores three encodings of the same numeric identity plus scale/local/cluster fields, but contains a call to a nonexistent accessor and accepts an empty digit-pair vector into an underflowing conversion loop. `0b0c0c4b` corrects the accessor and sketches Registered → MetadataLoaded → DataLoaded, but its payloads remain placeholder integers and the manager is empty with private transitions. The design vocabulary expands faster than the usable API or verified invariants.

November repeatedly redefines both how Rust code should be organized and what a chunk/entity identity means. `e05dc2f8` first copies the source tree to `newsrc` and fills each file with section headings as a formatting/organization experiment; `22ad31cd` manually moves declarations into those categories and deletes the duplicate tree, while explicitly leaving subcategories as undocumented implicit knowledge. `51374d80` soon replaces the earlier staged lifecycle with viewer-owned coordinate lists and a load/unload manager. That manager creates empty chunk marker entities only, does not deduplicate overlapping viewer requests, panics on duplicate loads/unloads, and removes its own resource without clearing loaded entities on exit. The viewer's 9×9 demand scan also calls coordinate helpers from the iteration-test module. The follow-on staged identity model (`81f48474`) adds separate chunk, cluster and entity residency enums over placeholder data and nested locks; `1d609519` then empties three non-unit cluster API methods. `6c20d5ba` starts converting panics into `Result`s but introduces source-visible return/type mismatches, followed by the file split in `4df99666`, whose constructors and field declarations still disagree. `1e960e02` introduces parent/local chunk positions and a request manager, while `a91b890d` replaces placeholder chunk data with Bevy run-state and simultaneously comments out the public transition methods. `2ebcd38d` changes the child map from global IDs to local positions, but leaves global position computation unfinished and comments out registration/query operations. On the identity side, depth and `CHUNK_SIZE` repeatedly change, and empty-input validation arrives alongside renewed API incompleteness. These are not only naming or formatting experiments: they expose unsettled policy at boundaries between world coordinates, chunk identity, ECS state and operation ownership. The companion review records exact patches and distinguishes visible source defects from unverified runtime behavior.

### 2024–2025: the engine becomes Rust-first, while the modding boundary remains unsettled

The project separates Engine and BaseMod into Rust crates, then experiments with build scripts, kernels, macros, registries, UI, commands and data systems. From May 2024 through early 2025, Prototype Mk0–Mk10 checkpoints record successive rewrites, rollbacks and new structures rather than a stable release line. Rust and Bevy gradually become the implementation foundation; old assets and ideas are selectively brought forward.

By September 2025, a Mk9 checkpoint explicitly de-prioritizes multiplayer and points toward modding and the Universal Scale Framework (USF). This is a key convergence: the engine’s hard problem is not only rendering or simulation, but how to let separately authored/reusable pieces participate in one coherent runtime. March 2026 still shows the work as modding/USF exploration in the Legacy history, including the “Crazy modding shit undso” checkpoint. It is evidence of a conceptual push, not proof that Vapor’s later code already existed.

### The bridge: from engine/modding questions to a named platform

The bridge is best understood as a change in the question being asked:

```text
Earlier:
  How should Loo-Cast's engine and mods be structured?

Emerging in 2026:
  How should content, source projects, tools, builds, distribution,
  installation, identity, and launch fit into one ecosystem?
```

The earlier work supplies the problems and some domain concepts; the 2026 Vapor work adds a system-level answer: typed manifests and identities, a pinned Rust toolchain, source workspaces, compiled artifacts, Steam Workshop as a distribution surface, and an orchestration/client layer that can acquire, validate, compose, build, install and launch content. The code and docs evolve quickly, so this should be read as the direction that emerged—not as a fully completed end-to-end contract on the first day.

There is no evidence that a single repository was simply renamed from Loo-Cast into Vapor. Instead, a fresh named Vapor workspace appears alongside a continuing Loo-Cast history, with engine and game work split into a new Loo-Cast repo shortly afterward. The new and legacy Loo-Cast histories overlap in time and are not Git-connected.

## How the named system appeared

### June 30–July 7: several seeds are planted in parallel

GitHub’s repository records and local Git roots show a burst of related starts around June 30, 2026:

- `Vapor` begins with an agent protocol, workspace skeleton and lockfile, followed by a shared content vocabulary and toolchain manifest on July 1.
- The repository that is now `Vapor-Studio` begins as a **Launcher** workspace and agent protocol. The earliest commits call it Launcher; “Studio” is a later product interpretation/rename, not its original scope.
- `Vapor-Examples`, `Vapor-SDK`, `Spacetime-Engine` and `Loo-Cast-Game` are also created as separate repository objects around the same period. Some are thin seeds or experiments rather than mature independent implementations.
- `Loo-Cast` starts on July 7 at a fresh Git root with “Bootstrap unified Loo-Cast workspace,” containing engine, game and packagepack roles in one Rust workspace. This is a new implementation history, not a continuation of the 2,350-commit Legacy graph.

This is the first visible phase where “Vapor” is more than an aspiration around Loo-Cast: it has a named shared workspace, typed content vocabulary and a managed toolchain direction. The shared repo’s first commits establish that the tool itself should be an authored, identified Vapor project; the Launcher prototype is being made into a Vapor project too. The system begins to describe its own source and products with its own vocabulary.

The first source contract is much narrower than the later ecosystem plan. On July 1, the initial `ContentType` table lists nine kinds, including four Packs, but not `Crate`; Packagepack can contain every listed kind, including another Packagepack, while the other pack lists are fixed shallow allowlists. These are kind labels and coarse parent/child filters, not the later dependency, compatibility, option, cardinality or conflict graph. On July 1, the first toolchain manifest pins `nightly-2026-01-30`, but its host/target set is Linux GNU plus Windows MSVC; Windows GNU-LLVM does not appear until the shipping workflow makes the mismatch concrete. The manifest identity changes from `[vapor] kind = vapor_root` to `[workspace] kind = core` on July 2. These fast changes show that Vapor began by giving the concepts names and compiling a shared core, while its identity schema and cross-target guarantees were still provisional. The source-level details are in the [early core hunk review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#june-30july-2--the-first-core-and-toolchain-contract).

July also records a change in how architecture decisions are produced. Vapor's first commit (`6db76f2`, June 30) bundled fourteen Q&A files at once, so their filenames preserve order but not authoring dates. The next record is timestamped: `020a` plus a pre-rewrite flat source arrives July 3 at 12:50; successive `020b`/`020c` queues revise it later that day; `020d` arrives July 4 alongside saved pre-collapse history and separate roadmap-hierarchy and glossary-migration branches. The queue spans fifteen domains—from documentation authority, repo/dependency topology and Steam bootstrap through toolchains, artifact identity, packs/Rhai, Workshop trust and command safety. This is a move from capturing answers to explicitly managing dependent unanswered questions. A pivot restores the legacy glossary as canonical source material rather than merely “legacy quarry,” but directs selective migration instead of wholesale copying. A subsequent commit creates a nested roadmap and six mdBook navigation trees. This is an attempt to make documentation an explicit product interface; most leaf pages are target outlines/placeholders, so the navigation structure is evidence of intended reader segmentation, not evidence that the books are complete or current. The exact commit sequence is in Vapor [`77a3676`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/77a3676), [`a25824b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/a25824b), and [`9134d3f`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/9134d3f); the order of Q&A answers is not a timestamp or proof of causal authorship.

The owner also shared a July 3 screenshot of the Vapor SDK demo workspace as the workbench mockup they meant: project tree, conventional IDE menus and file tabs, a Packagepack graph, a semantic inspector, build/package/publish actions and visible build output. The owner described it as a reference for growing the in-game script workbench into a fuller authoring environment; later messages make the target a distinct Vapor IDE with workspace/content understanding, in-game scripting, Rust Analyzer/LSP and managed Rust tooling. The image records design intent and one demo build pane, not proof that every shown workflow was shipped. Its filesystem timestamp is 2026-07-03 21:37:22 +02; see [the screenshot](</home/leslieghf/Pictures/Screenshots/Screenshot_20260703_213719.png>) and the [origin analysis](loo-cast-vapor-origin-and-intent.md).

### July 3–5: the first container-and-submodule model

The future `Vapor-Client` repo was initially known in the migration corpus as `Vapor-Root`. Its early commits anchor Vapor, SDK and Launcher as submodules. A July 4 commit then removes the Loo-Cast-Game and Spacetime-Engine submodules, explaining that they should be default/automatically subscribed Workshop content rather than part of the Vapor app root. This is a consequential boundary decision:

- the **Vapor app/depot** is the product/tooling environment;
- the **game, engine and packagepack** are content, even when first-party and needed for the default experience;
- the container may pin source repositories for building Vapor, but the user-facing installation model should acquire content through content semantics.

A July 7 topology commit establishes the unified workspace/project identity approach. July 9 quickly replaces a toolchain-first Shell surface with a setup flow and splits host facades from shell commands; July 10 starts implementing Workshop content lifecycle. These commits show the conceptual workload swelling from “a CLI wrapper” to cross-cutting source, setup, content and distribution semantics.

The initial Vapor pieces already contain both a product vision and a mismatch that later work must resolve. The shared Vapor workspace calls itself the root ecosystem layer and sketches a `vapor_core`/`vapor_macros` foundation, but its first crates are scaffolding. The Launcher repo’s opening protocol assigns install/select/validate/compose/launch to a Launcher and publishing to a separate SDK, while the first CLI is instead a small Rhai REPL whose state is inferred from the current directory and a string mode. The Client container briefly gathers Vapor, SDK, Launcher and Examples as submodules, then removes the Engine and Game submodules because they should be Workshop content. The intended content/source separation appears before the machinery that can actually deliver compiled content is established.

The July 2 Registry seed adds a distinct trust idea: a Git-reviewed machine-readable manifest maps GitHub identities and organization roles to first-party Steam app/depot permissions, while Steam still enforces the final Steamworks permission. Its initial grant binds the GitHub account and GHF-Studios owner role to Loo-Cast app 2122620/root depot 2122621. The manifest schema then moves from a custom `[workspace] kind = "registry"` identity to the shared `schema = 1` form, changes the explicit dotted ID to a slash ID, then replaces that ID with `name` plus `organization`; on July 19 the filename becomes `Registry.vapor.toml`. This is a declarative, reviewed authority layer over Steam operations, not an alternative to Steam authorization or evidence of a live authorization service. The fast schema changes show Vapor’s manifest vocabulary was still actively being negotiated.

The glossary history is a distinct part of the same design-formation period. On July 5, `Vapor-Client/b7fd414` imports a 125-page scattered glossary and raw information corpus from the Loo-Cast `origin/develop` source snapshot. A few hours later, `6ca90c3` establishes persistent planning intake/evidence/atomization stages and the 27-page technical glossary set. The register explicitly marks those imported glossary pages unprocessed and unvetted; the extraction preserves statements and terminology, not truth. Its `USF.md` entry already contains an owner-answer correction: USF is a Spacetime Engine subsystem, not a Vapor product pillar or a Vapor-level capability, while Capability is broader Vapor runtime/contract machinery. Aug 30 then adds a focused USF monolith; Sep 9 organizes a separate Vapor monolith and says each concept needs one normative owner. The current book glossary begins as a July stub and is expanded in October but still retains a Composition distinction later challenged by the owner. This history is a staged preservation → consolidation → product-book summary sequence, not proof that each old page was faithfully migrated into a final canonical glossary. The exact status and term crosswalk are in the [current atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#archived-vapor-glossary-cross-check--2026-10-25) and [source-corpus register](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/planning-intake/corpus-register.md>).

### July 17–23: shipping and operating Vapor creates new boundaries

Cross-target packaging becomes explicit: Linux and Windows target artifacts, setup prerequisites and Steam launch wrappers are handled separately. On July 19, root publishing pivots to installer-managed split depots. On July 20, the Steam entrypoint is extracted into its own repo so Steam’s native launch boundary can route into Vapor without making every app frontend a separate bootstrap.

On July 23, four service briefs appear within minutes: [Docs](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Docs-Server/commit/c435add6d62b3973b3f35919444336c386f5c22b), [Homepage](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Homepage-Server/commit/f6f92104d6747517733c6bc7677ff91f245cbb26), [Identity](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Identity-Server/commit/0759b49178f94eb0163ac2fc84f828f31c48b4ef) and [Diagnostics](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Diagnostics-Server/commit/14e1381564a1f37e46e7c3c349d71cf524eb0820). They define separate data, privacy and trust responsibilities before implementing them. The [Platform Server root](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/e8e63df8e421b1a68eb94c3c8a7fa6f6c2fcde8b) follows about two hours later with submodule pins, a Caddy example routing the four localhost services under one domain, and a manifest for routes/state owners; it labels itself planning-only and contains no accepted server implementation yet. Later the Registry service gains its own repository. This split has a stronger operational rationale than the early UI-repository multiplication: server services have distinct data, trust, deployment and recovery boundaries, while `Vapor-Platform-Server` owns orchestration and deployment. A separate `Vapor-Registry` repo holds the Registry manifest/catalog identity; `Vapor-Registry-Server` is the executable service implementation. The similar names are historically easy to confuse, but the roles are not identical.

The trust distinction is important: Identity is intended to authenticate linked Steam/GitHub identities and authorize developer/root actions; Registry is a reviewed semantic catalog mapping identities/roles to first-party Steam permissions; Steam remains the final enforcement point for Steamworks. The first Platform root does not route a Registry service yet, so that authority layer joins later. Its initial README also says service repositories are empty and should later be added as submodules, although the same root commit already contains their initial gitlinks—a small docs/tree synchronization failure visible at the starting boundary.

The early service code is a series of scaffolds followed by rapid implementation. Identity moves to SQLite and Steam/GitHub verification seams; Diagnostics states explicit opt-in/privacy and retention constraints; Docs accepts bounded tar-gzip static trees for serving. Docs briefly gains immutable content-derived releases with promotion/rollback, then removes that design and returns to a simpler current-tree API. This is a useful example of the project revising complexity downward when a stronger versioning model is not justified.

The Registry service does not join the initial July route map. Its first implementation appears on September 7, after the separate Registry manifest repository had already established a Git-reviewed first-party permission seed. The service’s SQLite schema and GET routes describe provider accounts, repositories, and an ecosystem’s acquisition topology; its bootstrap transaction seeds those records at startup. This is useful for discovering the source roots needed to reconstruct Vapor, but it is not yet the typed content/Workshop catalog later called for by the October 21 Platform Server decision. The distinction is important: a repository topology API is not Workshop type filtering, content version/channel authority, or identity authorization. Those later contracts are a target, not a feature implied by the service name. The same day's `Vapor-Platform-Server/e9e4ba3` commit adds Registry's server-local directory/configuration but accidentally truncates `bootstrap-ubuntu.sh`, deleting its shebang, host/root preflight, package and user setup, and completion reporting. The first-run deployment guide continues to call that file directly, and subsequent commits preserve the damage; this is a clean-install/rebuild regression in source, not evidence that the previously configured VPS failed. See the [current bootstrap trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#current-root-deployment-bootstrap-and-recovery-cross-check).

### August 30–September 12: rewrite doctrine and documentation ownership become explicit

The documentary record shows a second architecture shift, this time in how design knowledge is organized. On August 30, the focused [USF Model glossary](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/c8b91a3ef83628e5105a2a8c6bc99c66ce231458) is added as a compact ontology, including distinct entries for State Authority, State Representation, Mechanism, Simulation Regime, Phenomenon, spatial scale and temporal scale. It defines 71 logarithmic **spatial** levels, while temporal scale is mechanism- and context-dependent rather than derived automatically from that coordinate. That is a dated model snapshot, not evidence that the runtime implements it or that every later owner discussion retained every definition.

On September 4, [`Vapor Rewrite Bootstrap.md`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/7c529304f7543862520c630bc52d22cb3b2d2c0e) first appears. Its initial framing is implementation-oriented: the current Premium Docs define the model, and the bootstrap supplies the first architecture-proving slice. On September 8, a [large rewrite](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/fa0fe19057f0e3eb177056911fdf0bba3272361b) changes its role to a **historical record**: why the rewrite began, how to treat old source, what Vertical Slice 0 aimed to prove, what it actually proved, and what it did not. The central thesis is that legacy Vapor is useful archaeology but not the authority that new code must imitate. The same rewrite restructures the progress roadmap around three evidence states—**Proven**, **Proven but Requiring Migration**, and **Designed / Pending Implementation**—then lays out 23 milestones and three concurrent tracks. This explicitly prevents “proven once” from being mistaken for current API, source topology, UX, or production completeness.

An owner-authored design brief on August 30, in projectless Codex thread `01a0548a-a330-7400-a4dc-e27dcdb67670`, proposes a deliberately tiny “Hello World on Steroids” proof: a String Engine and Guess-the-Number Game with Engine/Game/Mod/ExtensionMod manifests, composition-time selection, and one ordinary Cargo-built executable. It explicitly retires the then-universal Capability Architecture outside USF, rejecting a custom Rust compiler layer, capability supergraph, compilation strata, and call tracker for that prototype; it also excludes Steam, Workshop, and USF implementation. This is evidence of a dated proposed slice, not executed work: the thread ends after the initial prompt with a usage-limit failure and no response or follow-up. Later owner direction in the current project context deliberately reopens a broader scripting possibility—an immutable Rust core with recursive Rhai-defined capability/API stages, compiled Rust additions, and runtime WASM modules. These are successive design generations, not one simultaneous contract; the later direction supersedes the August exclusion for the future scripting architecture, while the August brief remains evidence of the static-composition proof the owner wanted.

The September 4–6 source sequence shows the first content graph taking shape, including a quick correction to its ownership model. `fedee520` converts the earlier nine-name vocabulary into a serializable `ContentKind`, introduces a versioned dependency declaration and an exact-identity graph type, but the resolution module explicitly says the algorithm will come later. On September 5, `c65f1e7` adds the first local catalog, pinned-toolchain/Cargo support, workspace discovery and a CLI, then implements a recursive “highest locally matching version” resolver. That first resolver makes the root a Packagepack and immediately validates it as a runnable composition. In `cce0630`, committed later the same day, the implementation separates generic recursive Content resolution from pack-specific validation and keeps `ResolvedComposition` as a Packagepack-only projection. This is the first source-level correction against treating every dependency graph as a playable selection. The algorithm still resolves only local candidates, chooses each edge independently without global version unification, and has only the fixed role rules then modeled; it is an architecture-proving slice, not the later ecosystem resolver.

The validation entrypoint also changes ownership across that history. In `cce0630`, both kind-specific and Packagepack resolution call the Core wrapper `validate_resolved_content_graph`, whose narrow implementation checks direct Game/mod target relationships; pack rules are a second call. The October 18 `f9e8b13` extraction moves the graph contract into provider-neutral `vapor_content`, expands relationship validation, and makes `validate_content_graph` the path used by kind-specific resolution, Packagepack projection, and the new shared install planner. It leaves `vapor_core::validate_resolved_content_graph` publicly re-exported, but the October 26 source snapshot has no callsite for that wrapper. This is a concrete extraction residue, not evidence that graph validation as a whole is unused: the underlying validator has active call paths. The change relocates and broadens the semantic check while retaining a stale-looking facade; the diff does not explain whether that wrapper was intentionally kept for external callers.

On September 6, `26a3785` adds `Library` as the tenth kind. That name remains in the code until the October 18 domain extraction renames the kind to `Crate`, preserving the owner’s distinction between ordinary Rust content and Vapor’s user-facing local Library. This is a historical vocabulary detour, not a present-day eleventh kind. The distinction later matters because the player-facing Library means acquired/available local content, while `Crate` is one manifest/content kind.

On September 9, the [former bundled glossary/model documents are reorganized](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/5b7ef29a317926b511d4b5954405574bd0b29e6b) into focused owners under `Architecture/`, `Development/`, `Experience/`, `Migration/` and `Reference/`. The new Premium Docs README states the rule “Every concept has one normative owner”; the Vapor Glossary becomes quick lookup that points to focused owners rather than a second architecture corpus. The USF glossary remains separate, focused on USF vocabulary. This is more than a file move: it replaces most of the broad flat model-document set with an ownership-and-navigation policy. The README also describes a `Process/` category, but the inspected tree has no such directory: Bootstrap and Progress/Roadmap remain at the Premium Docs root. So the document describes an ownership category the physical navigation has not fully realized. The rule itself is intended documentation policy, not proof that every page or website route follows it. The September 12 [roadmap status update](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/b99b83863d5d0bacf2f91f61fddf58516165f49b) marks the two GitHub repo names as “provider renamed” while leaving semantic identity and checkout path pending. That distinction explicitly avoids treating a repository rename as a complete migration.

Together these records explain an important part of how Vapor formed: implementation was deliberately reset from legacy authority, a small end-to-end composition slice was used to test whether the new semantics could affect a real Rust build, and the docs were then reorganized to keep architecture, implementation progress, experience, migration and lookup from collapsing into one undifferentiated “spec.” The roadmap and glossaries are documentary evidence of intent and status classification; actual code and artifact builds remain the evidence for implementation claims.

### September: names and containers are corrected

The migration corpus explicitly records `Vapor-Root → Vapor-Client` and `Vapor-Server-Root → Vapor-Platform-Server`. The recorded `gh` lifecycle script changed the GitHub repository names; the [Sept 12 reference update](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/b99b838) and [Sept 14 repo-rename checkpoint](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/4c061ca) reconcile source references and migration state. At roughly the same time, product vocabulary is clarified: `Vapor-Shell` becomes `Vapor-CLI`; `Vapor-Launcher` becomes `Vapor-Studio`; `Vapor-Entrypoint` becomes `Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint`. `Vapor-SDK` is archived after the owner chooses to dissolve its standalone boundary. The migration plan calls for useful implementation to be consolidated into shared Vapor/Client, but the archive itself does not prove that every SDK feature was carried forward. These are repository/provider lifecycle events and product-meaning changes, not merely cosmetic strings.

The renames expose a design correction: **an executable, a user-facing mode, a semantic service, and a Git repository are different kinds of boundary**. The early layout often treated a product label as a repo; the target model treats Client/Core and Platform Server as stable source containers, with frontends and independent services nested underneath where useful.

### October: frontend repos consolidate; service repos remain

On October 14, `Vapor-GUI` is created as a host/shared graphical layer. The [Studio-boundary design](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/dda18dd) and Client’s [frontend consolidation](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/41c62e6) move the prior Entrypoint/Launcher/SDK/Shell submodule arrangement toward the current `Vapor-GUI`, `Vapor-Studio`, `Vapor-CLI`, `Vapor-Installer` and `Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint` set. The Studio-specific design and consolidation commits distinguish the GUI host from Studio’s product UI rather than treating “GUI” as the whole product.

That same day, [`Vapor-CLI/0b64cc4a`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/0b64cc4afffc6c77f9eb78f4388e586b9382060a) embeds an SDK authoring CLI under the existing `vapor sdk` command and keeps the terminal executable named `vapor`. It introduces typed nested command families for every content kind, workspace, toolchain, Steam and root publishing, but the dispatcher executes only selected families; the remaining parsed commands fall through to a generic stub. So this is a command-vocabulary consolidation and early facade integration, not evidence that all advertised operations were ready or that the CLI already consumed the later shared local Client service. The exact dispatch map is recorded in the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#cross-repository-hunk-supplement--sdk-authoring-enters-vapor-cli-0b64cc4a-october-14-2026).

The initial GUI host still puts Installer UI inline and models Play as a boolean variant of Studio. Within a week, Installer UI moves into its own product crate, Launcher receives its own binary/UI and consumes shared composition actions, and a small chooser dispatches to Launcher, Studio, IDE, Installer or Shell through the Steam entrypoint. IDE begins as service-backed file editing; by October 23, selected patches add bounded semantic objects for Rust/Rhai/TOML/XML, structured diagnostics, canonical Rust authoring operations, and version-aware LSP request state. This is a real move from “IDE as a mode” toward a semantic workbench. It is not evidence that rust-analyzer is bundled/launched correctly or that all Rust organization conventions are enforced.

The Steam entrypoint likewise changes role. Its July implementation is a mode-agnostic terminal wrapper that forwards arguments to a launch script; successive Windows patches revise command payload quoting and switch to a relative script path. October briefly routes directly to Studio/GUI, then the October 21 entrypoint makes the no-argument path launch the default composition and reserves `chooser` for selecting Launcher, Studio, IDE, Installer or Shell. The owner later confirmed those two Steam options are the intended configuration for both Linux GNU and Windows GNU-LLVM. This establishes source-level intent and configured launch shape, not runtime success for every mode.

The current Client container pins shared Vapor, GUI host, Studio, CLI, Examples, Installer and Steam Entrypoint. The Platform container pins the service implementations and owns deployment orchestration. Loo-Cast remains its own content/source workspace and is not a Client app-source submodule. This is closer to semantic ownership, but the number of repositories still carries prior generations and needs to be read with its lifecycle history attached.

October also corrects the service boundary in two stages. Studio first gains its own typed stdio child service, fixture simulator and process scenarios; workspace discovery, profile state, file operations, Workshop metadata and authoring are moved behind its protocol over successive commits. Within roughly a day, that service/client/protocol code is deleted from the Studio repo and Studio is switched to the shared Vapor Client service. Its old service design is explicitly marked historical and superseded. This is a meaningful migration rather than simple code deduplication: it changes process ownership and routes major Studio and ordinary CLI-shell capabilities through shared service contracts. The SDK subcommand remains a direct in-process exception, recorded below. The source history shows the old boundary was consciously abandoned, but does not alone prove lifecycle works on both operating systems.

On October 19, `d7e21dc3` makes the shared Client service a real owner of work, not merely a common snapshot endpoint. The 74-file change removes CLI dispatch from `vapor_core`, expands the Client application API, routes authoring/catalog/composition/Library/publishing/Workshop/workspace operations through a typed service session, and makes Devtools a protocol-consuming GUI library. It also moves build/release and profiling operations behind the same application boundary and packages Steamworks runtime libraries alongside the service binary. The diff introduces process-handshake improvements and fixture process coverage, while retaining a single active-operation slot that rejects many overlapping requests. This is a substantial implementation of the user’s “one service, many facades” model, but it does not yet equal a queued job system or prove startup, shutdown, publishing, and profiling on all target systems.

The same migration creates the present provider-side content authoring model in a concentrated diff: `content/authoring.rs` adds 2,516 lines and `content/model.rs` 632. The source keeps a typed `ContentArtifact` with kind, dependencies/conflicts, Workshop policy and runtime declarations; Studio-facing graph, Workshop and runtime-output editors are separate projections over the exact manifest text. Save paths compare that whole-file snapshot, validate the requested change, edit through `toml_edit`, serialize writes with a per-manifest lock, and restore a backup if the edited artifact fails to reopen. This means structured manifest editing predates the later Rust/Rhai/XML semantic IDE workbench: the provider owns domain edits, while the IDE workbench addresses source navigation and editor-level semantics. It also means graph/Workshop/runtime edits share a whole-manifest stale-write boundary rather than merging independently. These details are source-derived from the current provider and the original `d7e21dc3` insertion; they do not show how the product UI presented those panels in the 2026 user’s run. See the [source-manifest editor cross-check](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--source-manifest-editors-are-typed-views-over-one-optimistic-snapshot).

The shared service source at this revision also defines an explicit lifecycle: it returns after all clients disconnect, no background operation remains, and a 20-second idle window expires. A brief `vapor-client-service` process after closing a frontend is therefore expected by this code; whether every frontend closes cleanly and the process exits on Windows/Linux is a runtime question. The next two commits make managed process output part of the same boundary. [`aac30bd7`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/aac30bd7e581c49fa4ba2308b73ffcc7393ec7a9) adds protocol-versioned stdout/stderr events for workspace Cargo actions. [`cbb72d35`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/cbb72d359cef7bdc6a491c637f0841385d82a363) factors bounded child-output forwarding into a shared helper and applies it to release builds: output is read concurrently from both pipes, emitted line by line, with an 8 KiB line cap and a 128-event queue. This provides a transport path for logs; it is not itself the styled, retained, filterable console later requested for the frontends.

The current provider clarifies the workload behind that transport. Application-release staging runs fmt/check/test/Clippy/docs/release-build across each binary-bearing Cargo project and target before promoting the declared binaries/libraries. Because progress advances per completed Cargo command, a long compile can produce logs while its step counter stays still; target-independent formatting is also repeated in the target loop. The files are swapped individually, so the batch is not one rollback-capable transaction. This is a current-source refinement of the October 19 service/output history, not evidence that any specific user run took a particular time or left partial outputs. See the [current release-pipeline analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--cargo-tool-identity-is-shared-build-outputs-are-not).

On October 21, [`92ab2b9b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/92ab2b9b075a3d52976b9ce5e2ec99ea4d0278a2) shortens the service's idle grace from 20 to 15 seconds while adding the service-owned Rust Analyzer path. The current Oct 23 local source still uses 15 seconds and exits only when clients and active operations are both absent. A short post-close process lifetime is therefore expected by design; longer persistence is not explained by the grace period alone and would need process/client/runtime evidence.

The shared-service boundary still has a concrete exception in the latest inspected `Vapor-CLI` default branch (Oct. 23): ordinary shell operations use `vapor_client`/protocol, but `vapor sdk` remains a separate crate that depends on `vapor_sdk_core` and calls its functions directly. The SDK dispatcher routes unmatched typed command variants to a generic stub. Thus the integration is real but incomplete: one CLI binary still contains a service-backed shell surface and an in-process SDK surface with different operation ownership. The live source evidence and affected commands are recorded in the [evidence atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#3-shared-service-operations-logs-and-cross-frontend-behavior) and [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#cross-repository-hunk-supplement--sdk-authoring-enters-vapor-cli-0b64cc4a-october-14-2026).

That same commit provides a particularly strong test of whether the content design is implemented end to end. The basic workspace template makes all four Pack kinds metadata-only, but creates no Packagepack Cargo project or executable; the launch provider nevertheless resolves and runs a binary from the Packagepack root. The generic single-content scaffold makes Engine binary-only. A separate basic-workspace helper writes both `src/lib.rs` and `src/main.rs` for Engine, so Cargo auto-discovers a library and binary, while `Engine.vapor.toml` declares only its binary. Game is `rlib`/`cdylib`, and Crate is `rlib`/`staticlib`. The package provider only stages declared outputs already present in Cargo output directories; a separate workspace runner builds projects with per-project target directories while invoking Cargo `--workspace` for each selected member. Thus the generator, build selector, packager and launch provider do not yet form a dependency-aware Packagepack composition pipeline in this revision. October 21’s hand-authored wheel Packagepack binary supplies one concrete composition example, but does not prove the general generator was repaired. Conversely, the authoring implementation includes real safeguards—workspace locking, symlink/path checks, manifest revalidation, rollback, and symlink-refusing forks—which are useful pieces of machinery rather than disposable ad-hoc scaffolding. More detailed contract analysis is in the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

## Why the organization reached 21 repositories

A snapshot of the public `GHF-Studios` organization on 2026-10-24 returned 21 repository objects. Twenty belong to the Loo-Cast/Vapor/Spacetime project lineage; `clubrust` is separate and excluded from this lineage. The 20 related repositories do **not** mean there were 20 simultaneously active, equally important products:

- some are enduring content/source roots;
- some are parent/container repositories that pin submodules;
- some isolate a server process or operational owner;
- some are historical product names preserved by GitHub rename;
- some are archived or near-empty experiments;
- some existed because the product boundary had not yet settled.

The proliferation happened through **three overlapping mechanisms**:

1. **Product-first splitting:** Launcher, SDK, Shell, Installer and Entrypoint each briefly appeared as repo boundaries. This made local ownership easy to see, but duplicated integration/configuration overhead and overstated how independent their semantics were.
2. **Containerization by submodules:** `Vapor-Root`/`Vapor-Client` and `Vapor-Server-Root`/`Vapor-Platform-Server` became parent repos that pin child source repos. This makes app/deployment composition explicit, but adds revision synchronization and risks confusing checkout topology with semantic ownership.
3. **Service/content separation:** Workshop content, the shared client, and independently deployed server services were separated as distinct source roots. This is often justified by different lifecycle/security/build needs, but only when the underlying contracts remain shared and the boundary is genuinely owned.

The sequence is therefore not “every repo was deliberately designed as part of the final topology.” It is “fast experiments made responsibilities visible; later work is trying to keep the useful boundaries and collapse the accidental ones.” The October architecture corpus says the same in normative terms: one semantic owner per concept, product/executable/repository counts are not equivalent, and Core semantics should be consumed by frontends.

**Counting note:** the table contains 21 organization repositories because it includes the unrelated `clubrust`; the project lineage itself accounts for 20 repository objects. GitHub rename preserves repository identity and history, so the earlier names (`Vapor-Root`, `Vapor-Server-Root`, `Vapor-Launcher`, `Vapor-Shell`, `Vapor-Entrypoint`) do not necessarily appear as separate current repository objects. Archived `Vapor-SDK` still counts as a repository object. An empty or superseded repo also counts in this historical inventory, but not as an active implementation boundary.

## The repository graph at the current evidence cutoff

```text
~/Vapor  (local Superworkspace; not itself one of the 21 GitHub repositories)
├── Loo-Cast                         first-party content/source workspace
│   ├── spacetime-engine             Engine content role
│   ├── loo-cast-game                Game content role
│   └── loo-cast-packagepack         playable Packagepack role
├── Vapor-Client                     app/depot source container (historically Vapor-Root)
│   ├── Vapor                        shared semantic/service workspace
│   ├── Vapor-GUI                    graphical host and shared UI layer
│   ├── Vapor-Studio                 creator-facing product UI
│   ├── Vapor-CLI                    command-line frontend
│   ├── Vapor-Installer              setup/recovery frontend
│   ├── Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint       Steam launch bootstrap
│   └── Vapor-Examples               example/test content
└── Vapor-Platform-Server            deployment/orchestration container
    ├── Homepage / Docs / Identity / Diagnostics / Registry services
    └── deploy, health, backup and recovery tooling
```

This graph is not the whole runtime dependency graph. Loo-Cast is not a Client submodule; its content is independently identified/acquired and delivered through Vapor’s content/Workshop path. Conversely, Client submodules are source-build inputs and repository revision pins, not player-installed mods. The distinction is one of the core semantic lessons of the reorganization.

## What the repo expansion accomplished—and what it cost

### Boundaries that have a defensible operational rationale

- **Client versus Platform Server:** different machines, privileges, deployment lifecycles and secrets.
- **Server service boundaries:** Homepage, Docs, Identity, Diagnostics and Registry own different data and trust responsibilities; the parent server repo composes deployment, reverse proxy and recovery.
- **Shared Vapor core versus frontends:** CLI, GUI, Installer and Steam bootstrap are distinct user/process surfaces, but should consume common semantics and service contracts.
- **Content versus app source:** a Workshop-delivered Game/Engine/Packagepack should not become a hidden part of the launcher depot simply because it is first-party or default content.

### Boundaries whose history warns against taking names literally

- **Launcher → Studio:** product intent changed; its Git root did not start as a creator IDE.
- **Shell → CLI:** an implementation vocabulary was renamed as the canonical command frontend clarified.
- **SDK:** a standalone repository was tried, then archived/consolidated; “SDK” was too broad/ambiguous to serve as the permanent boundary.
- **Entrypoint:** its purpose narrowed to Steam-specific launch/bootstrap behavior, hence the explicit rename.
- **Spacetime-Engine and Loo-Cast-Game repos:** the identities were explored separately, but the current Loo-Cast source is a unified workspace with engine/game/packagepack role manifests.
- **Vapor-GUI:** this is a host/shared-GUI layer introduced after it became clear Launcher/Studio/IDE/Installer are products or modes, not one generic “GUI” responsibility.

### The structural tension left visible

The architecture wants one coherent semantic core, but its implementation was born as several fast-moving repositories. Parent repositories pin child repositories; the same vocabulary appears across source identity, project roles, Steam depots and content manifests; “first-party” does not mean “same lifecycle.” This creates real costs: synchronized revisions, partial checkouts, version/config duplication, and a risk that one frontend or service silently owns policy that belongs in shared Vapor semantics.

The history therefore supports neither “all repos are wrong” nor “the current graph is final.” It supports a more useful conclusion: repository boundaries should now be judged against semantic ownership and independent lifecycle, while historical renames and thin repositories are retained as evidence of how the boundary was discovered. The companion evidence atlas audits whether the current code has actually achieved those ownership boundaries; this timeline explains why those questions accumulated.

## Loo-Cast chronology

The numbered Loo-Cast periods below retain the previous historical synthesis. The much longer commit register that follows is a complete reachable-commit index for the two audited Loo-Cast Git histories, not a claim that every individual diff has been semantically narrated.

### 1. Unity foundations and gameplay systems — June 2022 to January 2023

The first reachable commit is `29109ac` on 2022-06-07 and contains only `.gitignore`, `LICENSE`, and a one-line `README`. Less than three hours later, `922b9c8` (“Initial commit”) introduces 793 blobs and 238,704 added lines. The earlier figure of 300 paths came from GitHub’s capped changed-files response, not the complete commit tree. The full tree contains 170 C# scripts, three enabled build scenes, a template scene, 13 prefabs, and the Unity assets/settings around them. The code spans Player and movement, enemies and bosses, health, stations, generators/spawners, targeting, weapons/projectiles, experience/currency, attributes/stats, UI, and shared managers/utilities. This is a broad game snapshot; source-level presence does not prove a successful Unity build or playable runtime. June 13’s `9d78bbf` (“Actual initial commit”) modifies nine scene, volume-profile and editor-state files; its subject is not a reliable description of the repository’s first code import. June 7 remains the earliest verifiable Git start, not evidence against the owner’s recollected 2021 beginning. See the [diff-level origin correction](loo-cast-vapor-origin-and-intent.md#june-2022-repository-shell-then-a-complete-looking-unity-game-snapshot).

The June–August diff sequence shows an already developed Unity game moving toward data-driven authoring: ScriptableObject variables/events, typed weapon/station/attribute assets, custom editor drawers, runtime sets and interfaces. The change is not simply “add ScriptableObjects”; it migrates existing runtime parameters into a large serialized asset graph and introduces defects/complexity along the way. One concrete example appears by June 20: EnemyStation data gains experience-drop settings and a matching initializer, but the station’s actual generic initialization path still calls only the inherited health initializer. The June 21 rewrite moves these values into a typed data asset, yet generic overload resolution still calls the non-virtual StationHealth initializer, so the specialized drop initializer remains unreachable. That same health rewrite mutates base fields directly while PlayerHealth’s UI update overrides remain unused, and initialization replaces the serialized kill event. Persistence was tried; an August commit notes the first Steam build. Asteroids, inventory/item upgrades, stations, missions, targeting and AI continue evolving in parallel.

A complete source pass verifies the startup route in this snapshot: `ApplicationManager.Start()` initializes the attribute/stat registries and initialization scene manager, then requests `MainMenu`; `GameSceneManager.Start()` initializes the Player, background, UI, generators and related scene systems before resuming. `ExtendedMonoBehaviour` is defined in the tree and owns pause-aware update/fixed-update hooks. This disproves the earlier “no initializer call” and “missing base class” findings, which resulted from the 300-entry API cap. It remains source review, not a historical Unity build/run. See the [source-level registry audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#hunk-level-semantic-supplement-922b9c84-imported-c-snapshot).

The complete serialized reference cross-check covers 4 scenes and 13 prefabs: 194 script-component references and 73 unique GUIDs, of which 57 resolve to project C# metadata. Game resolves 30/45 unique script GUIDs, Initialization 4/9; the remainder are not automatically missing scripts because Unity package and built-in components also appear in these assets. The full manifest contains UGUI, TextMeshPro, URP, VFX Graph and other Unity packages. These counts establish broad source/scene linkage, not a clean Unity editor validation.

November 2022 contains two distinct WIP arcs. On Nov 8–11, computed weapon stats, inventory removal and dynamic item upgrades are rapidly introduced, repaired in part, then several upgrade/inventory commits are explicitly reverted; the branch merge retains some intervening item changes, so “reverted” applies to those patches, not every item-system addition. On Nov 15–25, a Game/save-slot idea expands into a large identity and persistence experiment, then pivots into hierarchical Universe chunks. A `Game` JSON record, generated Universe, chunk identity and parent-child coordinate wrappers appear, but source review finds a mismatched Game save/load path, no completed loaded-chunk restore, and a `UniverseObserver` whose final November state does one synchronous startup neighborhood pass while `Update` is empty. Several parent-coordinate formulas are revised repeatedly; no reviewed runtime evidence establishes correct negative-coordinate or hierarchy-boundary behavior. The earlier hand-spawned UniverseGenerator harness is deleted before this replacement is proven. The detailed patch sequence and precise code findings are in the [November hunk-level review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#november-1525-2022--save-slot-scaffolding-turns-into-a-synchronous-chunk-world-prototype).

December 2022 does not settle on one generation owner. The `955e9f2f` worker-thread patch adds a main-thread completion queue, but its consumer does not take the producer lock. The large `3274e40c` rewrite changes observer neighborhood loading back to a synchronous `Update` call while **retaining** coroutine queue pumps for density generation and adding GPU compute shaders; it is a mixed pipeline, not a wholesale return to synchronous generation. That same patch has source-visible GPU contract defects: the Universe kernel dispatch count exceeds its `Size × Size` buffer by a factor of 16 per axis, the selected cellular-noise function is a constant-zero stub, and the Region settings stride is one float short. Runtime impact was not tested. Finally, [`fd6be1b6`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/fd6be1b64fedf3a612d8a265627ff039d5f6d74b) explicitly removes 673 lines of persistent assets and says only Default Data remains. Save slots and persistent user data were experiments, not a delivered feature in this branch. The detailed review traces these ownership reversals, GPU contracts and explicit deletion in the [December hunk-level review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#december-hunk-review-worker-completion-mixed-sync-and-gpu-rewrite-persistence-deletion).

January 2023 begins a modding framework and identity system; that is a new architecture attempt after the save/chunk prototype’s persistence retreat, not a continuation of a stable saved-world runtime. It also adds a Unity editor action that recursively deletes project data under `Application.dataPath/Data` without a confirmation dialog. In the chunk loader, a per-frame invalidation pass has inverted predicates for SectorChunk and FilamentChunk requests and removes from the `List<T>` it is currently enumerating; the later rewrite disables that pass but its queue processors snapshot pending requests, so removing an item from the live queue cannot cancel work already copied into a coroutine. The follow-up also leaves density completion queues with both an `Update` pump and coroutine consumers, while their names resemble the separate map-element request processors. These source findings expose a recurring gap between naming lifecycle operations and specifying their ownership/timing. See the [January review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#january-2023-an-explicit-modding-framework-appears-beside-dynamic-data-and-identity-machinery) and its [load-cancellation follow-up](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#january-follow-up-hunk-review-data-reset-scope-and-invalidated-load-requests).

The January work shows two pressures beginning to converge: dynamic game data needs a persistence/host boundary, and mods need identity, lifecycle and loading contracts. The first Mod/Module loader is still embedded in Unity and its sample `.LCMOD`/`.LCMODULE` descriptors do not match the paths and JSON deserialization used by the loader; lifecycle methods exist without the startup path that populates their collections. The first IdentifierManager similarly has constructor/registration/query mismatches visible in source.
