These failures are important because they expose the actual missing machinery behind “modding,” but they are not evidence of a usable mod ecosystem. February then responds by moving the project toward a Base Mod/engine boundary and replacing large parts of the prototype, rather than stabilizing this January implementation.

### 2. Engine extraction and replacement of the original game code — February to December 2023

On 2023-02-03, [`2176ae0`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/2176ae0af4cd8b2e8cc21ac6d1139499cab569ce) moves the codebase into “Base Mod,” explicitly describing the work as reconnecting pieces while constructing the new foundation. On 2023-04-12, [`941b201`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/941b2010c1d11ec1620bfb7ade12c14c3a6fd3b5) deliberately wipes legacy game code and assets “to provide a starting point for the engine without the legacy code interfering.” This is a real architectural break: the older Unity gameplay implementation becomes historical material rather than the base of the engine rewrite.

The February move does not immediately yield a clean mod boundary. The first loader discovers directories but feeds `.cs` source paths to assembly-loading APIs, while its reflected type names disagree with the classes actually added; the next CoreManager/manager pass adds thousands of lines of bespoke lifecycle and registry machinery before the engine/game split is stable. CoreManager holds a fixed list of feature managers and still marks dependency ordering as TODO; many of the introduced managers are empty lifecycle shells. The Feb 13 revision has a direct source-level C# mismatch: `CoreManager` overrides hooks that `Manager` does not mark virtual, while the `ModuleManager` inheritance chain has no constructor to forward its parameterized base constructor. The next manager commit replaces this arrangement with constructor-injected arrays, but still hard-codes dependencies and ordering. By Feb 14, MainManager refers to a removed `games` field and repeatedly iterates an unassigned `CoreModuleManagers` array; it also removes public game-selection operations while retaining a scene-based startup fragment. The shared manager phase API duplicates many flags/action lists and its “completely initialized/terminated” predicates omit the late post-phase. The type/instance/namespace graph is declared broadly, but constructors do not populate the parent-owned child lists and the central “register all” block remains a placeholder. In parallel, a February BigFloat/BigVector3 sketch makes large-coordinate intent explicit; the next arithmetic pass adds a broad API but still has an empty root operation, recursive floating construction/logarithm paths, wrong exponent alignment and a zero-normalization loop. Thus the month reveals both the ambition—mods as independently identifiable, lifecycle-managed modules—and the recurring gap between naming a general facility and wiring its complete data/control path. The patch-level evidence is in the [February review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#february-2023-base-mod-makes-the-engine-boundary-explicit-then-builds-a-custom-runtime-framework) and the [February hunk supplement](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#february-follow-up-hunk-review-a-fixed-manager-graph-and-the-first-large-number-sketch).

March multiplies the vocabulary—Object, Instance, Type, Identifier, Data, MetaData, Resource, File, Folder, registries—then deletes thousands of lines and reintroduces narrower variants. The month does briefly sketch a useful distinction between logical data and stored resources, but the first interfaces put recursive serialization on both sides; a concrete `Data` base then leaves serialization as `throw null`, and a later `Load`/`Save`/`Deserialize` split has no demonstrated converter. Namespace organization also expands without removing the manually enumerated root registration catalogue; 130 Unity `.meta` files change in the same relocation, a serialized-reference risk whose actual fallout cannot be established from that diff alone. The durable question is still who owns identity, persistence and runtime objects; the March interface matrix does not become a stable contract. April makes the break explicit: a custom Engine Integration Mockup briefly separates metadata, persisted state and logic, then on the next day reshapes Enemy into an entity composed from health/movement components and submodules; even the sketches contain mismatched semantic annotations and type names. Then [`941b2010`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/941b2010c1d11ec1620bfb7ade12c14c3a6fd3b5) removes the old Unity code/assets (270,716 deleted lines in the indexed summary) to start the engine without the game. In the short post-reset implementation, the first wrapper-based Component constructor dereferences its not-yet-assigned containing GameObject and reflects an `AddComponent` signature incompatible with its invocation; the rewrite back to a MonoBehaviour factory avoids that wrapper but does not define how its custom construct callbacks order against Unity callbacks. This is a clean-start trade: freedom to redesign the engine is purchased by discarding the active game implementation, and the mockup’s semantic split is not yet a working mod/compiler pipeline. The [March](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#march-2023-the-custom-instancetypedata-model-is-formalized-and-repeatedly-rewritten) and [April](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#april-2023-the-project-deliberately-clears-the-game-then-rebuilds-a-custom-engine-model) reviews retain the commit-level details and exact source limitations.

May–June 2023 shifts the framework’s center from generic data and metadata toward a universal hierarchy. On May 18, `IRegistry` itself records a proposed simplification: remove its specialized metadata/data classes; the next day deletes those contracts, while the replacement hierarchy remains incomplete. Data nodes gain mutable parent/child relationships; hierarchy then absorbs files, folders, registries and engine objects. The abstraction expands faster than its behavior: path methods are added as empty bodies or explicit `NotImplementedException`s, and a large hierarchy/path layer is deleted before concrete lifecycle-managed File/Folder objects reappear. The June 8 path snapshot makes the gap concrete: newly added methods have empty non-void bodies and duplicate existing typed `Equals` signatures. The parsers index empty inputs before validation; the FilePath guard does not protect the later two-segment indexing for a name without an extension; root folders become relative empty values, absolute folders retain a leading empty segment and serialize with an extra slash, and ObjectPath inverts its slash test. These source defects imply the path layer was not build-ready at that revision; no historical build was run here. This is not a stable authoring filesystem; it is an attempt to make identity, containment and runtime organization share one model.

July runs three related but distinct prototypes in parallel. A recursive hierarchy inspector visualizes the bespoke File/Folder/Object graph. A custom Entity–Logic–Data model separates identity, state and behavior, briefly bridges entities into Unity `GameObject`s, then is replaced by a home-grown Entity/Component system with its own managers and many setup/initialization/termination phases. Serialization is attached directly to entities, components and managers, making persistence part of object construction and lifecycle; the serializer, path model and hierarchy are repeatedly removed and reintroduced. A third track begins the nested Universe/Scale/Chunk model, abandoning BigDecimal for BigInteger coordinates while converting distance back to `float` for observation. These are meaningful expressions of the recurring aim—explicit structure, reusable runtime machinery and worlds beyond ordinary coordinate ranges—but no single July framework reaches a settled contract. The author’s temporary ~6,000-line deletion to isolate a fatal bug is restored, so it is diagnostic bisection, not a lasting architecture rollback. Patch-level findings and limits are in the [May](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#may-2023-datametadata-and-hierarchies-become-the-frameworks-central-model), [June](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#june-2023-hierarchy-paths-and-filesfolders-become-runtime-framework-objects), and [July](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#july-2023-hierarchy-ui-custom-ecs-universe-prototype-and-repeated-framework-resets) reviews.

The August transition is a sharper break. On August 21, the `Modding_Framework_Test` branch is merged at 19:26:22 UTC, bringing in a substantial Unity mod-framework experiment: an XML `.LCMOD` manifest with nested modules, data categories, and asset/file registries. The sampled loader path is not operationally coherent, however: the manifest is parsed as JSON, dictionaries are used before initialization, and the entrypoint tries to load a C# source-file path as an assembly. At 19:40:04 UTC—13 minutes 42 seconds later—“THE GREAT RESET” replaces the Unity root with a Rust/Cargo/Bevy project. Complete tree comparison shows 1,748 paths removed and 56 added; only five paths are shared, and none is Unity runtime content. The Rust project is a separate small arcade-game prototype, not a port of the Unity ECS or the mod framework. Before the reset, serialization receives another broad custom-framework push, while the command system is removed for Lua. The Lua experiment exposes host C# methods to scripts through reflection and keeps `LoadCLRPackage()` enabled; the console also imports `UnityEditor` from a runtime-path script, and its descriptors do not yet provide working invocation bodies. This is an incomplete, short-lived implementation, not the current Rhai runtime’s direct code lineage. The [August review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#august-2023-serialization-churn-console-and-lua-experiments-then-a-new-rust-game) distinguishes those experiments from the Rust reset.

The rest of August 2023 narrows the game prototype again. The August 21 “General cleanup” removes the enemy/star/score/game-over loop that existed in the first Rust snapshot, leaving a much smaller player-movement shell while renaming the menu to “Loo Cast”; it is not only file organization. The following background pass adds a 3×3 screen-tile background and camera follow, but its exit cleanup asks for a single background entity even though it spawned nine, so none are removed on game exit. The next day’s Rust `Universe` begins as component/resource sketches and a serialized string printed to stdout, then one commit later switches startup to loading a fixed `data/saves/universe.json` file and panicking if it is absent or invalid. This is a distinct prototype from the later save-slot metadata: on August 25, [`142e9cf5`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/142e9cf5b267dd38116811bd32c48edf0a451c10) scans `data/saves` for `SaveGameInfo` records, but loading a named save only reports the metadata; it does not restore Universe state. [`ddbab001`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/ddbab001cfab69178f1e279fb5604cd018ebe070) then places each record at `data/saves/<name>/info.json` and deletes the whole named directory, still without adding world payload or path validation in these handlers. About an hour after that directory change, [`7b388def`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/7b388def42b1469b749d433b95e82b511ae31968) removes the Universe creation, file save/load and print systems, and removes Serde derives from the Universe resource. It adds a `LooCastBasePlugins` grouping and an empty `GameConfigurationPlugin`, but those are organizational scaffolds at this snapshot. Over the following two days, [`40850c07`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/40850c07e83fc37c2c7846e3bce17fe2a6f97d27) models save→config→state→Universe as event confirmations that mostly create empty directories/markers and insert empty managers; [`7d98cf2a`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/7d98cf2a31ad41590f871343bb351306b37d8806) folds those stages into synchronous game loading, while its declared `LoadState` is not advanced. Neither revision restores save/config/state/world payload. By the end of the month, a player-attached observer tracks 25 neighboring chunk coordinates and creates/removes empty ECS markers; loading recursively generated data remains a TODO. Its coordinate debug helper also combines floor-based chunk coordinates with signed remainder, so negative positions report inconsistent local coordinates. A later pass extracts serializable `LocalChunkPosition`, `GlobalChunkPosition` and `GlobalEntityPosition` shapes, but the observer stores only local coordinates and a load event merely inserts a zeroed manager. `GlobalChunkPosition` has one optional parent-local position rather than a recursively represented ancestry path, and player speed changes back from 50 to 500; neither change makes saved world loading operational. The scale/chunk names recur from Unity, but the implementation is new and still has no functioning streaming/world ownership system at this point. See the [August hunk review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#hunk-level-semantic-supplement-august--reflection-serializer-command-ingress-lua-and-the-reset), [save-metadata supplement](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#hunk-level-semantic-supplement-142e9cf5-and-ddbab001--save-metadata-is-rediscovered-but-the-world-is-still-not-restored), [Universe rollback review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#hunk-level-semantic-supplement-7b388def--the-prototype-removes-universe-persistence-before-replacing-it), and [load-pipeline review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#hunk-level-semantic-supplement-40850c07-and-7d98cf2a--staged-loading-is-marker-creation-then-a-synchronous-foldback) for implementation details and limits.

September–December 2023 are cleanup and structural work: chunking, coordinate wrapping, a Universe module, and GlobalUniverse lifecycle APIs. September also contains the earliest direct written USF seed found so far: a 74-line prompt backup linking Phenomena, scale-specific ECS models, event durations, DPM/ZLM detail selection, transitions and chunk observation. It is a conceptual prompt, not a finalized contract. The first worker-thread experiment is not end-to-end asynchronous: the live observer still generates/loads synchronously, and a generated chunk performs over a million Perlin samples plus JSON/PNG writes on that path; output goes beneath the source-like `assets/data/saves` tree relative to process CWD. Later worker revisions can mark lifecycle states complete without calling the corresponding generation/load functions. In October, `ChunkCluster` introduces staged Registered/MetadataLoaded/DataLoaded states and reverse unload guards, but its transition methods are private and its manager has no implementation; the state model cannot yet be used outside its module. November’s local-view observer updates its “currently viewed” list even when queuing requests fails and supplies empty callbacks, so its bookkeeping can diverge from accepted operations. The ID sequence then corrects empty-input handling and root depth after an earlier parent-ID patch left inconsistent root depth and incomplete methods. December’s `f44c1f5` moves the existing Bevy game under `engine::kernel`, but the new `base_mod` and `engine::system` are empty scaffolds; it is a directory split, not yet a reusable engine/game boundary. A separate GlobalUniverse rewrite moves lookup/mutable-borrow responsibility to callers, makes root operations explicit and changes completion callbacks to one-shot closures, while retaining the shared nested chunk graph and queued Bevy operations. The `7f0e7a9b` root-map conversion is not fully threaded through the following lookup implementation: the fetched `58e76c43` source still locks the now-plain root map and uses its former position key. At `58e76c43`, the dispatcher also calls one-argument callbacks with older multi-argument shapes and omits the new root-operation match arms. `spawn_chunk` changes a state flag but does not use its Bevy `Commands` argument to create a runtime entity. These are source-level signs of an incomplete, likely non-compiling API snapshot, not a reproduced historical build. See the [September chunk/USF review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#september-2023-asynchronous-chunk-generation-and-a-written-usf-concept), [October cluster/ID review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-2023-chunk-clusters-and-numeric-id-experiments) and [November and December hunk-level review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#hunk-level-semantic-supplement-december-2023--moving-the-tree-versus-changing-ownership) for source-level evidence and limits.

### 3. Rust crates, engine kernel and prototype succession — January 2024 to August 2025

January 2024 separates Engine and BaseMod into workspace crates (`9028dce`), but the first split commit contains a template-only BaseMod and source moves rather than a working game/mod API. Its root workspace spells the member `loo_cast_base_mod`, while the committed directory is `loo_Cast_base_mod`; this case mismatch makes the declared path fail on case-sensitive filesystems. It also leaves a nested Engine lockfile beside the workspace-root lockfile. The immediate follow-up (`0721ede3`, January 16) adds a BaseMod→Engine dependency but comments out the player’s chunk/entity interaction and the local observer’s chunk lifecycle submissions, replacing them with TODOs. The observer still mutates its viewed-position list as if those requests ran, making its local view disagree with chunk registration. The split therefore formalizes the desired boundary while temporarily removing live paths to get past compile errors; it does not yet deliver a usable composition. The accompanying PowerShell workflow quickly becomes self-inconsistent. `55fd70f8` changes into `spacetime_engine` and then tries to enter the sibling BaseMod path relative to that directory; it later pops only once and enters the engine path again. `9734a7f5` replaces this with a destructive clean-and-stage flow for release output. `a8f18fcd` renames the path variables but leaves the rest of the script using the old undefined names, so its defined source/target layout is not connected to cleanup, build, copy or launch. `fac1f839` later builds release output but launches from `build\debug`. These are source-level defects, not claims that a recorded execution failed. February then prototypes a second UI object/scene system beside Bevy UI and begins routing Universe mutations through command-like requests; startup stops invoking the prior mod-discovery path, and the custom UI is deleted/restored within days. By February 19 (`b43031a2`), the command boundary is still incomplete: Player startup no longer registers a local universe, while the registered detection system still calls the local-chunk processor with two old arguments after its signature changes to one `UniverseCommands` argument. The helper body also retains references to the removed local/global state and submits operations directly to `GlobalUniverse`. March turns the command idea into a Rust procedural-macro DSL. The March 21 Assets/Files scaffold is similarly early: its asset methods and `Asset` implementation are empty, while its example imports an asset macro that the derive crate does not define and file commands stop after opening a file without returning their declared result. By April the macro has a compiler-like pipeline—parse declarations, extract normalized meaning, generate Rust/Bevy types and call paths—but the extracted-info layer is explicitly judged inconsistent and removed. The proc-macro entrypoint shrinks from roughly 1,300 lines to a delegating adapter, a sound boundary improvement inside an unstable DSL. In May, a two-commit reset first removes the generated Kernel examples, then deletes the BaseMod/macro crates, their design notes, and the Engine’s previous background/camera/game/player/savegame/UI modules; `main.rs` becomes only a default Bevy app. Mk0 then introduces a different chunk-streaming sandbox. This is a product/runtime reset, not an incremental evolution of the macro workspace. This is an important historical ancestor to codegen-in-Rhai discussions: the recurring need is to let concise authored declarations shape Rust APIs, but the 2024 proc-macro implementation is neither the later recursive Rhai evaluator nor a surviving subsystem. The exact sequence and limitations are in the [February](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#february-2024-a-bespoke-ui-is-explored-universe-operations-become-named-commands), [March](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#march-2024-commands-become-a-procedural-macro-dsl-assetsfilesregistries-are-prototyped), [April](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#april-2024-the-command-macro-is-split-into-compiler-like-stages-kernel-taxonomy-expands), and [May](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#may-2024-the-kernelmacro-experiment-is-discarded-chunk-streaming-becomes-a-new-engine-prototype) reviews.

The February command attempt has an additional ownership wrinkle: after temporarily commenting out both Player and LocalUniverse's direct operations, the code re-enables those legacy request paths while introducing empty/incomplete command resources. A later pass comments out the Player's click-to-spawn body again as commands are injected. By Feb 20, the proposed `InfoHierarchy` centralizes metadata lookup but remains directly mutated by GlobalUniverse methods; it is not yet the exclusive command-owned state described in its TODO. Parent and child records hold strong `Arc` references in both directions, and root removal does not recursively detach descendants, creating a source-visible reference-cycle risk for a removed hierarchy. This is not a measured runtime leak. The February review records the exact transitions and limits.

The same January contains a second, more generalizable attempt to own runtime composition. `dbcbfc03` gives Data, Config, Event, Resource and related managers duplicated `TypeId` dependency maps, mutex-protected trait objects, and initialize/finalize states. `2c45a355` starts a worker that locks the root and all managers, then registers the root as a dependency of each child. It then initializes those children while still holding the root mutex; each child tries to lock that same root dependency, a direct non-reentrant mutex self-deadlock visible from the source. The caller has no completion barrier before the Bevy app continues, and the displayed finalization path neither joins the worker nor can acquire the mutex it retains. On January 31, `c2c20a3e` makes native mods loadable by a Rust trait-object pointer exported as `extern "C"`. Its discovery helper searches for `mod.dll`, but the loader instead constructs `<folder-name>.dll` and discards the search result. The host calls `register_mod`, which adds plugin systems to Bevy, but its local `Library` drops as the function returns; scheduled function pointers still target the unloaded module. The host also does not use the declared `id()` and `dependencies()` to order or validate modules. A separate Lua spike that day runs one hard-coded snippet on a worker thread, leaves failures unreported to app startup, and changes Engine from `rlib+dylib` to `rlib` while BaseMod remains a dependent `cdylib`; this can create duplicate Engine global state and does not declare vendored Lua. These are source-visible lifecycle, ABI and packaging hazards, not reproduced failures. The commit sequence puts lifecycle ownership, dependency direction, binary compatibility and unload semantics on the critical path much earlier than the later Vapor content model.

Exact-tree checks sharpen the early 2024 story. The January workspace member capitalization mismatch means the declared BaseMod package cannot be found on case-sensitive filesystems; a nested member lockfile also coexists with the root workspace lockfile. The follow-up adds an Engine dependency to BaseMod but comments out player chunk/entity interaction and the local observer’s full chunk lifecycle request path to get past compile errors; the replacement is explicitly deferred, not integrated. BaseMod itself remains template code. The February 7 custom UI file initially sits outside the declared Rust module graph: `system/mod.rs` does not declare it, and the registered UI plugin still wires the existing Bevy screens. On February 12, `new_ui` is added to the module graph, but its manager still has empty non-unit method bodies and is not installed into `SystemPlugins`; the result is compile-visible scaffolding, not an active second UI runtime. On February 19, Player startup drops local-universe registration; the registered detector calls the local processor with two arguments after its signature has changed to one, and the helper body still refers to the removed `local_universe` and `global_universe` names while issuing direct global operations. The intended command API has not replaced the old path or preserved its required inputs. The March 21 asset scaffold also has no complete path from declaration to output: the imported asset macro is absent from the derive crate at that tree, asset serialization methods are empty, and command closures do not return their declared values. In April, while a third `extracted_info` stage is added to the command macro pipeline, generated code still calls `.span()` on names already converted into `String`; the next extraction rewrite leaves an undefined `command_type` reference in `CommandInputInfo::extract`. The follow-up is evidence of design trouble, but also of a source-level implementation that still was not internally coherent. These findings come from commit-pinned manifests/source; no historical build was run.

A deliberate prototype sequence begins in May 2024: Mk0–Mk4 within days, followed by the long Mk5 line. The repository then carries many WIP commits, reverts and reapplications through late 2024 and into early 2025. Mk5 was not a single settled release; it was a prolonged, unstable implementation track. December 2024 records importing legacy assets into the newer prototype.

The first two revisions already show the core lifecycle problem. [Mk0](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/5c28c446a9be2ba6ec51d4aab98b1546ca3ce587) stores each chunk coordinate directly beside its live Bevy entity and has no unload path. [Mk1](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast-Legacy/commit/ce52a4803d74fcc1e3c1673b8a7c89c8c0109b83) separates loaded entities from registered coordinates and despawns chunks outside the single loader's window, but “load” and “create” both call the same placeholder-entity constructor; the registered list contains no saved chunk data. This is an early residency correction, not yet persistence. The Mk0 PowerShell script clears `build\debug`, a staging/output folder, rather than Cargo's `target` cache.

The May reset exposes a recurring ownership problem more clearly than the checkpoint names do. A world object needs an identity that can outlive its current Bevy entity realization, while that entity exists only while loaded. The prototype first tracks chunk registration and loaded entities together, then adds custom recyclable IDs, per-operation sets, registries, and separate actor identity. These additions make distinctions visible, but leave synchronization between registry-retained state and transient ECS state as a manual cross-system invariant. In the June source, `ChunkRegistry.serialized_chunks` is a Bevy resource's in-memory `HashMap<ChunkID, String>`, and `deserialize_chunk` removes its entry. The reviewed code does not establish durable save-to-disk behavior or process-restart recovery. Several `&mut World`/`SystemState` experiments are reverted or partly reapplied, and some branches discard registry errors. The patches therefore document an unresolved authority boundary, not a stable persistence or streaming guarantee.

The June conversion attempt shows why event names and request records cannot be counted as shipped lifecycle support: the new conversion handler is absent from the plugin's registered/scheduled systems. Its deferred handler also shadows the triggering chunk ID and compares a request ID with itself, while the failure branch cancels requests for other chunks and removes them from the creation map instead of the conversion map. These are exact-tree control-flow defects, not reproduced runtime failures. The source review records the details and evidence limits in the June supplement.

Within a week, that conversion branch is replaced by an “upgrade to chunk actor” path and handlers are added to the plugin. The integration commit also introduces `EntityReference` as a type alias—not a checked handle—and renames an unregister parameter in a way that makes its `HashSet::retain` predicate compare each ID to itself. Therefore any single-ID unregister clears the entire registered-ID set. This is a severe source-level registry defect in the June integration, not a runtime result from this research.

At the end of June, actor and loader registries replace request maps with sets of in-progress IDs, but actor systems still depend on the removed request payload APIs. The next patch only renames calls in an `_OLD` handler and passes a request struct to the new ID-only method. Source inspection therefore finds unresolved type-checking errors across the attempted repair; no historical build was run.

June makes the failure mode explicit: source TODOs report actor/loader upgrades silently failing and attribute them to timing races from deferred Bevy `Commands`; an internal schedule stage is proposed. The response expands toward request, internal-request, and completion events, event IDs and registries, while some advertised start/update paths remain TODOs or empty handlers. This improves the vocabulary for intent and outcome, but each subsystem still implements its own lifecycle path and correlation machinery. The more general queued-request and persistence-identity model belongs to July, so it should not be retroactively read into the June prototype. These are source and patch findings; this review did not reproduce the historical runtime failures.

See the [May review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#may-2024-the-kernelmacro-experiment-is-discarded-chunk-streaming-becomes-a-new-engine-prototype) and [June review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#june-2024-explicit-lifecycle-events-expand-while-registry-and-scheduling-gaps-remain-visible) for commit-level evidence and limits.

July begins with a naming change that should not be mistaken for the later architecture: `e3c62322` renames correlation IDs from “event” to “request,” but adds no payload records and changes no execution route. `23a2b4ea` then adds actor create/upgrade payload maps, yet leaves event-based handlers in place and introduces source-level unresolved references between removed event types, still-using handlers/plugin registration, and mismatched request type names. The following commits continue the stored-request experiment; the actor queue becomes an active readiness path by `b89e3cd8`, but with duplicated event-driven and polling spawn bodies. These are registry-owned records in an in-memory Bevy resource, not evidence of durable persistence. A generic entity request API is then scaffolded, but its create helper returns immediately after registering the entity, and the new component-hook lifecycle does not line up with the plain spawn/despawn handlers. Late July pushes an “entity first, capabilities transform it” model into chunks: chunk entities are upgraded/downgraded and serialized/saved through typed requests and component hooks. The first pass is empty stubs; the next fills request bodies but leaves the new event and hook path outside the old plugin schedule, with early-return request leaks and hooks that mutate identity before validating transitions. `serialized_chunks` remains a `HashMap<ChunkID, String>` inside the in-memory `ChunkRegistry`, so “save” here does not prove disk persistence or restart recovery. The lifecycle terms themselves quickly change from serialize/deserialize back to save/load. In parallel, chunk transition filters are repeatedly revised after the author records that they misclassify chunks; chunks, actors and entities keep parallel hand-maintained registries. The code is discovering the boundary between persistent data and loaded ECS objects, but has not converged on one lifecycle contract.

August opens a separate scripting/operation strand. One sketch explicitly assigns heavy primitive work to Rust and lets Lua sequence composite operations; a Rust `Operation` trait and typed registry are explored beside it, but the trait's execution method receives broad mutable access to both the registry and Bevy `World`. Type-erased global registries and mutex-protected values are added, then an early entity-registry consumer is removed. An async Rust caller uses one-shot channels, which makes the request/reply shape concrete but still depends on a separate queue runner. One terminology trap is now checked against the exact function bodies: `save_entity` and `save_chunk_actor` only remove live references from in-memory registries; teardown then unregisters/recycles entity IDs. They do not save entity or actor payloads. The separate chunk-scene serializer is the actual in-memory serialized-data path, and it still does not establish durable disk persistence. These are strong historical parallels to later host-capability and script-composition discussions, not a continuous Lua-to-Rhai implementation or a proven sandbox. The [July](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#july-2024-queued-lifecycle-work-moves-into-registries-chunk-allocation-and-entity-requests-are-reworked) and [August](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#august-2024-component-hooks-split-out-a-generic-operation-registry-and-lua-sketch-appear) reviews trace the exact patches and limits.

September tries to unify those operations around a process-global typed registry, generic instance IDs, and a request/execute/respond queue. Inputs and results become named types, but execution still receives `&mut World`, and the entity operations are marked `todo!()` while chunk operations remain incomplete. The queue’s callbacks can enqueue dependent work, yet ordering and world authority are not constrained by a narrow host capability. Component hooks assign identity and persist chunk/actor relationships as side effects; removing a `Chunk` marker can unregister identity, so classification and object lifetime are not cleanly separated. The September 6 `616306f2` patch goes beyond TODOs: it adds RON scene serialization/deserialization and Load/Unload bodies, but leaves Save/Unsave empty. The September 9 `b4a95769` patch fills Save/Unsave incompletely: storage remains a process-global in-memory map, success callbacks are missing, Unsave leaves the stored snapshot behind, and the save helper re-locks a mutex already held by its caller. The same code also despawns entities while holding that registry mutex, which re-enters an entity-removal hook that locks it again. These are source-level deadlock/callback findings; no historical runtime trace is claimed. The code is repeatedly moved into new module layouts, reverted, and reintroduced. At the September 30 `a0510a14` checkpoint, operation argument/result/callback traits are shared and chunk operations have moved into `chunk/operations.rs`, but `operations/mod.rs` still says chunk save/load and module integration are TODOs. The moved `LoadChunk` still deserializes before validation and omits success completion; `UnloadChunk` still holds the global registry lock over despawns and retains the inverted final-despawn callback; `SaveChunk` stores without success completion; and `UnsaveChunk` leaves the stored snapshot and has no success completion. The persistence defects therefore survive this organizational refactor in the source snapshot, although this is not a runtime reproduction. This is a stronger operation framework sketch than August’s, but evidence still describes an unfinished prototype whose generic machinery outruns its demonstrated consumers. It does not show historical build/runtime success. See the [September review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#september-2024-generic-operations-meet-lifecycle-hooks-serialization-and-async-calls).

October withdraws the global operation queue and tries a path-addressed “locking hierarchy” as the owner for types, registries, commands, operations and startup phases. It explicitly separates static from dynamic IDs, but its lock/unlock methods are empty or unfinished and path traversal still reaches `todo!()`; the accompanying large hierarchy diagram is therefore an intended topology, not enforced authority. A direct read of the October 27 locking snapshot sharpens this: the declared lock result is `LockedDataContainer`, but code paths return unit or a cloned mutex pointer; the container helper’s downcast type does not match what it stores; and the post-update system drains unlock requests into a node `unlock()` that is still a TODO. This is source-level evidence that the guard/authority mechanism is not implemented, not a claim from a historical build. November adds typed path bindings and briefly brings back blocking command dispatch and the operation queue beside hierarchy-managed lifecycle callbacks. Lua phase scripts and Rust bindings remain placeholders, while several hierarchy methods become `todo!()` and dispatch uses type-erased arguments. This is a particularly clear example of a concept becoming more comprehensive in documentation before its access rules or execution path work. See the [October](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-2024-a-typed-locking-hierarchy-replaces-the-global-operation-queue) and [November](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#november-2024-typed-path-bindings-and-nested-command-registries) reviews.

December first continues the hierarchy line: a lock guard API is introduced, but its implementation is changed to return no guard and only mutate lock metadata; the separate `TrackedMutex`/finalization sketch also does not finalize its payload. Later in the month, the active engine is archived and replaced by a smaller chunk/loader prototype. Lua task files now describe camera, chunk, actor and loader behavior through Rust operations, but the host contract remains underspecified. Ownership is split across mutex-backed globals, component hooks and systems; a failed retry can be requeued and consumed again in the same unbounded loop. This is another active-engine reset, not a port of the hierarchy into the new streaming model.

January removes the unused `ChunkStateManager`, then tries to centralize loaded chunks, owners and pending actions in a `ChunkManager`. The first despawn implementation mistakenly restores the chunk to the loaded/owned maps; the next patch fixes it. The action processor initially drains all work in one update; a later cap limits action count to 100 and adds high-water/counter diagnostics, but still clones the full map and selects from unspecified hash order. The source also says chunk construction remains synchronous and stalls, so the action budget bounds dispatch count rather than the expensive operation’s frame cost. An `Action` framework begins layering erased inputs, ECS/async stages and mutable `World` access on top, while completion/result bridges remain TODOs. These are patch-level findings, not historical build or runtime verification; see the [December review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#december-hunk-level-supplement-script-tasks-lock-guards-and-the-second-streaming-reset) and [January review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#january-2025-mk5-chunk-actions-consolidate-then-the-implementation-is-reset-again) for commit evidence and limits.

Mk6 becomes explicit in January/February 2025, then Mk7, Mk8 and Mk9 follow. The file paths in milestone diffs show the work shifting through workflow systems, GPU workflows, stage I/O, macros and increasingly separated engine/mod crates. The first February `request_action` path erases a present component as `&Component`, while the chunk validators try to downcast it as `Option<Component>` (and panic on an absent target); its ownership-transfer example also mutates a component obtained through an immutable query. The action plugin’s registered progression system is empty, so instances have no stage executor in that patch. These source mismatches show the new runtime API did not yet satisfy its own target-shape or execution contract. Bevy upgrades are recorded from 0.14.2 to 0.15.3 in August 2025 and later to 0.18 in February 2026. On 2025-09-17, the Mk9 checkpoint says multiplayer is off the table and that the next direction is modding plus USF. That is a meaningful scope decision in the recorded line, not merely a feature commit.

February 2025 then turns the action idea into staged workflows crossing ECS, asynchronous work, and Bevy’s render world. The API gains request buffers, active instances, generated modules, stage outputs, validation and completion relays; a GPU texture-generation example makes render-stage intent concrete. But workflow identity changes to a single `(module, action)` slot, making concurrent instances of the same named action unrepresentable, and the RenderApp queues initially lack extraction from MainWorld. A focused exact-source check also finds that one February runner discards stage output, repeatedly launches an async stage while it remains marked `Processing`, and accepts completion without checking its stage index. Several result/completion events are added and then removed or reshaped; type-erased IO and runtime downcasts remain, while one generated type bridge uses `unsafe transmute`. This is implementation-level evidence of the gap between a typed-looking workflow declaration and a safe, complete runtime contract.

In March, generated workflow code becomes the source of truth: hand-expanded chunk/GPU modules are replaced by macro inputs and generated Rust. Stage completion moves through separate ECS/render/async channels, then is repeatedly consolidated; “wait,” success, and failure become distinct lifecycle outcomes. The generated handlers, however, are duplicated across stage kinds, and reviewed patches contain internally inconsistent downcasts, missing generated syntax, incomplete pollers, and global sender ownership experiments. The commit register matches all 47 March commits, but neither the register nor source inspection proves generated code compiled or ran. The [February review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-02-staged-actions-mutate-into-workflows-then-into-a-macro-language) and [March review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-03-generated-workflow-code-becomes-the-product-surface-then-async-request-semantics-split) retain the patch-by-patch evidence and explicit limits.

April makes the stage lifecycle more legible: requests are initialized, `while` stages can return retained state or complete with output, and setup, wait, completion and failure each acquire event paths. Receive systems are ordered before pollers and channel capacity is reduced to one, trading unbounded accumulation for producer backpressure. At the same time, the macro generator expands across five stage kinds and eight input/output/error shapes, with intermediate omissions and temporary hand-expanded output. Workflow resumption retrieves and mutates a stage in the registered workflow definition, so the reviewed code still leaves per-invocation state ownership unclear; render-while polling adds a split/poll/fuse transaction whose restoration relies on scheduled reintegration. A late-April registry declaration further centralizes workflow/stage topology, but its initial catalog is inconsistent and several stage-forwarding functions are empty before follow-up wiring. April therefore improves lifecycle vocabulary and scheduling visibility without proving safe concurrent instances, complete message delivery, or a buildable runtime. See the [April review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-04-workflow-generation-absorbs-stage-ownership-dispatch-and-scheduling).

May tries to make those workflows own chunk streaming itself: chunk actions are batched by kind and routed through composites, GPU texture work is staged before spawning, and loader observer behavior moves into workflow declarations. The handoff is not transactional: actions leave the queue before job success is known, one `Local` handle per action kind blocks subsequent batches, and failure paths often panic or lose the request. Composite workflows also add captured values across an async boundary. A thread-local `AnyMap` first collides for same-typed captures and is unsafe across task migration; a later UUID/task-local context improves invocation identity but creates cleanup obligations on every exit path. A typed intent resolver is sketched but not made authoritative, and one validation branch reports failure even when no invalid actions were collected. The same month includes an engine/package naming move; it does not yet establish a clean engine/game/core ownership split. See the [May review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-05-workflow-staging-is-redirected-toward-chunk-actions-and-captured-composite-work).

June then moves from queued actions toward a proposal/commit intent model and a Bevy-entity-backed owner identity. The resolver and apply step are repeatedly stubbed, removed, or bypassed; pending and committed buffers appear without a demonstrated single transaction that resolves and applies every request. Reserved entities can exhaust through a panic, and the new owner wrapper compares by label while also storing an entity, so distinct entities with one label collapse under equality/hash. In parallel, the first custom tracing viewer gains split panes and severity/location filters, but its replacement `log_NEW` branch duplicates the store and indices before retirement of the original, leaves handlers empty, and ends with a source-inconsistent event extractor. June is thus both a failed attempt to formalize action authority and the start of a dedicated observability tool—two themes that later work will revisit separately. No build/runtime success is inferred. See the [June review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-06-chunk-intents-split-into-buffers-an-unfinished-log-viewer-is-prototyped-twice).

July does not finish that logger; it activates and then backs away from competing registry implementations while reworking selection state and recursive commands. A selected trace node’s privilege can be changed before recursion discovers a rejecting descendant, leaving a partially applied subtree; module/physical selection paths are still TODO. Log extraction initially records the event’s static metadata name rather than its message, assumes `/` path separators, and later dereferences required metadata with `expect`. A hand-written typed-DAG alternative is added and removed. The UI adds virtual row painting, but it eagerly gathers and sorts all selected records and retains history without a bound, so it is not data virtualization. July therefore carries forward observability as a product need while showing how typed path structure alone does not guarantee robust extraction or scalable presentation. See the [July review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-07-selection-semantics-churn-logger-cutoverreversal-and-windows-only-path-parsing).

August couples a Bevy 0.14→0.15 migration with lifecycle and product-surface changes: reflection registration expands, a developer toolbar appears, historical source/build snapshots are archived, and pause/step ownership moves from a copied `GameTime` under `game`, to a nominal `time` plugin, then back toward Bevy’s virtual clock. The sequence itself exposes the boundary problem: the first pause gate also stops infrastructure such as chunk loading/workflows, while the replacement `run_if_not_paused` temporarily returns true unconditionally. A chunk-debug dock grows into an in-game inspector with an offscreen game view and entity/asset/resource surfaces, but its window/context/resize assumptions remain prototype-level. The newly vendored consumable-event crate loses its two tests immediately, weakening evidence for the semantics now owned in-tree. This is a meaningful move toward an integrated workbench, but not evidence of a functioning editor or settled time contract. See the [August review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-08-bevy-migration-time-ownership-and-an-experimental-debug-workbench).

September is dominated by the first explicit scale-aware USF prototype and a simultaneous ownership split. Scale moves from compile-time generics (which multiply query/plugin shapes and prompt generated scale-specific workflow names) toward runtime values on chunks and a semantic `ChunkCoord`; the helper for scale-aware radius arithmetic is added and removed before rounding/overflow/canonical-coordinate rules settle. In parallel, `core`, `mod`, `api`, and `runtime` crates are repeatedly renamed and moved, while the dynamic-loading contract is not yet established. Pause policy and workflow timeout become configurable, but timeout is not coupled to cancellation or rollback. The owner’s September 17 Mk9 checkpoint makes a separate product-scope decision: multiplayer is deferred in favor of modding and USF. These are converging problem statements, not proof that the crate split, USF arithmetic, or timeout lifecycle worked. See the [September review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-09-input-modes-workflow-scheduling-and-the-first-runtimemod-split).

October makes the coordinate hierarchy tangible. `GridCoord`/`GridPos`, subgrid and unit-position types start distinguishing logical location at multiple resolutions, while camera scroll changes from projection-only zoom into a request to cross discrete scale charts. Repeated revert/reapply work shows that chart, target chart and continuous visual zoom are not yet one owned transition state. Conversion still reduces large integer coordinates through `f32`; broad zoom bounds do not establish representable precision. Carrying scale in coordinates is a real semantic improvement, and the logical/visual split begins to matter, but normalization/comparison operators still include panics or unfinished cases and origin rebasing only appears late in the month. This is directly relevant to the owner’s later insistence that scale/velocity/temporal effects need explicit coupled contracts, but October itself is a spatial prototype—not the later spacetime model. See the [October review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-10-nested-scale-coordinates-transition-heavy-zoom-and-logicalvisual-separation).

November consolidates camera, render-target and debug UI setup under a render-oriented module and begins separating logical position from Bevy transforms. That is a real ownership correction, but the bridge is schedule- and change-filter-dependent: proxy refresh listens to `ChunkActor` changes even when it reads a `Transform`, while loader movement performs origin normalization in another schedule. A change to only one side can leave the presentation stale unless the companion update path runs. Picking becomes a custom path that repeatedly changes candidates and screen/viewport/pixel coordinate formulas; a manual “it works” checkpoint appears, but no automated cross-case evidence is present. GPU texture readback likewise moves from placeholder to a synchronous `Maintain::Wait` and `recv().unwrap()` path, so the editor/debug path can block and has no typed failure completion. See the [November review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-11-camerarender-ownership-migration-and-experimental-picking).

December tries to make equivalent nested-grid positions compare/hash by normalized value and separately tracks loader position (`coord`) from render origin (`origin_offset`). This improves the vocabulary, but the two mutable coordinates are updated across zoom/rebase paths without one enforced synchronization rule; equality itself clones and normalizes positions. A native wrapping helper is introduced then removed, leaving hard-coded local bounds and bespoke wrap policy. When there is no loader, one patch chooses to despawn all chunks, making a temporary absence act like a destructive reset. A two-kind `Diegetic`/`Meta` context type appears for game-vs-overlay picking, but it is a fixed marker split rather than a general context system. The month’s manual report that picking works is preserved as author-observed evidence, separate from automated coverage. See the [December review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2025-12-runtime-coordinate-authority-and-local-wrapping-experiments).


January 2026 shifts the center of experimentation from world representation to authored behavior. A profile-aware shell build script starts assembling engine/game/mod inputs, but still deletes its profile output and calls host Cargo directly. In parallel, named Rhai startup hooks acquire ECS construction bindings; then the runtime grows a custom reflection registry and several forms of scoped Bevy access. The most consequential prototype stores Bevy borrows after erasing their lifetimes to `'static`, routes them through shared handles, and expects explicit hook teardown to close the access window. That makes the desired idea—temporary authority supplied for a call—visible in code, but expiration is a runtime convention backed by unsafe conversion, reference-count assumptions and panic paths, not a Rust lifetime guarantee. The reflection registry similarly describes Rust types separately from the Rust declarations and evolves through inventory/proc-macro and dynamic-trait experiments. Thus the month is a design laboratory for capabilities and discoverable APIs, not a safe or settled scripting substrate. It also reveals an enduring ownership split: content assembly is beginning, but build and cache policy are still bespoke shell behavior. See the [January review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2026-01-rhai-capability-experiments-and-reflection-substrate).

February 2026 takes two larger steps without closing January’s contract questions. The Rust workspace jumps directly from Bevy 0.16 to 0.18; keeping the app buildable means dropping integrations that do not yet support the new version, while dynamic linking changes repeatedly by profile. The Rhai side grows `AccessCell`, a runtime borrow-state abstraction built around raw pointers and `UnsafeCell`, and reflection develops into a nested graph of raw declarations, linked relationships, custom paths and generated registrations. Some commits leave parallel old/new registries in place, enable unstable Rust features, or temporarily break access operations; a recorded runtime panic and the hunk review’s safe clone/drop hazards show that the model is still being discovered in code. Documentation sometimes presents dynamic loading and engine/game boundaries as current capabilities even as nearby notes call them incomplete. This month therefore expands both the capability vocabulary and the amount of bespoke machinery, but does not yet provide a sound lifetime boundary or settled reflection contract. See the [February review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2026-02-bevy-018-migration-metadata-compiler-experiments-and-documentation-correction).

March 2026 is the first point where the script/host split is expressed as a concrete catalog boundary. Hook registration moves toward one Rhai-binding graph, but hook names still map through hand-written strings to Bevy schedules and asset paths. Generic query descriptors are authorable, while executable query combinations remain a finite Rust-registered set; this is a practical safety/performance boundary, not arbitrary runtime generics. A reviewed `AccessCell` revision makes ownership operations more explicit, but its soundness still depends on unsafe handles, reference accounting and the invocation scope. Meanwhile, the USF prototype starts using Rhai to register typed metrics, zones, density profiles and phenomena, with Rust-owned sampling/classification kernels and configuration selecting ordered content. This is stronger than merely exposing a text console: scripts begin composing domain data against host-provided operations. Yet the `.metric.rhai`/`.mod.rhai`/phenomenon-specific entrypoints and local profile/modpack structures are bespoke, not Vapor’s later canonical content lifecycle. The same month’s spatial work keeps revising coordinate, origin and presentation authority; tests and author-observed visuals cover particular cases, not a completed USF contract. March’s 151 commits are SHA-matched in the history register, but review status remains explicitly in progress. See the [March review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2026-03-rhai-bridge-becomes-a-catalog-driven-runtime-while-usf-prototype-restarts-in-parallel).

April is a recorded reset of design authority, not a continuation of the March USF code as if it were settled. A new intention-record format distinguishes owner direction, implementation observation, confidence and unresolved divergence; the USF flow is then reframed around canonical substrate, scale, realization and typed capability channels. Meanwhile a temporary math facade grows quickly, but inspected core operations remain `todo!()` stubs. In parallel, the repo begins contributor and verification rails: `xtask` docs/audit commands, workspace-aware hooks, issue forms, CODEOWNERS and CI scope. These are meaningful changes to how future work is planned and checked, but do not prove those checks were run or the new USF contract implemented. See the [April review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2026-04-typed-usf-content-contracts-a-clean-slate-correction-and-the-start-of-process-rails).

May alternates between the experimental Rust/math model and formal project governance. The numeric API gains constructors and tests while its abstraction is reshaped across crates; the reviewed implementation still contains unfinished operations and mutable/locking wrappers whose semantics are not established by API names. The same month makes process doctrine more explicit—phase gates, issue/PR links, labels, version policy and decisions—then refines that machinery as the first forms prove too ceremonial or awkward. The project is beginning to externalize architectural memory, but the process system is itself another evolving product surface. See the [May review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2026-05-phase-governance-an-expanding-knowledge-ontology-and-a-rustmath-restart).

June is the clearest change in how architecture is negotiated. The repository adds agent-operation rules, preserves raw owner answers and disagreement, and explicitly separates owner-confirmed direction from derived synthesis and implementation evidence. Those records correct several over-neat or overconfident interpretations: Vapor capability authority is not Spacetime Engine’s, USF depends on rather than defines the capability model, and script declarations may express local behavior while Rust retains schedule/kernel authority. A large glossary is summarized, corrected, converted into an alignment ledger and then made more concise; the owner rejects treating its earliest pages as uniformly canonical. June also deletes the May math experiment and resets diagram decomposition, so neither should be read as a surviving foundation. This is a pivot from “infer intent from prototype” to “preserve who said what, when, and with what authority.” See the [June review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#loo-cast-legacy--2026-06-agent-bootstrap-question-led-architecture-correction-and-knowledge-base-consolidation).
Scripting is a parallel, discontinuous line through those rewrites: Unity’s reflected command descriptors are replaced by NLua; the first Rust-era `mlua` callback experiment is withdrawn; a later Lua task tree composes Rust operations for chunk/actor behavior; then 2026 Rhai work explores typed schedules, finite Rust-registered signatures and temporary Bevy access. The recurring design problem is stable—how authored behavior composes with host-owned capabilities and lifecycle—but the language, runtime and execution boundary repeatedly change. The [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#august-2023-serialization-churn-console-and-lua-experiments-then-a-new-rust-game) records the earliest implementation defects; its January 2024, December 2024 and January–March 2026 sections review later attempts separately. This sequence is not evidence of one runtime/API surviving across the resets.

### 4. Mk9/Mk10, scripting, USF and process doctrine — September 2025 to June 2026

Mk9 and Mk10 dominate the late-2025/early-2026 history. Commit titles show continued chunk and module work, then a major scripting push beginning January 2026. Bevy 0.18 lands in February; dynamic linking is removed and the `core_mod_core` structure is heavily refactored. The names “Mk9” and “Mk10” designate exploratory checkpoints, not guarantees of backward-compatible architecture.

March–April 2026 is accompanied by planning and documentation accumulation, temporary renames/refactors, and frequent reversions. In May the repository formalizes “Phase 0”: branch/PR rules, phase gates, labels, release/version policy, and explicit decision records. The decision log dated 2026-04-28 through 2026-05-17 records a one-repo policy “for now,” Engine/BaseMod as first-party mods, composable mods, lockstep contract versioning, and capability/API lifecycle as projection-driven fixed-point bootstrap. June adds the agent bootstrap and question-batch process, legacy-corpus registers, phase plans and extensive vocabulary/glossary material.

This is when previously scattered design questions begin to be tracked as contracts, decisions, RFCs and owner-answer logs. It is also where proposals must be kept distinct from implementation: the glossary contains a very broad capability/USF/Rhai vocabulary, while the code’s actual implementation is narrower and continues to evolve.

### 5. Two overlapping Loo-Cast repo lines — July to October 2026

On July 3/7, the tiny `Loo-Cast-Game` repo experiment appears; its latest tree contains only a `Vapor.toml`. On July 7, [`GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/afe1d770cee8217f4100c7d4e8cd779677de2673) starts from a new root commit, “Bootstrap unified Loo-Cast workspace.” The local tree now has a Rust workspace containing `spacetime-engine`, `loo-cast-game`, and `loo-cast-packagepack`, with product version 0.5.0. The README states the intended boundary precisely: three sibling artifacts, with Packagepack referring to Engine and Game by Vapor identity; that composition does not create Cargo dependencies. At this commit the distinction is declarative only: Game and Packagepack each contain a one-line empty library, Engine is a `main.rs` binary, and all three Cargo manifests have no dependencies. Engine also declares one required renderer slot and the workspace declares its trait, but the fresh tree has no renderer implementation. This establishes the new semantic composition model while showing that it is not yet a compiler/linker graph. This is a semantic continuation of the project but a separate Git history.

The root README says the packagepack references engine and game by Vapor identity rather than Cargo dependency, and the root/children receive separate role manifests. That is an explicit manifest-level separation, not yet a working static composition: the initial Engine crate is a `main.rs` binary, while Game and Packagepack are empty library shells; no resolver/link step exists in the seed. Within ten days a host-only roundtrip script describes package/acquire/install/verify/select/update/repair/uninstall and Workshop previews. A week later the first-party content is reset to placeholders, with an Engine handoff executable, Game identity library and Workshop IDs. The new repository therefore begins as a schema/build-pipeline experiment, not as a port of the then-large Legacy engine implementation. On July 19, the manifest names change again to `Workspace.vapor.toml` plus `Engine.vapor.toml`, `Game.vapor.toml` and `Packagepack.vapor.toml`; this is the historical origin of a distinction later app tooling must honor between app metadata and authored workspace roots. A nine-commit exact-patch review now confirms the fast identity and renderer-cardinality experiments, the host-only/dry-run nature of the first lifecycle scripts, and that the Engine handoff remains printed environment diagnostics rather than typed composition IPC or a built packagepack. See the [July 7–28 hunk review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#ghf-studiosloo-cast--2026-07-clean-product-workspace-and-vapor-proof-scaffolding).

The new repo’s July commits rapidly add content identity inference, Workshop proof scripts, placeholders for first-party content, host-only local scripts, the Windows GNU-LLVM target and role-specific manifests. This shows Vapor requirements entering the engine/game repository early—not as a later packaging-only concern.

The first concrete cross-repo loop appears almost immediately: Vapor-Examples becomes a custom-content Cargo workspace, `workspace sync` generates Engine/Game/Packagepack crate and manifest stubs, and a follow-up marks their source files as user-owned after seeding. On the tooling side, Vapor-CLI adds a large first content lifecycle module covering discovery through install/update/repair and Workshop publication. That module is an early end-to-end-shaped prototype, not proof that composition, acquisition, subscription, or cross-platform delivery are complete. The root container itself adds then removes the Loo-Cast submodule and drops its `default-packagepack` field on the same day, showing that source topology and initial-player-selection ownership were still moving.

The content vocabulary was not complete at the first shared-core commit. On July 1, its nine-kind enum and permissive pack-child lists established names and a first compatibility filter, not dependency cardinality, mandatory composition roles, conflicts, or the eventual artifact contract. On July 2, the SDK replaced a single workspace anchor with one Cargo crate stub per declared content entry; a same-day follow-up guarded generated manifests from overwriting user-owned files while leaving seeded Rust editable. This was workspace scaffolding, not yet proof of static-library content acquisition or composition linking. `Library` was later added as a tenth kind on September 6. In the October 18 `vapor_content` extraction, the code’s name became `Crate`, with a source manifest filename and a Rust-only statically linked description. The extraction also introduced concrete graph constraints: exact Engine/Game role counts for composition packs, typed targets for Game/mods, and optional-edge omission; version resolution is highest-satisfying per edge without a global backtracking guarantee. Authored conflicts exist in the manifest shape, but enforcement is not established by the reviewed resolver. On October 21, an Engine-level `presentation` field began selecting Window or Terminal launch handling, making content metadata drive a typed host behavior; Linux requires the Entrypoint binary for the terminal route, Windows requests a new console, and other targets reject the route. This is implementation evidence, not proof of packaged end-to-end success. This source chronology aligns with the owner’s later clarification that “Library” as a content kind should be “Crate,” distinct from Vapor’s user-facing installed/acquirable Library. The richer intended meaning—packs are manifests, content carries implementation, and Composer combines both into packs—comes from owner direction; the enum and workspace generator do not by themselves implement that full lifecycle. See the content-model hunk supplement in the semantic review for exact patches and remaining evidence gaps.

The July 10 CLI lifecycle patch makes the gap between vocabulary and a complete provider loop especially visible. It is a substantial first local lifecycle prototype: a single 2,193-line module implements discovery, metadata checks, package/cache/install/update/repair/uninstall, selection, receipts, VDF preview and a SteamCMD publish path. Its focused fixture exercises local recursive package/install/repair and a publish dry-run. Uncached Workshop downloads are explicitly unavailable without a SteamUGC provider, and create/delete are previews; the hash is FNV-1a for local consistency, not content authenticity. The first uninstall contract also explicitly leaves dependency removal to the caller. The later design must therefore unify more than screens: provider authority, typed graph resolution, Packagepack ownership, source/binary artifacts and their release lifecycles all remain separate. The semantic review includes line-level representative findings for this 2,193-line insertion.

The Examples repository then makes the executable boundary concrete, but changes its answer over time. On July 17, `ce2d0adc` creates a terminal Engine that reads launch metadata, finds an installed Game library, and loads `terminal_game_definition_v1` through platform dynamic-loader APIs. That is a real Rust module-loading experiment: the ABI returns owned Rust strings and vectors, and the loader intentionally keeps the library mapped for process lifetime. It is not a stable plugin ABI, nor does the diff prove that Vapor built, published, acquired, or launched the shared library. On October 21, `c157496b` adds a Packagepack-owned binary which directly Cargo-links Engine, Game, and Tiny Game Mod and calls explicit install functions before the Engine loop. Its small test verifies the selected mod is present in the app's game state. This is closer to the intended statically composed executable, but the Cargo dependencies and calls are hand-authored for this one example; the reviewed change does not show the generic Vapor graph being transformed into that composition. These commits document a shift from dynamic library handoff to a compile-time composition seam, not a demonstrated end-to-end Workshop pipeline. Exact hunk findings and proof limits are in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

October 21–22 then tightens the client’s realization and ownership rules. `6efe082d` teaches the packager to recognize Windows GNU-LLVM Rust archive/import-library filenames; its test checks names, not a successful cross-target link. `28cc768c` makes an installed Packagepack own its dependency graph after unsubscribe, retaining shared dependencies until no installed or subscribed Packagepack needs them. Disabling auto-install now subscribes an item to preserve manual ownership, while a failed local state save can still leave the Steam-side subscription applied. The same change distinguishes cache and installed fingerprints because target-specific installation can legitimately narrow a full cache payload. These are direct responses to earlier “cache copy conflicts” and “unsubscribing removes what the composition still needs” failure modes. They move toward the owner’s lifecycle model, but partial-install ownership and real cross-platform Steam cleanup remain evidence gaps.

The Legacy repo continues in parallel. Its July changes add scratch/RFC material; the README divides `loo_cast_alpha/` (called active) from `loo_cast_legacy/` (read-only archive), then adds the blunt warning `DO NOT TRUST ANYTHING BEYOND THIS POINT. Legcay stuff.` The warning is ambiguous because the same README still identifies `loo_cast_alpha/` as active. On September 7, commit `49105303` reinforces that ambiguity rather than ending it: it renames the root Cargo manifest/config to `.DISABLED`, creates or expands a distinct `loo_cast_alpha/` workspace, adds 55 crate files and 180 documentation files, and restores phase-planning machinery. The README's simultaneous claim that `cargo xtask` works from the repository root conflicts with those disabled root paths; this was not executed. The new Alpha workspace has Bevy 0.18 and Rhai in its dependency catalog, but its `core_engine` entry point is still `fn main() {}` and the sampled math layer is a type alias. This is a substantial design/governance and scaffold event, not evidence of a working replacement engine. Meanwhile the new `GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast` repo continues through September and October. The repositories’ descriptions therefore do not prove which one superseded the other at every point; only current owner-directed workspace and current branch state can settle present authority. See the focused [September Alpha review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#september-alpha-revival-architecture-sketch-versus-executable-system).

The new repo’s September history becomes extremely dense: portal movement/collision, editor and debug tools, terrain/voxel rendering and collision, scale/USF restructuring, performance, bug fixes and repeated refactors. Many commit subjects are generic (“AI Stuff,” “Stuff,” “Schtuff”), so the commit register preserves them faithfully and links to the actual diffs rather than pretending the message alone explains the change. Two changes particularly clarify the architectural movement. On September 24, a commit explicitly titled “USF experiment part 42 (shit broke)” removes context-topology and hierarchical gravity-cache machinery, replaces it with sparse ancestor-closed runtime residency, and makes gravity sampling directly iterate source entities. This pivots from cached field representation toward a simpler canonical query, trading consistency machinery for potentially source-count-proportional query work. September 26's `2482e0d` creates the generic capability/coverage surface and removes most of the former monolithic refinement module: realized roles and bounded coverage become persistent producer evidence, while refinement describes the requested branch. On September 30, `757aab1` adds a cache keyed by source and canonical integer demand ranges, so motion inside an unchanged footprint avoids rebuilding the graph; October 6 extracts request facts, graph planning, range conversion and ECS scheduling into explicit modules (`0e48843`). This sequence answers motion-churn and ownership-separation concerns, but the current residency planner still lacks a total range-volume budget and the declared collision-query role remains unused. The later source audit distinguishes these structural boundaries from guarantees that providers publish accurate readiness or large authored demand cannot monopolize synchronous planning; see the [current demand/residency review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--generic-spatial-demand-and-usf-residency-are-separate-but-residency-expansion-has-no-total-work-bound) and [capability/refinement review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--capability-coverage-is-persistent-producer-evidence-refinement-is-a-separate-branch-request).

Collision representation then changes in two distinct steps rather than one monotonic split. On September 19, [`7966f1c3`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/7966f1c3925b7e622708f69a40a5cd9dfe30a34d) removes the configurable grouping strategy and moves the then-current Avian collider back to one-to-one voxel manifestations; its parent still built collision onto shared render aggregates. On September 29, [`3c57342d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/3c57342da9c2399da1a9f3ca7be04d2f73e4a538) reintroduces aggregation specifically for collision: aligned 4×4×4 materialization groups become collision-only proxies while presentation remains one-to-one. On September 30, [`1fa7d450`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/1fa7d4500f78d7b38e99145e611c8620ebcf660e) removes collision membership’s dependency on disposable presentation-runtime entities and gates presentation on publication of the same demanded rigid-surface revision. October 6’s [`0e48843`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf) adapts that backend to `VoxelScaleRealization` and chart-transition reprojection. These are source-level readiness and ownership changes, not runtime proof of complete geometric coverage, semantic/mesh equivalence, or safe braking. The next October fixed-step path tightens the controlled-motion transaction further, while universal writer coverage and runtime behavior remain open.

Portal physics follows a parallel authority refinement, but it is not the voxel collision path. On September 19, [`eaf0454`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/eaf0454ec87d52e0b82a2659abcbc2bc674919e7) adds an 853-line rigid split tranche: a persistent proxy collider, a temporary USF authority partition, mapped solver velocity baselines, inverse-mapped peer deltas, crossing reconciliation and a separate character-contact bridge. This turns the portal from a teleport/render effect into a topology-aware pairwise physics adapter. On October 5, [`e987230`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/e987230f240378353fe7afe1f5508649e318252b) restructures those paths and deletes the previous portal crossing/mapping tests; October 6's [`0e48843`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf) reorganizes and cleans the resulting subsystem. Current source still implements the peer contract, but contains no replacement portal test module. The progression is real integration with explicit single-authority intent; geometric and solver behavior remain runtime-unverified.

### September 19–October 6, 2026 — portal stencil fitting separates surface snapping from strict support

September 19 `f43573f` adds the first rectangular collision-stencil fitter as a single module with focused tests for flush support, face roll quantization, fit correction and size rejection. Its intended scope is a portal-independent cuboid-face geometry adapter: it resolves a nearby surface, clamps or magnetizes the aperture inside face bounds, and can alternatively answer strict support without moving the requested transform. October 5 `e987230` deletes the 66-line focused test module. October 6 `ab65b8e` extracts shared axis projection, fit placement and strict support into separate modules; `0e48843` adds their module map and public export surface. Current code still has only `CollisionClipSource::Cuboid`, and adding another source shape requires a corresponding collision-topology rebuild branch as well as fit logic. This history shows a real reusable seam, a lost visible regression suite, and a structural cleanup that did not expand supported geometry. It does not establish the deleted tests passed or that any current portal placement fails.
