See the [latest stencil-fit review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--stencil-fitting-is-cuboid-specific-and-currently-has-no-retained-focused-tests) and [current cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#collision-stencil-fitting-is-a-cuboid-adapter-not-general-support-surface-geometry).


The collision realization mechanism starts earlier: September 12 `6241440` adds immutable collision sources and the first convex clipping/decomposition path so portal holes alter the host Avian collider rather than only gameplay raycasts. The September 19 cleanup moves code out of the source module as the fitter is separately introduced; October 5 `e987230` removes the fitter's four focused geometry cases and trims CSG; October 6 `ab65b8e` separates local dirty-state indexing and ECS collider reconciliation, while `0e48843` documents the module surface. Current source makes the safety tradeoff visible: an unsupported/non-unit or failed clip conversion falls back to the original solid collider. The indexed host rebuild is deterministic by stencil entity order but has no explicit CSG piece budget or fallback diagnostic, and it watches source/Transform/stencil changes rather than independent Collider replacement. These are current source observations, not evidence of a collision failure; no result was executed. See the [focused collision-topology analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--collision-topology-derives-real-avian-colliders-from-authored-stencil-state) and [current-state comparison](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#collision-topology-replaces-collider-realization-rather-than-adding-portal-only-filters).

The same work keeps portal meaning and geometric mapping in separate source modules: `domain` holds the public command/types and fixed endpoint identity, while `topology` owns crossing and rigid-map math. `eaf0454` is the substantive move of the portal subtree into the Engine crate alongside the first pairwise rigid solver adapter; October 5 `e987230` and October 6 `0e48843` reorganize the subtree and add explanatory module maps, but do not turn the two-entity `PortalPair` into a registry. The current command path also makes an important lifecycle distinction visible: invalid placement and commands consumed before pair startup have no structured result, even though `PortalCommand` is described as the public requested-mutation route. This is current implementation evidence layered onto the chronology; no historical user-facing rejection behavior or runtime ordering was replayed. See the [domain/topology review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--portal-domain-commands-describe-a-built-in-pair-not-a-validated-extensible-portal-graph) and [cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#portal-topology-exposes-a-command-seam-over-a-fixed-pair-with-incomplete-rejection-feedback).

October commits show the line tightening around ownership and distribution: terrain/chart boundaries, canonical geometry, console observation/action separation, console/script/spacecraft ownership, a packagepack executable, a target matrix, debug build profiles, reusable cross-target content libraries and shared console/Rhai editor semantics. The current workspace is the clearest evidence of the present direction: a Vapor-managed playable Packagepack with an executable, reusable content libraries and Rust/Rhai tooling, built on Spacetime Engine.

The ECS identity graph followed a similar but distinct arc. The September 10 marker/manifestation model expanded on September 25 into semantic, authority-partition, realization and presentation relationships; September 27 added traversal and focused lifecycle tests. October 5’s consolidation deleted those assertions, and October 6’s ECS reorganization retained the relationship types and broad consumers without restoring a graph-level validator or equivalent tests. In the current snapshot, the ownership query is active, while the presentation-view reverse index is unused and constituency is only consumed directly. The latest-state distinction and exact call sites are documented in the [USF identity graph review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--usf-identity-graph-and-diagnostics-semantics-split-persistence-and-observability-still-separate) and [current-state cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#ecs-identity-and-manifestation-ownership-layers-exist-some-remain-descriptive). This is a loss of explicit regression coverage and partial enforcement, not evidence the graph fails at runtime.

The thermal domain is a compact example of the same “make the boundary explicit, then refine it” development arc. September 12's systemic fire slice put signed energy input, aggregate thermal bodies, fuel, derived combustion, game injury and derived flame presentation in separate roles. On September 19, `7402cc6` moved reusable thermal behavior out of game-owned health while retaining the game injury/presentation adapters; it also brought the finite-volume field and three focused domain/simulation/spatial test modules into the Engine. The field preserves gradients for selected local interactions while the aggregate remains a compatibility authority. On October 5, `dc69de6` removed those three test modules (91 lines) without a replacement in the current thermal source tree; on October 6, the cleanup deleted the 99-line thermal architecture note that had described the bridge and its limits. The current source still implements the bridge, but its focused historical verification was removed and its detailed architecture explanation was lost. Both removals are traced in the [October 25 thermal cross-check](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--thermal-subsystem-cross-check-against-its-deleted-architecture-note). This is an intentional approximation with a known information-loss path, not evidence that the complete USF-scale thermal model exists. Latest source review adds that the spatial adapter and aggregate simulation do not share one tick/coordinate contract; see the [current-state thermal cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#thermal-evolution-keeps-an-aggregate-compatibility-bridge-but-does-not-have-one-clock-or-one-coordinate-contract).

October also contains a sharp world-generation reversal. The October 6 tree (`0e48843`) carried a typed `PhenomenonRule` registry, sparse spatial/temporal evaluation cache, epoch metadata, deterministic noise and nine built-in descriptive domains. Its own module docs say it did not create live celestial identities, terrain, ecology or material state, and that the Loo-Cast fixture did not consume its outputs; its `TemporalScale` was a resolution label, not physical time. On October 8, `d806e3d` removed 1,382 lines of that model. Later that day, `0f153c5` introduced the narrower deterministic seed, authored/procedural constraint and provenance boundary; `b77a397` added a sparse canonical catalogue of construction facts. The current Earth-Moon fixture uses exact authored values, and the README calls the worldgen catalogue experimental rather than live world construction. This is not deletion of a working procedural-world pipeline; it is a move from disconnected generated descriptions toward stable construction inputs, with actual procedural recipes and orchestration still open. The [latest-state cross-check](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7a-worldgen-means-deterministic-construction-inputs-today-not-procedural-worlds) traces both ends.

That reversal must also be read against the September 30 proposal that preceded it. The archived [worldgen megapass design](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/5021345a88ad935a8cea460adb1b9feda02e792e/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-30-usf-sparse-procedural-celestial-worldgen-design.md) and task plan (`d44b3407`) had set a much larger end-to-end target: movable body frames, sparse realization, cubed-sphere whole-planet presentation, kilometer-scale continental/mountain morphology, canonical Moon orbit, and a future swept-collision seam. The October 6 cleanup deleted that design alongside other architecture documents. Present source later recovered portions of the body-authority, body-local edit, demand-selected realization and Moon-orbit architecture, but not the spec's adaptive surface or terrain morphology. That distinction explains the latest state better than either counting deleted lines as lost working behavior or treating surviving vocabulary as proof the proposal landed. The milestone audit is in [atlas section 7b](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7b-september-30-worldgen-megapass-milestone-to-current-source-audit) and the [semantic ledger](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#september-30-worldgen-megapass-design-versus-current-celestial-source).

The scale vocabulary also changed across these artifacts. The archived worldgen atlas describes a proposed 36-step S+35→S0 semantic descent and explicitly treats spatial and temporal scale as orthogonal. The current USF source instead implements 71 spatial exponents from S−35 through S+35; the October 9 owner-directed plan later describes a future coupled spatial/temporal index, with canonical time semantics still deferred. These are separate proposal, implementation and future-direction records. See the [scale-model crosswalk](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7d-the-old-world-generation-scale-atlas-is-not-the-current-scale-model).

One small but revealing remnant sits between design and implementation: current startup still generates a tectonic/biome-like 256×128 planet texture and stores its material in `ProceduralPresentationAssets`, while no current source consumer was found. The geometry authority remains an exact sphere. That is an authored visual hint without the semantic terrain or renderer it was meant to accompany, not evidence of a far-body planet implementation. The cross-check records this distinction in [atlas section 7b](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7b-september-30-worldgen-megapass-milestone-to-current-source-audit).

The narrower terrain-field lineage is more specific. On September 30, `b545e20` first reshapes the existing celestial field; later that evening `9ebd7da` adds semantic terrain bands and a seven-band deterministic Rocky morphology stack, with authored metre amplitudes and scale-introduction points. By October 3 (`fb58cef`) and October 4 (`f9a213e`), a separate rocky cave field is introduced and expanded: deterministic 3D noise defines bounded tunnel/chamber voids at specified crust depths, composed with the outer solid SDF. `0e48843` on October 6 reorganizes cave/noise and descriptive worldgen, but those worldgen rules remain disconnected from live fixture construction. On October 7, `69780e1` removes the terrain bands, Rocky implementation/development path, profiles, residual sampling and cave field together with much of the GPU density/descriptor code. It leaves the radius-backed field as the canonical sampler. The code deletion is unambiguous; the commit title says the removed terrain was “unoptimized,” but no benchmark or replacement is in that diff. The inspected old and current field/rocky/cave modules have no local field-shape or cave tests, so this is not a case where a verified suite was simply removed. This establishes a design/prototype that reached semantic sampling and was then deliberately withdrawn, not a feature that was simply forgotten or proven to work at production quality. The October 25 latest-state cross-check details the consequence: dense voxelization and swept collision now agree on the simplified sphere, while the old morphology contract is not active. See [current field audit](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#the-collision-query-is-authoritative-for-a-sphere-not-for-the-terrain-that-was-planned).

The authored-map system has its own shorter arc. On **September 12**, `00f2727` adds the `.spacemap` RON asset, schema, compiler, prism mesh and playground map adapter in one 2,311-line change; the same day `c87bf81` revises the format and coordinate conventions. It is a functional reusable scene-authoring pipeline, with a README that explicitly keeps gameplay meaning in adapters. The geometry tests are extracted/refined through the later cleanup sequence, but on **October 5**, `e987230` deletes the focused asset/compile tests and the procedural-texture storage test; no replacements are present in the October 25 tree. The current audit also identifies that runtime teardown does not follow the stated “disposable manifestation” ownership: removed assets are ignored, and source entities do not own their generated entities through linked-spawn/children. This is source-derived, not runtime-proven.

A current-state nuance is that file watching rebuilds the map’s generated geometry, but the Playground’s player-spawn and portal-marker consumers each retain one-shot local state; subsequent edits to those markers do not reapply their gameplay effects. The current `.spacemap` path is therefore live for authored object geometry, not a fully live game-scene authoring transaction. The [latest-state geometry audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--authored-geometry-and-procedural-assets-reusable-pipeline-incomplete-lifecycle-and-recipe-authority) records the direct source paths and separates this adapter limitation from the separate stale-entity teardown hole.

Procedural presentation assets begin as a generated material/texture facility on **September 19** (`c19a905`), then gain stable-handle lifecycle and analytic-grid separation during the September 19–20 cleanup. The current module retains several built-in surfaces, but only the debug-grid material is consumed in the searched source. In particular, the planet texture is not the September 30 promised shared terrain field; it is a visual recipe beside the exact spherical celestial field. The [October 25 semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--authored-geometry-and-procedural-assets-reusable-pipeline-incomplete-lifecycle-and-recipe-authority) records the present consumer/lifecycle checks and their limits.

The October 2 [`segmented materialization design`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/020877577d1c1c0f86b69a519b43d5af2dcea844/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-02-segmented-voxel-materialization-design.md) records explicit approval and a frozen architecture before implementation: classify occupancy before allocating dense samples; publish empty facts without ECS manifestations; separate presentation, collision and editing; batch coverage; and schedule capability work by role. That document was also removed October 6. The October 25 source does contain a store/entity split, no-surface manifestation elision, batched coverage facts, role-aware demand ranking and fair worker lanes. Sphere-shell demand pruning avoids requesting some off-surface addresses, but a demanded address still produces and retains the full padded dense lattice before its uniform no-surface result is known; the proposed compact occupancy classifier and one cross-stage work-ticket scheduler are absent. So the approved design left a real lineage in code, but not its core pre-generation memory-saving stage. The [tranche cross-check](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7c-october-2-voxel-design-which-sparsity-contracts-survived) explains the difference.

The parallel `Vapor-Examples` history gives this architecture a deliberately small test subject. On October 21, [`07ae8f0c`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Examples/commit/07ae8f0c9969090eabc3a2e280fa08f490464b57) turns the earlier terminal reel into a wheel-based salvage roguelike, splits its rules, engine, game, mod and packagepack into separate typed content, and adds source tests for wheel extension and run progression. [`aca638c4`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Examples/commit/aca638c42e2deb03f516d6e345605a6aa1f7d888) adds private Workshop identities and static-library crate types. Later that day, [`c157496b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Examples/commit/c157496b46404d79309a61cf3551073b8f3bc1c3) puts the executable on Packagepack and Cargo-links the Engine/Game/Mod with explicit Rust install calls. This is a useful architectural progression—manifest graph, private provider references, hand-composed runnable product—but not evidence of public distribution or of Vapor generating the Rust graph from manifests. The exact hunks and limits are recorded in the [Examples supplement](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#cross-repository-hunk-supplement--examples-dynamic-handoff-to-compiled-composition-julyoctober-2026).

Two later same-day commits refine what that proof means: [`04479b10`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Examples/commit/04479b10727cd30909a910f41963e7fcde52a359) only reorders the lockfile’s package block, while [`80a30d2`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Examples/commit/80a30d2882ac210277d84c490a193106014602e1) moves all six manifests to public visibility and `0.5.0` alpha constraints. The latter is the repository’s request for public Workshop state, not independent proof the remote Workshop accepted it. It documents the transition from a private integration graph to intended public alpha example content.

## Abandoned, superseded, or unresolved directions

| Direction | Historical evidence | Status supported by the record |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 Unity gameplay code as the active base | Explicit 2023-04 wipe to clear game code/assets for engine work; later repo map archives Unity material under nested legacy folders. | **Superseded as implementation base.** Valuable historical/design material remains archived; do not assume Unity gameplay code migrated into the Rust game. |
| Persistent data/save-load in the 2022 game | World creation/save-load work followed by an explicit removal of Persistent Data in Dec 2022; 2026 Contracts says save-data compatibility is outside Phase 3. | **Attempted, rolled back, deferred.** No evidence here of a shipped carry-forward save contract. |
| Custom Command System | Removed 2023-08-16 in favor of Lua. | **Replaced at that time.** Later Rhai work is a later scripting era, not automatically the same code/API. |
| BigDecimal coordinate/numeric path | July 2023 commit says abandoned for BigInteger/BigVec2Int. | **Explicitly abandoned.** |
| Multiplayer | Mk9 checkpoint (2025-09-17) says definitively off the table. | **Abandoned at that checkpoint.** Later docs/code should be checked before assuming it was revived. |
| Prototype Mk0–Mk10 implementations | Dense WIP sequences, reversions/reapplications, and changing crate/file boundaries. | **Exploratory checkpoints, not a chain of stable releases.** Preserve only the design/code proven to survive into active code. |
| Separate `Loo-Cast-Game` repository | Two commits; latest tree is only `Vapor.toml`; subsequent active workspace embeds `loo-cast-game`. | **Appears to have been superseded by the unified repository**, though the two-commit experiment is preserved in GitHub. |
| Standalone Vapor-SDK repository | Repo archived; migration ledger directs useful implementation toward shared Vapor/Client. | **Historical boundary retired.** The archive is provenance; exact feature-by-feature carryover remains unverified. |
| Frontend-per-repo arrangement | Launcher/SDK/Shell/Entrypoint were split, then renamed and frontend repos consolidated in Oct 2026. | **Partially superseded.** User/process boundaries remain; source repo boundaries narrowed to shared core plus product surfaces. |
| Legacy repo as a whole | Its latest README says `loo_cast_alpha/` is “currently developed”; meanwhile the new repo has independent active history from July–October. | **Ambiguous overlapping authority.** The README and simultaneous repo history do not establish a clean retirement date. |
| 2021 project origin | Owner recollection; no 2021 commit or dated source located in the examined history. | **Open historical lead.** First provable repo root remains June 2022. |

**July 24–25 deployment and recovery arc:** GitHub Actions gains a restricted VPS deploy trigger and optional public health/auth smoke checks; an initial oneshot-status failure is corrected by making that status diagnostic-only. A root-owned hourly backup timer then records one observed state export with secrets excluded. The next restore-validation pass adds structural checks, but source review finds the validator accepts a regular file named `state` as the required state directory, allowing restore to move live state aside before failing. Current scripts also omit the fifth, SQLite-backed Registry service from restore quiescing; changing the database path while its process remains alive can leave requests bound to the old database inode. A failed copy/permission/health check has no automatic rollback, and configured state roots are not constrained to a safe subtree. The history records backup execution, not a successful restore rehearsal. Detailed evidence and the failure path are in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

**July 25 API-swarm experiment and contraction:** a local, API-funded planning harness grows from a 10-worker/two-manager read-only architecture review into workload profiles and a 12-worker/two-manager source-aware implementation-campaign profile. It reads an external prompt pack, stores its API key outside the checkout, estimates spend, confirms before calls, and writes reports locally; its own prompt forbids source mutation, deployment, SSH and secret access. The same day, the root integrates Diagnostics v2 and immutable Docs release contracts into service-source changes, but the available commits do not prove the harness caused or authored those changes. `ecf1b4e9` then removes the complete harness and release contract, collapses Docs and Diagnostics back to simpler unversioned routes, and replaces the `local-qa.sh` wrapper with a narrower explicit CI list. The record does not explain why these designs were reversed. See the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#july-25-api-swarm-planning-harness-externalized-analysis-then-removed).

The diagnostics slice exposes a long-lived integration seam. The July 22 Client planning intake makes local capture the active deliverable and leaves whether/how to upload unresolved; on July 25 the server API gains structured reports, then is simplified to an unversioned `/reports` route, while the Client's same-day local-capture revision adds a future transport seam that remains stubbed in the October CLI. The current cross-boundary behavior and privacy implications are in the [latest-state review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25-diagnostics-server-exists-but-the-client-upload-path-is-still-a-stub). This is evidence of two service slices, not proof the API-swarm experiment caused the split.

**October 20 operational turn:** the Platform Server begins generating a docs landing index from the content it bundles, repairs a missing VPS-side docs token configuration during deploy, and changes publication to stage a public archive with SCP before the VPS authenticates to its loopback Docs service. This closes a real operator gap, while leaving two distinct publication paths (direct HTTP with a locally supplied token, or SSH/SCP with server-side token access). The uploader’s new test uses mocked SSH/SCP; it is not a live VPS or rendered-page verification. Full diff interpretation is in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

**October 25 live-site checkpoint (observed, not a commit):** the deployed `/docs/` page lists curated HTML books, 18 direct Shell links, and a Client-context list containing README/manifests/roadmap under broad headings. This means the generated index is not yet an audience-first documentation map: current guides, design checkpoints, platform proof, raw manifests and roadmap appear as peers. However, the nested [Books chooser](https://vapor.ghf-studios.site/docs/books/index/which-book.html) routes readers by task, and its status page distinguishes current behavior, approved direction and unverified behavior. The target policy already exists in that book but is not reflected by the landing page. This browser observation is separate from source-level upload tests; a direct attempt to open a raw `.md` link was blocked by the browser, so its end-user behavior remains unverified. See the [evidence atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#live-navigation-observation--2026-10-25) for the precise inventory and the limits of this observation.

**Docs service lifecycle:** the July release work briefly introduced immutable content-addressed docs releases, promotion and rollback; the later October simplification removed those routes and retained only replacement of the current tree. Full publication history and the operational consequences are recorded in the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#docs-server-immutable-release-history-is-added-then-removed).

**October 22 workspace metadata rollout:** the Platform Server advances four service submodules to commits that add the same `Workspace.vapor.toml` envelope and single-project declaration. This makes the repos recognizable in Vapor’s workspace model, but deployment still calls `cargo build --release --locked` directly; `--locked` fixes dependency resolution, not the Rust toolchain, so the recorded Rust 1.97 pin is not enforced by the checked build path. Metadata presence is not proof of Vapor-managed builds. The per-repo diffs and boundary limits are in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-22-four-server-repositories-adopt-one-vapor-workspace-envelope).

#### Identity implementation and its later authority contract

Identity's July 23–24 history is a compressed vertical slice: a scaffold becomes an Axum service, SQLite becomes the owned persistence layer, external Steam/GitHub verification and linked profiles are added, then browser sessions and role administration follow within roughly one day. The July 24 module split and role/audit UI make the service a usable identity-admin product. This is genuine implemented authority for its own sessions and admin decisions, not a token-only placeholder.

The operator scripts appeared in the Platform Server on July 23, alongside the first Identity vertical slice. `2feb0f9` introduced provider configuration and the auth smoke; the later smoke implementation ties GitHub Device Flow state to a single newly-created attempt. Its `--no-wait` branch exits without preserving that attempt ID, although it tells the operator to rerun and poll. The companion config script atomically replaces a setting at a time, but validates options interleaved with writes, allowing earlier valid settings to persist when a later option fails. This is an operational interface gap beside a real Identity service: convenient shell operations exist, but neither resumable CLI state nor request-level transactionality. It is source evidence, not a report of a live failure. See the [current-state analysis](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#identity-operator-scripts-expose-two-workflow-mismatches) and [focused review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--identity-operator-scripts-have-non-resumable-and-partial-apply-paths).

The scope widens after that code burst. The July 25 Platform Server cross-service contract names Identity as the source of role facts and proposes audience-bound introspection for Docs/Diagnostics first, with Publishing later; it explicitly labels the transport “not implemented yet.” September adds the Registry service as a distinct catalog boundary, and the October 22 server-domain decision assigns it content types, Workshop bindings and releases while Identity remains people/role authority. The current Identity route table still has no introspection endpoint; Registry exposes public status/ecosystem/provider reads and has no content or authorization routes, while a production-source search found no Identity client in the Vapor Client. Consequently, the chronology is: identity administration implemented first, ecosystem authorization/catalog roles defined afterward, integration remains unfinished. The design lineage is documented in [cross-service authorization](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/cross-service-authorization-contract.md>) and [server boundaries](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/server-domain-boundaries.md>); exact commit chronology is in the [Identity register](#vapor-identity-server--19-commits) and [Registry register](#vapor-registry-server--6-commits). Source/docs cross-check only; no service request or VPS deployment was inspected.

## Semantic diff review status

This file is the chronological commit register. Its entries are not, by themselves, evidence that every historical patch has received a line-by-line semantic review. The separately maintained [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md) records reviewed historical intervals, the superseded Loo-Cast checkpoint `b77a397`, and the current local head `c070bf3` (with only `Cargo.lock` modified); it also lists intervals and patches still outside the selected hunk review. The focused 2026 review now includes the October 15–19 Steam UGC, subscription, operation-lifecycle and acquisition sequence; the October 23 semantic workbench, canonical module creation, local/Rust Analyzer boundary, Rhai parsing and content-authoring UI; and October 25 cross-repository source checks, including engine foundation call sites and portal's current pairwise physics contract against the older WIP traversal concepts. Further repository/commit slices remain open. Do not treat an indexed commit as semantically verified unless that review ledger says so.

### Local content proof scripts: authored path and current CLI contract diverge (July–October 2026)

Loo-Cast `ff16e4c` (July 10) adds `content-roundtrip.vapor` and `content-publish-preview.vapor` under `.vapor/scripts/`; `2f87384` (July 17) narrows package/create/publish steps to host-only behavior. The July 19 root README retains `script run` instructions for those names. The present Vapor CLI contract instead resolves line-oriented scripts from `resources/vapor/vapor-scripts/` (source tree first, installed app fallback); its current app payload contains only `default.vapor`. It also defines `content subscribe` as an operation requiring a Steam PublishedFileId, while the old roundtrip passes authored Vapor content IDs. The scripts remain present but have not been migrated to the current resolver/argument contract. The exact old executor semantics are not established here, and no command was run; this is a current code/document compatibility gap, not evidence that a user mutated Steam subscriptions. See the [October 25 path/side-effect audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-documented-local-content-scripts-are-stranded-on-the-old-path).

## Vapor-Examples: from dynamic library loading to a statically composed game probe (July–October 2026)

The example repository captures a compact version of Vapor’s changing composition idea. July’s `ce2d0adc` has a separately built Game library loaded by the Engine through a handwritten Rust ABI. On September 5, [`f38932de`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Examples/commit/f38932de06c101f0a359e475535a847fabd42756) deletes that prototype and replaces it with a very small Engine call that accepts Game and Mod installation closures. On September 6, [`89e4ff59`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Examples/commit/89e4ff59cbc341eca6330e7f65cffb7cfd767fc9) expands the Engine into a Bevy/Crossterm runtime and the Game into registered wheel behavior with a Mod extension seam. The transition is a shift from runtime-loaded independent code to code composed in one Rust process; it is not yet a general Vapor-generated build pipeline. A root Vapor workspace manifest is removed in the September 5 reset and restored by [`a8448f63`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Examples/commit/a8448f639f9f8a2d525e8136209c0603de604444) the next day.

The wheel API also changes quickly: September 7 removes the `wheel-core` Cargo dependency from `wheel-rules` while leaving its Rust import, then restores that dependency and richer outcome/table types two hours later. The source history demonstrates the instability, but no build was run on the intermediate commit. October 21 makes the Packagepack own a Cargo binary that links Engine, Game, and Mod by local path and passes installation closures into the Engine. This is the strongest example-level evidence yet for the later static-composition direction, while still being hand-authored package wiring rather than proof of generic composition from Vapor manifests. The same day the six-artifact graph is completed with PublishedFileIds and private visibility; on October 21's later alpha-version commit `80a30d2`, those manifests are changed to Vapor content version `0.5.0` and declare public visibility. Cargo package versions remain `0.1.0`, a separate namespace documented in the workspace README. This chronology proves what the repository declared, not that Steam's live items or cross-target binaries matched those declarations. The [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#september-57--prototype-reset-terminal-runtime-and-unstable-wheel-api) details the prototype-to-static-link arc, and its [latest-state comparison](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--the-wheel-salvage-graph-proves-a-hand-wired-static-composition-not-generic-pack-realization) records current limits.

## Reconstructible-work pacing enters the voxel pipeline (2026-10-02–06)

Loo-Cast commit [`cb094c12`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/cb094c12d9459ff105fab2de8b692da6c6bc5f85) adds a generic frame-budget resource while reshaping voxel demand, generation, derived-surface work and manifestation reconciliation. The resource measures wall-clock spacing between `First` stages (not isolated simulation CPU time), carries a decaying overshoot debt into the next allowance, and keeps an EWMA estimate for three classes: planning, publication and maintenance. Its first admission per class is unconditional, and an admitted synchronous unit cannot be interrupted; the implementation is therefore cooperative pacing, not a frame-time guarantee. October 6 commit [`0e488433`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf) adds a closure helper but does not alter the budget policy.

Following its current callers changes the historical interpretation: the shared `Publication` estimate now covers queue/publication bookkeeping, membership reconciliation and mesh construction, while the mesh-rebuild caller drops its timing token. The policy has no direct focused tests in the inspected source module. Thus the October integration did establish one shared pacing resource across important voxel paths, but source does not establish a well-calibrated cross-domain cost model or a reliable cap. No runtime frame-time measurement was performed. See the [current semantic trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#reconstructible-work-is-a-soft-admission-heuristic-with-one-unclosed-measurement-path).

## Script Workbench crosses into the game build as source data on 2026-10-02

Loo-Cast commit [`fdc8fb26`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/fdc8fb26d8b9ce055cc7eb16ccc581433aed94a6) creates `spacetime-engine/build.rs`, `scripts/README.md`, the first repository Rhai examples, and a larger in-game Script Workbench path. The build script walks the sibling repository `scripts/` tree and writes every `.rhai` source as string data into a generated Rust constant; at runtime, the Engine materializes build defaults and seeds a separate writable live tree. It does not generate Rust logic from Rhai, compile Rhai to an AST at build time, or establish the previously discussed generalized capability graph. The October 6 cleanup commit [`0e488433`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf) changes this build script's formatting only; its large deletion of design documents should not be read as an implementation change to the embedding mechanism. Current source retains the source/default/live split, with a 1,024-file build cap and a 256-file runtime discovery cap; the current tree has two scripts, one live freecam policy and one compile-only scratch document. This marks an important transition from script-host/capability exploration toward a real but narrow game-integrated editing and execution path. [Current source-to-runtime assessment](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-in-game-rhai-workbench-executes-a-narrow-committed-hook).

The editor's shared action row exposes a further semantic seam: compile-only scratch documents still have Commit and Revert Runtime controls. Their “commit” merely selects a compiled AST as that document's local committed revision; only the path-bound freecam document has a host call site and a Live toggle. That difference is not a chronological change to Rhai's execution model, but it matters to reading the October 2 feature accurately: the workbench supports several document lifecycle states, while only one stateful host contract currently gives a committed script runtime effect.

The October 6 `ab65b8e` extraction makes the live failure policy easy to locate in `workspace.rs`: runtime Rhai errors return the original scalar through `unwrap_or(value)` without updating the editor diagnostic. The following `0e48843` change generalizes the method signature to take a `ScriptTarget`; it retains that fallback. Current compilation also executes the bound function at a preview value, so “Compile” can emit host logs, and preview success is not proof for all runtime inputs. This is a later source-level refinement of the October 2 workbench story, not evidence that the owner’s broader scoped-capability design was implemented. See the [runtime/preview source finding](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#follow-up--the-scalar-workbench-validates-by-execution-and-hides-live-call-failures).

## Spatial authority and fixed-step collision transaction on 2026-10-09

[`46e1eac`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6) is a 64-file spatial/flight tranche (+2,476/−547) with an in-repository implementation plan. The inspected path changes the collision journal from a `PostUpdate` shadow observation into a `FixedUpdate` transaction: controlled flight prepares one canonical SI displacement, submits it, the voxel provider searches semantic body and edit bounds and refines signed distance for at most 256 steps, then flight commits only after the provider/finalization sets. No request or uncertain query means zero safe fraction; contact advances only to the reported safe fraction and clips inward velocity along a valid normal, or stops if the normal is unavailable. This source evidence confirms a real collision response path for canonical controlled flight against the included semantic voxel field. It does not prove general collision coverage, other motion owners, runtime robustness at 147 km/s, or terrain interaction.

The query frame accepts provider-labelled results, but this commit wires only the voxel provider, so provider neutrality is an API seam rather than a working multi-provider registry. A smaller contract gap is that `Contact` documents a unit normal while result publication accepts arbitrary values; the voxel resolver normalizes its own gradient, but flight's response formula relies on that normalization without enforcing it for other providers.

A follow-up source search finds no direct tests of the voxel candidate/refinement path, even though tests were added for neighboring flight/travel policies. The failure, contact and safe-fraction behavior therefore remains unverified by an automated test in the inspected tree; see the [semantic collision audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

The same commit changes authority selection from only a detailed/coarse scale check to a compound condition involving numerical step representability and local collision readiness. Yet the motion contract still maps detailed interaction scale to `DetailedBody` and other scales to `ScaleProxy`, so scale remains coupled to collision backend. A new coverage-gated transition admission path requeues a one-shot relocation when destination roles are not ready and treats a canonical motion reanchor as representation-only. A flight safety supervisor calculates radial TTC/braking warnings but remains observational and does not actuate the sweep result. Its calculation combines body-relative radial direction with the ship's absolute velocity; the body velocity is not included, even though orbital bodies have canonical velocity. Thus moving-target TTC/braking is incomplete when body radial motion matters. Its scalar deceleration estimate also does not account for whether the ship can orient thrust against its actual trajectory. These are source-level model gaps, not an explanation proven for the reported Moon incident; tests in the commit were not run during this historical review.

The same diff adds a signed persistent ship throttle, independent angular-assist state and a distinct attitude-rate control law. W/S feed the throttle axis; the wheel trims it except when modifiers/debug traversal route the wheel to pace. Camera mode expands to cockpit, chase and observer orbit, with per-mode orientation policy and separate zoom intent. Travel-neighborhood refresh now accounts for semantic speed so fast movement refreshes the influence set before crossing half its cached margin. These are source-level affordances toward the requested ED-like control/camera split and motion-aware navigation; visual/runtime feel and streaming latency remain unverified. The systems still select a single `LocalControlSubject`, notwithstanding the generic locomotion documentation.

The focused source review resolves more of that transition: the fixed-main-loop ordering evaluates radial flight safety after navigation observation and before Cruise request resolution. An emergency transition leaves capture pending; fixed-step flight then clamps the resolved velocity, clears the pending state, and submits the resulting motion for collision handling. This is an integrated handoff, but the risk supervisor does not itself steer braking or use the subsequent collision result. Input defaults also change (`E` becomes roll-right, `F` becomes interact); F5 cycles cockpit/chase/orbit instead of presenting a mode picker. The new HUD reads `FlightTelemetry` for persistent throttle, forward/lateral velocity, assist state, cooldown/charge and TTC, and draws a camera-relative velocity marker with a fixed pixel clamp. The telemetry producer is ordered before the primary-view/HUD projection, so same-frame source ordering is explicit; the marker itself uses a fixed 90 px scale rather than camera projection/FOV and clamps at ±110 px. The October collision pass adds a semantic voxel sweep for canonical flight, but numeric f32 step representability—not sweep readiness or tunneling risk—selects canonical authority; representable high-speed movement can continue through the distinct runtime physics path. These are implemented data paths, not proof of feel, discoverability, screen-space correctness or universal collision safety. See the [October 9 focused source pass](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-9-controls-travel-handoff-camera-and-telemetry--focused-source-pass).

The same patch adds console `camera` and `debugfly` commands and enriches the spatial developer panel with canonical SI velocity and sweep-resolution text. Context action help now changes with on-foot versus ship flight and lists flight axes/assist/camera operations, but the focused source audit finds it still hardcodes Shift/Ctrl wheel labels, omits Alt+wheel view-scale guidance, and omits on-foot camera/view-scale wheel help. Rebinding these modifiers can make the displayed actions false. This exposes the new path to player/developer UX; it remains a Loo-Cast-owned console and HUD, not a shared generic command/console system. The precise binding/help audit is in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-9-controls-travel-handoff-camera-and-telemetry--focused-source-pass).

The editor receives a separate Bevy relationship for organizational groups; the code explicitly avoids `ChildOf` transform parentage. The initial UI can create/nest/select groups, but the inspected slice does not show persistence or richer hierarchy editing. The 64-file commit also changes camera, controls, travel commands, navigation and HUD; those call sites remain partly reviewed. See the [semantic diff ledger](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-9-spatial-tranche-broad-integration-review-still-open) for exact limits and selected hunk findings.

A targeted writer search also finds semantic-position updates in separate orbital, landing, ship-exit and fixture-bootstrap paths alongside the new fixed-step flight commit. These may be correctly exclusive/domain-owned, but they mean the “one motion owner” claim requires auditing each owner and schedule; the new commit does not make all semantic pose changes flow through one transition API. A follow-up source audit separates these into projection sync, Keplerian ephemeris, controlled-flight commit, admitted rechart and event-scoped placement. The current fixture assigns the orbital component to scenery, but the propagator has no guard against the same semantic authority being used as a controlled subject; that is a conditional dual-owner risk, not a reproduced runtime case. The detailed writer table is in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#follow-up-audit--semantic-position-writer-domains).

The latest source check sharpens the phrase “one motion owner.” The controlled-locomotion plugin has a real per-subject `MotionKernel` choice: Character simulation is scheduled before flight preparation, and the inertial-flight resolver runs after canonical collision-query finalization. `UsfMotionAuthority` is a separate question about whether SI velocity or the Avian velocity cache is authoritative. This supports one selected controlled-subject integrator per tick; it does not prove global disjointness from orbital ephemeris, spatial rechart or event-placement writers. No schedule-level test or runtime trace was performed. See the [current locomotion executor trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#follow-up-audit--semantic-position-writer-domains).

**Further source audit of collision-query cost and failure locality:** the voxel provider scans every semantic voxel authority for every requested sweep. A single failed global coordinate conversion sets query-wide `complete=false`; resolution then returns zero-safe-fraction `Unknown` before using any nearby candidates, so an unrelated unrepresentable authority can conservatively halt local flight. Within a candidate, the narrow phase reapplies every Add/Remove edit at each sphere-trace sample, and each intersecting edit bound can itself produce another candidate. With up to 256 trace iterations, edit-heavy bodies can therefore multiply the per-sweep cost roughly with candidate-count × total-edit-count; the publisher also repeats broad-phase collection to publish candidates and then resolve. This is a source-derived complexity risk, not measured timing. It qualifies the claim of a bounded query: the trace loop is bounded per candidate, but authority count, candidate count and edit count are not bounded in this path. See the [additional collision-query audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#additional-collision-query-audit--spatial-global-failure-and-edit-count-scaling).

No later Loo-Cast commit from Oct 17 through the local Oct 22 head touches the collision, voxel-query, flight-safety, locomotion-flight, transition or camera paths from this tranche. The inspected Oct 9 design and implementation therefore remain the current committed baseline at `c070bf3`; runtime evidence is absent from this audit.

A second focused pass traces two limits inside the transition/travel claims. The normal spacecraft installs its safety state and the fixed-step order evaluates it before Cruise resolution, but the resolver accepts that component as optional: a custom Cruise-capable subject with no safety state is treated as non-emergency. Likewise, an empty travel neighborhood refreshes continuously and is indistinguishable from temporarily unavailable influence data; the default state permits Cruise, which is appropriate in known empty space but assumes the world query is complete. Transition coverage is opt-in on each request. The overlap guard examines continuous coarsening requirements, while one-shot requested transitions are admitted without that backend veto. These are source-confirmed contract boundaries and conditional risks, not reproduced incidents; the [second focused admission/readiness pass](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#second-focused-source-pass--travel-readiness-and-transition-admission) records the call paths and test gaps.

A final targeted look at the same tranche's help UI finds that most action labels come from the binding registry, but wheel-modifier hints are literal `SHIFT`/`CTRL` strings. The runtime routes those gestures through rebindable FastModifier/Descend actions; Alt wheel changes observer scale but is not listed, and the on-foot help branch does not show its available camera/view-scale wheel gestures. A 16-row cap also silently drops trailing hints in a sufficiently feature-rich flight state. This is a small but concrete example of a broader boundary: input execution and input explanation are coupled by convention rather than generated from one binding-aware action description. It is source-confirmed UX behavior, not a report of a particular player's rebinding or HUD state. See the [focused input-help audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#focused-input-help-pass--the-hud-is-only-partly-binding-aware).

The control audit also distinguishes three meanings of “brake.” Manual flight's signed throttle moves by 0.5 per second, and while a nonzero thrust command remains, RCS velocity damping is suppressed; Cruise clamps throttle to nonnegative values and logarithmically smooths its speed toward the commanded cap; emergency dropout directly caps velocity magnitude before the next proposed displacement. These are materially different responses, and the last is a discontinuous speed capture rather than force-based deceleration. The code contains arithmetic coverage for the cap, but not an end-to-end test of approach braking, dropout displacement, collision admission or energy consequences. This makes the user's earlier braking report an unresolved behavioral issue with several plausible interacting control paths; source alone cannot identify which path was active. See the [focused braking-policy audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#focused-braking-pass--cruise-throttle-and-emergency-capture-are-three-different-policies).

**Current-state cross-check of control handoff:** the October 6 control/transition extraction (`ab65b8e`, then structural cleanup in `0e48843`) gives semantic authority transfer and spatial chart application separate messages and owners. October 9's `46e1eac` adds an explicit motion-reanchor channel and keeps one-shot relocation requests pending until declared coverage is present, but does not join those two lifecycles into one completion result. At the October 25 source snapshot, a control request can be accepted and focus markers moved before the queued destination transition is admitted; a coverage miss requeues the transition. This is a supported staged policy in code, not proof of a failed spacecraft interaction. It leaves the meaning of “transfer applied” narrower than “the controller, view and collision-ready chart have all arrived together.” The [current semantic trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--control-transfer-and-spatial-handoff-are-separate-transactions) records that consequence and the limits of available evidence.

The same audit also catches a stale generic-controller contract: `FlightControlIntent` describes forward movement inside its translation vector, but the executor replaces that vector's Z value with its separate throttle state. The local keyboard adapter writes the latter, so it works by convention; a future non-human controller following the public vector documentation could be ignored. This makes the patch's “device-independent” intent boundary less stable than its human-input path suggests.

The follow-on [`d7e1f589`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/d7e1f589386bc3702fba7bc871ff48197525a58c) adds a tiny local `cloc` wrapper for the Game, Packagepack and Engine directories. It is not evidence that Vapor owns build-cache policy or complete repository metrics.

## SDK workspace generation moves into shared Vapor (July–October 2026)

The July SDK first creates one Cargo crate per declared content item, with generated role-specific manifests and identity-only `lib.rs` stubs. [`a0c92232`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-SDK/commit/a0c922329e8def7d6354b2651a157d7fe05782ed) adds ownership markers so generated Cargo/manifest files cannot overwrite hand-authored replacements, treats seeded Rust as user-owned, and rejects duplicate normalized Cargo package names. That is a specific protection within one workspace.

On October 14, Vapor [`0e5789bf`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/0e5789bfe8d7590d401f33f7617ae75a6a2f023c) absorbs a 1,092-line, seven-file workspace/toolchain/deploy subsystem. Its generated Cargo target directory is keyed by a lossy slug of `organization/name`; this is a new namespace from the earlier per-crate name check and has no corresponding collision guard. The current manifest-driven project paths are also joined to the workspace root without containment checks, so traversal or symlinks can direct generated files outside that root. This differs from the Client provider's source-project validation, which rejects absolute/parent paths and canonicalizes role manifests; the SDK operation bypasses that boundary. October 18 [`f9e8b135`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9e8b135f3991f4eac43de6da964d0874504cde4) replaces the local content-kind/manifest-name list with the shared `ContentType::ALL` vocabulary and changes deploy from `vapor_shell` to `vapor_cli`, still producing one `vapor` alias. October 20–22 centralizes the managed Rust environment, uses the background process helper and appends Unix system utility paths. The current 05.02 roadmap's claim that sync generates per-content `Vapor.toml` therefore describes the July generator, not October's source: current sync requires that role-specific file already exist and creates Cargo scaffolding around it. The detailed diff/source comparison is in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--sdk-workspace-identity-can-collide-in-the-shared-cargo-output-root).

## Steam Workshop and the operation lifecycle begin to converge (October 15–19, 2026)

The October sequence starts with Steamworks UGC search and account subscriptions, then adds subscription metadata/state, a capped batch subscribe API, shared operation identity/progress, and finally a cache-aware acquisition lifecycle. The core operation contract deliberately leaves scheduling to the host: the initial `Queued` event is followed immediately by `Running`, and the October 19 Studio service still rejects all Workshop work while another operation is active. This is a lifecycle vocabulary before a shared queue.

By October 19, subscribing a Workshop item also attempts to acquire and import it into Vapor's app-owned Library. The service preserves the difference between a successful Steam subscription and a failed download/import, and it attempts to protect dependent compositions from incompatible Auto-Install updates. This sequence creates explicit states—discovered, subscribed, acquired, installed and composition-owned—but does not yet make them one transactional operation. The batch Steam provider returns an aggregate error instead of per-item outcomes; the service short-circuits before reloading subscriptions on that error, so partial Steam success can leave the displayed subscription snapshot stale. Later October ownership and resolver changes refine the intended model but retain exact-version and production-path gaps documented in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-15-19-steam-discovery-grows-into-a-separate-subscription-and-library-lifecycle).

## Packagepack executable, targets, and shared authoring/console pieces (October 17–22, 2026)

The Oct 17 Loo-Cast change moves the launchable program from `spacetime-engine` to a Packagepack binary. The root workspace registers Packagepack, Game and Engine as Vapor projects; the Packagepack directly depends on Engine and Game and calls the Engine host with the Game install function. This is a concrete statically linked example composition, although the dependency list is still manually authored rather than generated from an arbitrary resolved Vapor graph. The follow-up target matrix declares Linux GNU and Windows GNU-LLVM; separate `dev` line-table and opt-in `full-debug` profiles make debug-information cost explicit. Oct 21 adds declared reusable `spacetime_engine` and `loo_cast_game` library artifacts, while the demo executable continues using path dependencies. The manifest declaration and the currently linked executable are therefore related but not yet one demonstrated automated content-to-executable pipeline.

On Oct 18, [`7709f31b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/7709f31b3c0c69cc5c6077c9835ab3c9b7dcaf3b) adds the owner's mega-pass review method to `.ai_stuff/loo_cast_dev_startup_prompt.md`: diagnose evidence-backed problems across affected domains, map shared causes, separate facts from hypotheses, and carry implementation through integration rather than stopping at a plan. The adjacent text names a contract → proof path → runtime evidence → authority handoff → productionization progression. This is an important process artifact that influences how later work is requested and judged; the commit itself cannot show whether future sessions actually followed it.

On October 20, Vapor's [`a194167`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/a1941677450dfaec825837094c17e2bd5e34e3c5) is a 103-file documentation wave (+2,801/−235 lines), not just three chapter edits. It expands the reader-facing books across Vapor, Launcher, SDK, distribution and internals, while adding one publication guard in `docs_publish.rs`. Within the current Vapor book it turns July outline stubs into substantial descriptions of [`content-types`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/vapor/src/concepts/content-types.md>), [`packagepacks`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/vapor/src/concepts/packagepacks.md>), and [`packs-and-composition`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/vapor/src/concepts/packs-and-composition.md>). It does more than name the ten kinds: it promotes a separate durable player Composition record, a Packagepack-as-metadata boundary, fixed Engine/Game choices, compatible-mod grouping, and Composition-scoped install/version semantics as current descriptions. The timing exposes a real seam: Loo-Cast had moved its launchable program into a Packagepack binary three days earlier, and the runnable Hello World Packagepack example arrived the next day. The book's “not a Rust crate” sentence can coexist with those binaries only if “Pack kind” and “Cargo project that realizes the Pack” are explicitly distinguished; the current book does not explain that contract. Later owner direction in this audit treats “composition” as an informal synonym for the playable Packagepack selection, keeps Pack manifests separate from their referenced Content, and expects alternative paths/cardinality to be modeled. Current code still persists a `CompositionDocument` and enforces fixed graph cardinalities, so the book reflects a real implementation choice—but not the latest owner-approved semantic endpoint. This is a design transition and unresolved reconciliation, not evidence that the latest direction has already been implemented. The same commit adds a documentation gate for blank Markdown, missing summaries and three exact placeholder strings, not editorial prompts or semantic accuracy. It does not remove earlier July editorial lines: `Explain…` prompts in the Steam/GitHub and Rationale chapters date to the July 4 stub commit `9134d3f` and remain after the October expansion. The gate raises the floor against known exact stubs but does not certify a truthful or complete manual. [Guard implementation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/docs_publish.rs#L229-L288>). See the [current-state reconciliation](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#the-current-vapor-book-is-not-yet-aligned-to-the-latest-packagepack-model) and the [relevant resolver contracts](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/resolution.rs>).

One Oct 21 commit titled “formatting” also changes runtime config/asset root discovery: explicit config wins, then `VAPOR_ENGINE_ROOT`, then source/current-directory fallback; Bevy assets similarly resolve beneath the Engine root when composed. Its USF scale tables are reformatted, with inspected values textually preserved. Oct 22 then connects a new Vapor `vapor_console_core` to the game and developer tooling. Vapor Devtools uses structured records, bounded history and text filtering; Loo-Cast adopts that record schema and takes Rhai highlighting vocabularies from the shared crate. They still retain separate command execution, record wrappers, widgets and tokenization paths. The shared Rhai tokenizer is not the one used by the game editor; the current integration shares vocabulary and data contracts, not a unified editor/console implementation.

The current in-game Rhai workbench is an independently bounded execution slice: one path maps to `debug.freecam.speed`, whose committed `transform(value)` AST may alter freecam speed only when its Live control is enabled; scratch files are compile-only. On October 5, `e3d558d9` split the existing workbench into host, storage and UI modules as part of a console/spacecraft ownership cleanup. On October 22, `c070bf3c` switched its editor highlight syntax from a Rust preset to shared Rhai keyword/type/literal vocabularies. These commits make ownership and lexical presentation clearer, but they do not connect the current tool to the older lifetime-erased ECS bridge or the owner's proposed capability-graph/Rust-generation runtime. See the [October 25 execution trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-in-game-rhai-workbench-executes-a-narrow-committed-hook); the roadmap's “no Rhai parser/executor” sentence is stale, while the broader design remains unrealized.

In the same Vapor change, Workshop search gains a typed `ContentKind` field across domain, protocol, service and Steam provider. Kind filtering is implemented as a required canonical Workshop tag and a local post-filter, so existing items must carry the exact type tag; the code change does not establish that all published items do. A one-time-looking migration helper seeds an empty legacy `default` composition from the selected Packagepack but retains the legacy `default` identity, so it does not by itself solve the product-level duplicate-default/selection model. The cross-repository hunk review records these limits alongside the source links.

## Semantic IDE workbench and service-owned authoring (October 23, 2026)

The language-server boundary was built in the shared Vapor service just before the GUI workbench matured. [`92ab2b9b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/92ab2b9b075a3d52976b9ce5e2ec99ea4d0278a2) adds a per-client managed Rust Analyzer process and protocol-routed start/stop and LSP messages; [`60ff4eee`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/60ff4eee92a02f768d14625a51b77e3eee385027) then changes toolchain discovery to use the source workspace selected in the IDE, rather than the service process's installed-app working directory. The source includes bounded message queues and generation checks. Stop kills and waits for the direct child; it does not show an LSP shutdown/exit exchange, process-tree cleanup, or joins for the worker threads. These omissions are source-confirmed, while descendant or thread leakage is not established without runtime evidence. The GUI-side request extraction described below is therefore a client of an existing service path, not the whole implementation.

The protocol's later typed addition is intentionally narrower than “Vapor speaks typed LSP”: [`4fe3ab21`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/4fe3ab2121b81c4eaeb62effaf16ac298607d6da) introduces a bounded decoder for `textDocument/publishDiagnostics`, while preserving other JSON-RPC messages as generic values. Current code still applies document-version freshness only when a version is present. Thus the history has three separate steps—service-owned process/transport, IDE-owned request/edit semantics, then a shared typed diagnostic projection—not one completed LSP abstraction. The precise limits are recorded in the [Oct 23 IDE review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-23--lsp-edits-gain-explicit-safety-rails-the-ide-grows-into-a-separate-subsystem).

That same [`4fe3ab21`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/4fe3ab2121b81c4eaeb62effaf16ac298607d6da) also creates the first shared `SemanticObject` DTO. It is later re-exported by GUI core, where [`e30cdac`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/e30cdac915397f95107eff63f2f20e5402a034bb) introduces the bounded document index and Rust/Rhai/TOML/XML adapters, followed by [`16df77e`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/16df77eadc55967bedbe288f05933d940b26f258), which expands local Rust projections. This chronology connects the owner's wish for addressable objects to real code, while preserving an important boundary: the shared DTO standardizes shape and revision-scoped navigation, not the underlying language/content semantics. See the [current model finding](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#the-semantic-object-is-a-shared-wire-shape-not-yet-a-shared-semantic-authority).

The October 23 sequence is a notable transition from “IDE as editor” toward “IDE as semantic workbench.” In `Vapor-GUI`, commit [`e30cdac9`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/e30cdac915397f95107eff63f2f20e5402a034bb) introduces a bounded, versioned semantic index and distinct projections for Rust, Vapor TOML, XML and Rhai. It adds Structure/Inspector navigation and structured Problems while retaining the original files as authoritative. The projections have different implementations and limits: Rust uses `syn`, Rhai a custom declaration tokenizer, with format-specific TOML/XML parsers. This is a shared *object model*, not evidence of one shared parser or complete semantic coverage. The commit documentation explicitly leaves broader LSP support and external dependency source editing under development.

The final same-day Rhai diagnostic change, [`972a3f60`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc), adds a regression case with an astral Unicode character before a syntax error. It covers conversion from Rhai parser character positions to byte spans and the IDE's UTF-16 columns; it adds test coverage without changing the mapping implementation. The test was not run for this historical review.

Later that morning, Vapor commit [`868bbc1d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/868bbc1d28d89beb46a6e2ae7299c8ba533e5f76) puts one concrete structural edit behind the client service: create a canonical Rust module, validate Cargo `src` placement/syntax/current file fingerprint, then update the parent and create the module. `Vapor-GUI/320541c3` adds the IDE dialog and applies the returned parent/child contents and fingerprints to its document model. Ten minutes after the initial service implementation, [`57430651`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/574306517d60d6be7f165481881fa85c373d1d51) replaces a free-form module-name string and duplicated allowlist/docs with a shared typed `CanonicalRustModuleKind` enum. The synchronized `Vapor-Client` commits propagate the operation into the multi-workspace checkout.

**What changed architecturally:** a semantic representation is now shared across views, and at least one file-creating action follows the intended direction of UI → client protocol/service → application filesystem operation → typed result → updated UI model. This is a more substantive ownership boundary than letting the IDE write arbitrary files itself.

**What the evidence does not establish:** that all Rust source organization rules are enforced, that existing source is classified/migrated, that semantic adapters are reusable outside the GUI, or that “canonical modules” understand Rust visibility and all valid workspace arrangements. The service action is opt-in and narrow; it scaffolds one of nine module kinds. The GUI also contains domain-specific parsing and Rust-item template operations. Neither repository diffs nor focused tests reviewed here prove end-to-end IDE runtime behavior. The fuller hunk analysis is in the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

Other Oct 23 commits refine the distinction between fast local outlines and workspace-language intelligence: Rust Analyzer requests are extracted into their own IDE module; Rhai syntax checking advances from delimiter heuristics to bounded parser compilation without script evaluation; and a shared result-publication helper rejects stale local diagnostics. The IDE also adds “New Vapor content,” with one content-creation action for every selected `ContentKind`. The backend is more differentiated than that UI suggests: its generic scaffold returns metadata-only output for the four Pack kinds and Rust/Cargo output for the six implementation kinds. However, the generated Rust contract is inconsistent across creation paths. `scaffold_content_project` gives Engine a binary-only scaffold, while `init_basic_content` creates an Engine Cargo package with both `src/lib.rs` and `src/main.rs`; the latter is not a Pack and has a separate “basic workspace” entry point. In both paths, Packagepack is metadata-only; this code does not build the Packagepack-owned executable described in the owner’s target. The UI’s one form still hides the distinction between authoring a manifest composition and authoring implementation code. These are chronological implementation steps, not a final statement of the desired authoring design.

The late-morning service changes make two pieces of that work less GUI-owned. `1a5796a1` gives diagnostics a shared scope/domain/context record with backward-compatible deserialization; Cargo and Rust Analyzer begin to populate selected fields, but the producers leave workspace/semantic identity/operation linkage incomplete. `Vapor-GUI/96314884` projects those available context fields into console records and adds domain/scope selectors, completing the visible bridge for values that exist without inventing the missing values. `4fe3ab21` carries structured Cargo diagnostics and launched-composition output through operation events, and tags requests using executable-name inference. This improves the service’s ability to explain where work and errors came from, while leaving attribution dependent on binary naming and context still sparse. `868bbc1d` then moves canonical Rust module creation behind a typed service action; `57430651` centralizes its nine module categories and starter docs. The operation validates the selected Cargo source parent and protects against a stale editor buffer, but only scaffolds an empty module—it does not classify or reorganize an existing crate. Its operation is currently assigned the `Building` phase alongside ordinary save/create-file actions, showing that the new operation-phase vocabulary still groups semantically different work together. These source changes are evidence of a functional path being assembled, not confirmation of a completed or running IDE.

The Oct 22–23 Studio console sequence also directly addresses earlier layout/performance complaints in source: it introduces the docked operation console, separates Problems from Console, replaces the first per-frame Problems scan with a history-revision cache, reuses the shared indexed record view, and permits a 140–520 px expanded dock. That is a measurable implementation change, but no runtime capture here establishes that sizing, virtualization or readability now feels right at real workloads or on Windows.

The Oct 21–23 frontend audit closes one source-level gap left open in the first Workshop/console summary. Both Launcher and Studio pass a typed `ContentKind` through the common service action; Steam publishing writes the canonical kind tag, and Steam search requires and post-filters that same tag. Consequently the implementation is coherent for items carrying the expected metadata, while actual Workshop coverage remains dependent on existing records being tagged consistently. Current tests exercise local matching and fixture data, not Steam's public index or the published catalog, so the reported live filter failure is still unexplained. The shared console is likewise more limited than a unified F2/Vapor command surface: Vapor frontends share structured records and indexed rendering, but game command execution, Rhai editor tokenization, and CLI/GUI input remain separate. See the [cross-frontend hunk review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

The local Vapor checkout also contains an untracked Oct 24 content-graph spec and task plan at commit base `5743065`. The proposal preserves the ten-kind vocabulary, distinguishes manifest Packs from implementation Content, and sequences relationship semantics, selection-aware resolution, pack alternatives, Packagepack source/runtime projections, and examples. It is valuable evidence of the current design direction but is not a committed decision or implementation. The source cross-check finds real precursors—required Engine/Game slots, Engine-vs-Enginepack and Game-vs-Gamepack choice groups, optional dependencies, recursive highest-matching-version selection, and separate runtime conflict checks—but those rules live across string relationships, fixed validators and install records rather than one resolver contract. It also finds that authoring can accept an EngineMod/GameMod/ExtensionMod without its required target even though later graph validation rejects that structure; non-Pack kind restrictions are not rechecked uniformly, and Pack cardinality is applied at the selected root rather than to each nested Pack. Generic feature/alternative selection and conflict-aware catalog solving are not yet represented. The Packagepack release/source provenance question remains open: Packs must stay manifests while an editable source closure and executable are exposed under a coherent release identity. See the [Oct 24 proposal review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-24-local-wip-the-content-graph-model-becomes-an-ordered-implementation-proposal).

The Oct 23 CLI follow-up (`Vapor-CLI/a09c49c5`) adds each operation event’s origin and optional composition ID to its rendered record, so CLI output can participate in the same provenance filters. This is a presentation of service-provided metadata, not an independent origin detector; if the Client stamps the wrong origin or omits the composition, the CLI preserves that omission.

Follow-ups link that authoring surface to registered local source projects: semantic manifest references can open the referenced source manifest; a dependency picker filters the registered projects through the current kind-compatibility predicate and pins their listed versions; workspace-symbol navigation tries to resolve a unique current semantic object rather than blindly selecting an old range; and workspace switching clears much of the pending navigation/diagnostic state. The reset is incomplete: current source retains Inspector hover/reference results across the switch. This reduces some fragmentation, while leaving the type predicate narrower than the owner’s full relationship/cardinality model and keeping advanced free-form selectors available. The incomplete reset is source-reviewed in the [semantic diff ledger](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

At the backend, this one action does branch on kind: the four Packs produce metadata-only projects with no Cargo workspace member. In the generic `scaffold_content_project` path, Engine is scaffolded as a binary; Game and three mod kinds as `rlib`+`cdylib`; Crate as `rlib`+`staticlib`. A different helper, `init_basic_content`, writes a basic Engine project with both a `lib.rs` and `main.rs` (and a Game library), so the Engine output policy is not uniform across authoring paths. These are real scaffold contracts from the inspected source, while the owner’s target is prebuilt reusable Engine/Game/mod libraries linked into a Packagepack-owned executable. The basic template does not itself add a Packagepack Cargo target, and neither path proves a completed package build. These are skeletal outputs, not proof of the final build architecture; the reason for the differing Engine shapes is undocumented in this slice.

The canonical-module response is then handled by both the IDE and Studio against their respective editor models. The IDE opens the returned child file directly and indexes it; Studio reconciles the service-returned parent baseline with its live buffer and opens the child. Thus the file operation is shared, while document-buffer synchronization remains implemented separately in each frontend. This distinction matters to the later goal of one semantic authoring core: a shared service API alone does not make editor-state behavior shared.

### October 20 — runtime deployment and app-release staging grow separate promotion paths

The October 20 provider changes also left two promotion owners at the same runtime boundary. [`d0cc4ba`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/d0cc4bae6bcf39a9cd10e28304b91a569ceb484c) added the target-aware workspace/package promotion module. Later [`f9f129e`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9f129ee0413bf53fafc371690f5c0b8f098861b) consolidated build output roots in the broader application-release path, which retained its own artifact promotion loop. Their current replacements differ in whether a failed final rename can remove the old executable; see the [latest source comparison](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--runtime-promotion-has-parallel-writers-with-different-replacement-guarantees). This does not show that either path failed during actual Steam or local deployment.

### October 20 — documentation gets a generated bundle and remote publication path

Platform Server [`40a7c57`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/40a7c57bac1872cf24ddbdb34758177c0d19997b) replaces a fixed docs landing-page list with a generator over book metadata and Markdown guide files.
