The source roots remain deliberately curated, but every Markdown guide in its CLI docs subtree is flattened into one list; the generator has no audience/status hierarchy. The subsequent [`01ee1b7`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/01ee1b7e4ff197701d9d302742ef3500303aab77) restores missing docs service configuration during deploy; [`647f14c`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/647f14cc4baa517c624a3006f6971f1bb9560632) changes publication to SCP a public bundle, then load the token and POST from the VPS, allowing sudo to prompt through SSH. The owner later confirmed a 412-file bundle upload succeeded. The detailed review finds a key limit: when mdBook is unavailable, the bundle builder publishes Markdown source/summary links, while the server only serves static files. So the transport path worked, but that alone does not prove a readable rendered book. The upload test mocks SSH/SCP and token placement; it does not exercise the real VPS or rendered site. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

The Client provider separately grew a local Rustdoc pipeline: managed Cargo builds docs for discovered Cargo projects, then installs the result under the local Vapor docs tree. Discovery currently opts every Cargo workspace into this path. Packaging and normal deployment can trigger this compile, while public docs publication builds a curated authored-book bundle without including Rustdoc. This distinction helps explain some explicit build work, but does not establish the cause of any reported Studio startup compile. The current review traces the [Rustdoc and authored-doc split](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--installed-rustdoc-and-public-docs-are-separate-products); those findings were not runtime-verified.

Server auto-deploy checks the Platform Server repo on a five-minute timer, but this does not regenerate or publish Client docs: that uses a distinct bundle/upload command. The root README also still describes a four-service topology after Registry has joined the manifest and deploy scripts. This is a useful example of why “server deployment works” and “docs are current” are separate state claims.

The docs server's staged replacement protects the previous tree if promotion fails, but it moves `current/` aside before placing the replacement, leaving a brief source-visible gap for reads; a late cleanup failure can also report an error after the replacement is live. No concurrent request was reproduced.

The checked-in VPS deployment-status file remains dated July 25 and reports 410 files, whereas the owner-provided Oct 20 upload result reports 412. The later successful response establishes that bundle was accepted at that moment; the checked-in status did not advance to record it, so it cannot prove what is live now.

### October 21 — CLI composition lifecycle becomes service-backed

Vapor-CLI [`061eb7ba`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/061eb7baf22139c815898196ae7a5572d1aa1aab) adds typed `composition list`, `install`, `verify`, `repair`, `update`, and `launch` operations. Lifecycle commands send typed composition actions through the shared Client service; listing reads the latest service snapshot and marks its active selection. `client launch play` is redefined as an alias for the player Launcher, with explicit composition launch moved to its own command. The list can show “not checked” after a service restart because it does not itself verify content. No command was run during this source review. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-21--cli-gains-explicit-composition-lifecycle-commands).

### October 22 — Registry is assigned canonical Workshop catalog authority

Platform Server commit [`d02a0c6a`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/d02a0c6acf083a00f06d62b35cff49852ed3cab1) accepts a higher-level ownership split: Registry is intended to own Vapor content types/identities, Workshop-item bindings, discovery metadata, and version/channel records; Identity remains the authority for people and roles and supplies authorization facts; Steam remains the distribution transport, with tags treated only as hints. This is an important shift from the earlier Registry service, whose concrete implementation reconstructs first-party source repositories and ecosystem topology.

The Registry source history makes that earlier purpose concrete: its September 7 seed includes only provider/repository/ecosystem tables and read routes; September 12 renames provider records but briefly leaves obsolete `Vapor-Root`/`Vapor-Server-Root` checkout paths; September 15 adds Loo-Cast and fixes the root path set. The initial service commits also tracked a compiled `target/` tree, which the September 7 `7f5fb1e` cleanup removes and replaces with a `target/` ignore rule. That build-output accident is historical repository hygiene evidence, not part of Registry's present service contract.

This commit changes documentation only. At the current Platform Server revision `a98770ad`, Registry schema v1 still stores provider accounts, repositories, ecosystems, and their membership; its routes remain public health/status and ecosystem/provider-account reads. No Workshop catalog, publication write route, or Identity authorization integration is present. Identity does expose sessions and role administration, but no Registry-specific authorization-check contract is visible in its current routes. The accepted semantic boundary therefore precedes its enforcement: it is a design decision, not a deployed capability. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-22--accepted-workshop-authority-boundary-implementation-still-topology-only).

### October 22 — Steam Play begins launching the persistent selection

`Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/c6e178fa` changes the no-argument Steam Play path from `vapor launch default` to `vapor launch selected`, aligning the executable route with the owner-approved persistent composition selection. The CLI implementation confirms that `default` and `selected` currently reach the same selected-composition path; `default` is a compatibility spelling. The source therefore implements a meaningful product semantics change, while the Entrypoint README and some Vapor/CLI book pages still describe `default` as the app-manifest default composition. This is a confirmed cross-repository documentation mismatch. No Steam launch was run as part of this historical review. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-22--steam-direct-launch-follows-the-persistent-selection-reference-docs-lag).

This endpoint followed a week of reversals in the installed-product contract. On October 14, commits `16c605a` and `79c8f0f` first routed Steam launches through Studio and then through Vapor-GUI; October 18–19 added shared-service startup; October 21 (`43b2ba8`) made the default Steam option launch the game directly, while `332e8c5` added required first-launch setup and the IDE got its own route; October 22 (`c6e178f`) switched the direct path from manifest “default” to the durable selected composition. The current source reflects the resulting two-entrypoint product intent (direct Play versus a chooser), but it remains an installed-App host adapter with separate Linux/Windows terminal implementations and an append-only per-App log; it is not itself proof that Steam launch-option configuration or either target's published depot matches the source. See the [detailed Entrypoint analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--steam-entrypoint-is-a-real-host-router-not-just-a-launch-string-shim).

### October 22 — workflow tiers and concurrent operations enter the Client service

Vapor commit [`3b692e7d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/3b692e7d8f89d6b07f51dcb2befd8698e8ed9b16) adds progressive `Player`/`Composer`/`Developer` profiles and a service `OperationRegistry` that allows independent jobs while rejecting conflicting resource reservations. The profiles classify navigation and name local tool/external authority prerequisites; they are not themselves authorization. Resource ownership is partly mapped from string domain/action pairs, and the service returns a retryable conflict rather than owning a general queued-work scheduler. [`f2058b8b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f2058b87818f090bf59c06ef1489e2b99750391c) then tracks each accepted operation through its originating service request. This is a substantive move away from one global operation lock, but the concurrency contract and queue behavior are not yet uniform across frontends. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-22--progressive-workflow-labels-and-resource-aware-concurrency-are-introduced).

The October 18 [`f9e8b13`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9e8b135f3991f4eac43de6da964d0874504cde4) extraction is the transition from product-local operation ownership to a shared local-client architecture: protocol, client transport, service process, provider/domain/application crates and persistence are introduced together. The October 19 [`d7e21dc`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/d7e21dc332a8b8874541eeb5ca0a4fffeeb655d0) follow-up moves service operations behind that boundary and removes the old 2,704-line Core CLI. Later changes add bounded startup/readiness, cross-platform endpoint locks, output/client limits, origin-aware operations, and resource-key concurrency; this culminates in the present service behavior summarized in the [current-state cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#the-local-vapor-client-service-implements-the-shared-backend-model-across-frontends). The design's current limits are also explicit: service conflicts reject rather than queue; the service idles out after 15 seconds; path-derived endpoint identity is not stable across moved installations. This timeline records the sequence and intent signals, not proof that startup and reconnect work on every platform.

### October 22 — source content is deliberately removed from the acquired Library projection

The October 18 shared Client extraction (`f9e8b13`) introduced one local catalog with `Workspace`, `Cache` and `Installed` locations merged by exact content identity. Its catalog kind was already a string, so the shared service/domain boundary began with weaker typing than `vapor_content::ContentKind`. On October 22, `3b692e7` changed the contract: `discover_content_catalog` became `discover_local_content_catalog`, Workspace enumeration was removed, and the docs now call authored source a separate workspace-discovery surface. This clarified that player Library should show acquired content rather than source projects, but separated projections instead of keeping source/acquired/installed observations under one typed identity with workflow-specific views. It is an important product boundary decision and an implementation trade-off, not simply a regression; the latest-state review records the remaining seam. See [catalog history and current boundary](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-ten-kind-vocabulary-loses-semantic-resolution-at-the-client-catalog-boundary).

### October 22 — shared operation output and a limited service-backed console

Vapor [`8e3d1bac`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/8e3d1bac841d05faacbca9ce3309ac71277c6bf9) adds shared console records/tokenization, a small typed command parser, and structured operation output with origin/action/process/severity fields; managed Rustup output now reaches the operation stream after terminal control sequences are stripped and output size is bounded. `Vapor-GUI/dab912cd` wires the model into IDE and Launcher views, while `Vapor-Studio/13b829df` docks it in Studio and sends its supported commands through the Client service. The resulting command vocabulary is intentionally much smaller than the CLI, and the game F2 console/Rhai paths remain separate. This is foundational sharing, not the fully unified in-game/IDE/CLI console envisioned by the owner. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-22--a-shared-vapor-console-model-reaches-studio-and-ide-but-not-the-game-f2-console).

### October 22 — Auto-Install becomes Packagepack-owned and subscription-aware

Vapor [`25aeced4`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/25aeced4d8be2f2ecf05b531f11760649d559919) changes dependency descriptions into catalog records and persists Packagepack owner IDs plus whether the user explicitly chose an Auto-Install value. A subscribed/acquired Packagepack can enable default dependency management; a user opt-out survives owner changes. Unsubscribing the root releases its dependency owners, and cleanup can remove unused local items and invoke Steam unsubscription. [`28cc768c`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/28cc768c8d31c03f57c32ea00e59d0ac5366e87d) then establishes installed Packagepack compositions as a second owner, preserving their resolved graph after Steam unsubscribe. This is the first clear code expression of the owner’s distinction between subscribed pack ownership and installed playable composition ownership. The catalog dependency relationship and content kind remain string-valued in this model, and no external Steam/filesystem lifecycle was executed during review. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-22--packagepack-owned-auto-install-begins-as-a-persisted-lifecycle-graph).

### October 22 — managed toolchains distinguish Windows runtime and Rustup host triples

Vapor [`1c92bd78`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/1c92bd7822949e8823ac279245135c2fadf5109c) maps the app's Windows GNU-LLVM runtime triple to Rustup's Windows MSVC host triple, resolving a host-vs-target identity mismatch that surfaced as “host not supported.” A focused test checks the mapping, but does not install a target toolchain or link an artifact. Later [`2897a810`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/2897a810a5d002bd81f411ab772603a76d53cd48) appends existing Unix system utility directories to managed Cargo subprocess paths so builds can find host tools. This is an intentional fallback to OS-provided executables; it does not change the Rust toolchain pin. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-22--windows-gnu-llvm-runtime-is-separated-from-the-rustup-host-identity).

### October 22 — installed app identity is separated from source-workspace identity

The manifest API names distinct markers for an installed app (`App.vapor.toml`), app source (`App-Source.vapor.toml`), ordinary source workspaces (`Workspace.vapor.toml`), and Registry checkouts. `InstallationPaths` requires the installed app marker; source-root discovery deliberately accepts the source/workspace/Registry markers and excludes the installed-app marker. This makes the Steam depot an installation root, not an implicit Cargo authoring workspace.

Commit [`8259961`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/825996195c054ed2808573ca4bee7e6e4e5a5153) clears a persisted authoring-workspace path when it points at a directory containing `App.vapor.toml` but no `Workspace.vapor.toml`. The added fixture test starts a Linux-configured service in fixture mode and verifies that stale saved value is removed; it does not exercise Windows Installer discovery, live service startup, or toolchain installation. The separate Rust Analyzer change [`60ff4eee`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/60ff4eee92a02f768d14625a51b77e3eee385027e) selects its toolchain from the IDE's source workspace rather than the service's installed-app working directory. Together these changes address related root-selection hazards, but the source evidence does not prove the reported Windows Installer failure is fully resolved. See the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-22-installed-app-roots-and-source-workspaces-have-distinct-markers).

### October 23 — the IDE becomes a bounded semantic workbench

The Vapor-GUI series grows from a raw-file editor into an IDE with syntax-derived semantic objects, Rust Analyzer navigation/refactoring, typed canonical Rust-module creation, Rhai parse diagnostics, content-manifest navigation, and structured Problems/Console views. Workspace edits are constrained to previewable changes in already-open files inside the selected workspace; direct command actions and filesystem operations from the language server are refused. This is meaningful editor safety and semantic navigation, while still leaving different sources of truth—local syntax projections, Rust Analyzer, Cargo, Vapor content metadata—as separate authorities. The detailed source findings and limits are in the [Oct 23 IDE review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-23--lsp-edits-gain-explicit-safety-rails-the-ide-grows-into-a-separate-subsystem). No compile, tests, LSP session, or UI run was performed for this historical review.

The local Rust outline is intentionally only a fast syntax projection: it recognizes a selected subset of Rust items, infers some domain labels from filenames and derive-token names, and silently omits unsupported syntax. Rust Analyzer supplies a later, separate symbol tree. Canonical file placement is reported as a warning rather than enforced. These distinctions matter because the IDE is beginning to model declarations as selectable objects, but those labels are not yet compiler-resolved identities or build rules. The detailed coverage limits and affected source locations are in the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-23--lsp-edits-gain-explicit-safety-rails-the-ide-grows-into-a-separate-subsystem).

The other adapters share the object envelope, not one semantic depth: TOML displays field paths and value types/counts, XML displays element and attribute names without text/value content, and Rhai displays functions/bindings without runtime meaning or nested local-scope structure. These domain distinctions are part of the new IDE’s actual behavior and matter before a common inspector can be treated as a common authoring model. Details are in the [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#vapor-guie30cdac9-a-semantic-outline-layer-not-yet-a-semantic-source-of-truth-editor).

The local Rust projection also runs synchronously after editor changes, with a per-document size cap but no incremental or debounced parse shown in this path. A malformed in-progress buffer can temporarily clear the outline. No responsiveness benchmark or live UI test was run, so this is a scaling and feedback limitation identified from source, not an observed freeze.

The file tree adds semantic Rust labels and strict ordering, but is not virtualized. Filtering expands matching directories and creates labels against the workspace-wide Rust path list; source inspection flags a possible large-workspace cost and a duplicate-crate-name label collision, neither measured or reproduced. These are specific remaining IDE concerns, not evidence the recent workbench is unusable.

Rust Analyzer is launched by the Client service per connected frontend, from the toolchain pinned to the selected source workspace; it must already be installed, so language intelligence depends on Developer setup. This avoids tying tool discovery to the installed Steam app root but can duplicate analyzer processes when multiple frontends open the same workspace. The lifecycle and setup boundary are reviewed in detail alongside the IDE and Installer sections.

The same service extraction also leaves a workspace-identity split visible in the Oct 23 tree. The service stores one active `workspace_root` and persists it globally for the local service, while each IDE instance retains its own displayed root. File operations carry only a relative path, so the service resolves them against its latest global root. Snapshots and shared operation output are broadcast to all clients; operation-output diagnostics have no workspace ID, and the IDE stamps its local root onto those received records. Rust Analyzer diagnostics are different: each analyzer is per client, messages return to that client, and the IDE drops a diagnostic URI outside its displayed root. This creates a plausible wrong-project file/operation-diagnostic context when clients differ, without a reproduced incident. It also conflicts with the intended future of multiple independently opened IDE workspaces unless the service gains stable workspace IDs per request or the product explicitly enforces and synchronizes one active workspace. The source-level finding is detailed in the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md).

The same day, [`Vapor-Installer/b3ddcf9`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Installer/commit/b3ddcf9) changes role recovery: an unreadable readiness snapshot no longer hides a role that is known, so the user can still attempt promotion. The source adds tests for that distinction, but they were not run; successful promotion and cross-platform tool installation remain unverified. See the [Installer review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-23--installer-separates-known-role-from-tool-readiness-failure).

## Latest-source review appendix — findings checked October 25–26, 2026

The chronological history above remains ordered by the event or commit dates. This appendix records later source audits and cross-checks; the review date is October 25–26, while dates within each note refer to the historical change being explained.

### October 25 — Engine validation documentation lags the managed toolchain path

At this snapshot, the Engine README still teaches raw `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo check -p spacetime-engine` as its normal structural loop. The instruction dates to the README's first appearance, Loo-Cast `76d1d84` (September 18). October 5–8 edits changed its source map and Celestial Fixture claims but left that validation block untouched. Meanwhile, Vapor CLI gained `fmt`, `check`, `test` and `validate` commands routed through the shared Client service to app-local Cargo; `validate` adds format-check, tests, Clippy and Rustdoc to compilation. This leaves the README anchored to the direct Cargo habit even after Vapor has taken on a managed path. It is one concrete example of an architectural intention arriving in tooling before all its consuming documentation. Platform Server CI/deployment also remains outside the managed path, so the broader toolchain-centralization story is incomplete. Source inspection only; neither the managed commands nor raw Cargo were run for this comparison. See the [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--vapor-owned-validation-exists-but-the-engine-readme-bypasses-it).

### October 25 — Loo-Cast test annotations remain, but their Cargo harnesses are disabled

The current Engine has inline unit-test annotations, including worldgen invariants, while Engine, Game and Packagepack manifests disable automatic test discovery and their library/binary test harnesses. This means current `vapor validate` reaches a Cargo test command but does not execute these annotations under the present manifest configuration. The tests remain valuable as evidence of intended invariants, but the repository should not be described as having active regression coverage for them. This configuration nuance matters when reading the October cleanup's test deletions and later source additions: the count of test functions does not equal tests that validate a build. No test command was run here. See the [full current-state finding](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--loo-cast-has-test-code-but-disables-its-test-harnesses).

The state began with the October 5 `e987230` consolidation: it disabled Cargo test targets and doctests while deleting several existing test modules. Later commits added new `#[test]` functions without turning the targets back on. On October 17, the former Packagepack library's disabled test harness became a disabled binary test harness. Thus this is a deliberate test-execution policy that later source additions did not consistently account for—not merely a test suite that nobody has run yet.

### October 25 — the Game artifact is distinct, but Game implementation remains in Engine

The October 17 Packagepack executable conversion made the product composition statically link `spacetime-engine` and `loo-cast-game`, but source ownership remains mixed: the Game crate's installer calls `spacetime_engine::game::LooCastGamePlugin`, while the Engine's `game` subtree contains substantial game implementation alongside modules that describe themselves as generic or shared. The latest Git-tracked inventory is 158 Rust files/20,226 lines, not a semantic classification of every file. The Game adapter previously documented this as temporary housing; the commit that introduced the Packagepack binary removed that caveat but did not relocate implementation. This changes the reader's impression without changing the underlying ownership boundary. Current manifests and code prove separate Rust artifacts and explicit local Cargo edges; they do not prove the Vapor content graph generates those edges or that an independently acquired Game library can be composed by another Packagepack. A direct Engine-physics-to-Game-schedule reference also crosses back against the Engine root's own dependency rule. See the [detailed latest-state source and limits](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-enginegame-split-is-a-package-label-boundary-not-yet-a-source-or-dependency-boundary). The same October 17 diff deletes the Engine `main.rs` and creates the Packagepack executable without changing the existing `[[run]]` package/binary selection; Oct 20 profile/target changes leave it stale. See the [run-path finding](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-checked-in-default-vapor-run-configuration-names-a-removed-engine-binary).

### October 25 — current-tree service/IDE race found during history cross-check

This is a source-tree observation, not a new commit. `WorkspaceAction::Open` immediately replaces the one service-wide root and is handled outside the operation registry. A concurrent save/create/module action captures the old root, writes under it, then has its completion rejected if the active root changed while it ran. Because the completion handler constructs the file-result event only after this root check, the write can succeed on disk while the initiating editor receives a failed operation and no reconciliation result. Operation diagnostics are broadcast to all authenticated clients, and the IDE fills missing workspace context from its own currently open root; another IDE can label the same diagnostic with the wrong project. The root-switch UI clears documents and many semantic views but retains Rust Analyzer hover text and references, which the Inspector continues displaying. A narrow related mismatch exists for `RunConfiguration`: it executes the explicit root in its request, but reserves the service’s selected-root key, so CLI current-directory runs can be serialized under the wrong workspace when those roots differ. The service rejects resource conflicts, while the IDE disables most workspace controls behind one pending slot and lets console commands use a separate request path; neither path queues a blocked action in one shared scheduler. These are source-confirmed possible states; no concurrent-client runtime reproduction was performed. The immediate design implication is that immutable workspace identity must travel with each operation, its reservation, diagnostics, file result and completion; changing one client’s selected project must not rewrite another operation’s context. The separate [detailed service/IDE review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--workspace-switching-can-invalidate-completed-edits-after-they-write) traces the exact checks and consequences.

The same source snapshot makes the reported service process tail more specific: the local singleton stays alive while a client or operation remains active, then exits after a 15-second idle grace. Short invocations can therefore leave a bounded service process behind; this source does not establish the duration of the user’s observed process list. The Windows spawn path includes `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`, stderr log routing, and child cleanup on startup failure, but no Windows process run was performed. See the [service-lifetime trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--shared-service-lifetime-is-intentionally-idle-not-invocation-scoped).

An exact-version audit of the Packagepack Auto-Install ownership pass found that its traversal keys visited roots and required dependencies only by stable ID, discarding Packagepack root versions and dependency version requirements. It then chooses the first cached catalog row for an owned ID. The existing test covers required/optional edges with one version per ID. This is a possible wrong-owner/cleanup path when multiple versions exist, not a reproduced data-loss event. The detailed [October 25 ownership trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--auto-install-ownership-traversal-drops-exact-versions) follows the edge from composition state through subscription cleanup.

The same current-tree review found an authored-conflict projection gap. Source manifests and deployed artifacts preserve `conflicts`, and both install planning and launch validation check them, but the Library projection emits an empty `CatalogContent.conflicts` for cached and installed items. That field currently represents disagreements between duplicate local observations, so it is not interchangeable with authored incompatibility. Composition eligibility and Auto-Install can consequently treat an authored-conflicting artifact as clean; setup's install plan then blocks the conflict before materialization, while the launcher checks it again. The generic resolver separately omits optional edges and selects the highest satisfying version independently per edge, with global unification/backtracking explicitly deferred; the install planner catches multiple versions of one ID before install. This is a confirmed source-contract mismatch with the desired richer dependency model, not a reproduced user incident. See [the detailed October 25 conflict/resolution review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--authored-content-conflicts-disappear-from-the-library-projection).

The package boundary is similarly flatter than the intended vocabulary. The same authored record accepts binary and library payloads for any content kind, and generic deployment copies each authored project tree before adding any declared payloads. The code does not enforce “Packagepack is the executable root; other packs are manifest-only” as a kind-specific packaging rule. The SteamCMD VDF points `contentfolder` at that staged output, so its copied source files are included in the upload input; no remote upload was performed during this review. The exclusion-list copier also admits any non-excluded file from a project tree, a conditional publication-hygiene risk. This is a verified implementation mismatch with Leslie’s stated model. The [detailed packaging trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--pack-and-code-artifacts-share-an-unrestricted-packaging-path) records the exact boundary.

The same Auto-Install review found an asymmetric state transition in the real Client service. Turning Auto-Install off subscribes the item first and persists the manual-retention choice after that succeeds. Turning it on is accepted as a background operation, but the worker routes it to an application handler that explicitly rejects policy changes; the service completion code persists only the off transition. The fixture-mode path updates the policy directly, so fixture success does not establish real-service success. This is a confirmed current-source defect, not a Steam/UI reproduction. See the [exact dispatch trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--enabling-auto-install-has-no-successful-real-service-path).

The October 21–22 service update also separates file verification from host launch readiness. It reports a verified composition as `OutOfDate` when its Packagepack lacks a ready executable for the current runtime target, then lets explicit Update refresh Workshop-backed members and reinstall the root so it can select a target build. This addresses the Windows missing-`gnullvm` executable state in source; the owner later reported a successful Windows launch for the deployed build. The refresh path is not a guarantee for all content targets, and the “update required” label currently wraps any launch-plan error, including some manifest/configuration failures. Steam acquisition and launch were not independently run in this history review. The [host-readiness trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-2122--host-specific-verification-becomes-an-explicit-composition-update) records the distinction and verification boundary.

### October 25 — startup, snapshots and Library refresh repeat filesystem work

The current service creates its persistent session synchronously on the first authenticated connection. Before sending the initial snapshot, it discovers the installed Vapor root and ensures the canonical Superworkspace, defaulting to `~/Vapor`. That routine can create/adopt the directory and manifest and load immediate Container Repo / Workspace entries and their declared source submodules; it does not recursively search arbitrary descendants or invoke Git/network in the inspected path. The subsequent Library refresh is a background operation, but it reports progress only before and after the full scan. Its current projection reloads and reparses the complete app-owned content index once per cached/installed artifact while also reading each artifact manifest, giving a source-derived superlinear scaling risk as the index grows. In addition, every client snapshot rediscovers that Superworkspace from disk; ordinary actions create a response snapshot and another broadcast snapshot, both on the service loop. That repeats workspace-manifest I/O and can delay other requests if the tree or storage is slow. This live-discovery-inside-snapshot design first appears in the Oct 18 shared-service extraction, then remains in the Oct 19 operation migration. None of these paths was timed or tied conclusively to the reported hang. Details and exact source anchors are in the [October 25 service bootstrap/snapshot/refresh review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--startup-snapshots-and-library-refresh-repeat-filesystem-work).

### October 25 — source management remains split across three lifecycles

The current snapshot exposes three adjacent but non-equivalent source paths: Vapor CLI indexes and opens authored source, with `source sync` still a printed stub; Installer exposes one-source preset-based clone; Studio calls the shared Client service for Registry-backed discovery and repository acquisition. Roadmap 11 proposes a unified shell lifecycle (`source setup/acquire/remove/teardown`) and marks much of it complete, but the root roadmap omits chapter 11 and still points to glossary migration as active. Studio has no multi-select presentation in the inspected panel, source removal/teardown is not the same as CLI index removal, Git remains a host prerequisite, and automatic IDE reconciliation is not in the acquisition path. This is a current-state finding, not a historical commit claim; exact command boundaries and links are in the [October 25 semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--roadmap-11-spans-multiple-still-disconnected-source-workflows).

#### Source lifecycle lineage — July to October

The present split has a traceable history rather than being a single recent regression:

- **July 18, [`Vapor-Installer/b0e9e78`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Installer/commit/b0e9e78):** the first bootstrap tool bundled app-local Git alongside SteamCMD and source-oriented bootstrap state. Two days later, **[`1404db3`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Installer/commit/1404db3a17640a26d0047b97e7edf8b6d2f3ebcf) explicitly removes Git from player bootstrap** (558 deletions across ten files). This preserves a simple player install but creates a developer-source prerequisite boundary: Git must come from somewhere else.
- **July 28, [`Vapor-Installer/6603574`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Installer/commit/6603574):** workflows move into compiled Rust control surfaces, while shared app-root tool implementations still supply explicit `source status` and one-at-a-time `source clone`. The current RustRover setup offers individual clone actions for four preset repositories; the implementation rejects bulk clone.
- **September 15, [`Vapor/46a92d1`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/46a92d1f6b945cc3eb09d0f31334e30e82789773):** Roadmap 11 is changed from an uncompleted configurable setup/acquisition plan to “automatic canonical root” plus an `acquire first-party-all` normal onboarding path; many workflow items are checked complete. It simultaneously retains the explicit clean-machine caveat that Composer-or-higher promotion requires Git on PATH. The contradiction is already visible in that document: bulk first-party acquisition is marked done while Git provisioning is explicitly not done.
- **October 14–19, [`Vapor/f9e8b13`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9e8b135f3991f4eac43de6da964d0874504cde4) and [`Vapor-Installer/2547b88`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Installer/commit/2547b88):** the Client service becomes the CLI's source-index/open authority; Installer removes its duplicate Client-service bootstrap. These changes do not replace its older first-party source clone path with the proposed Registry-backed `source acquire` lifecycle.
- **October 22 onward:** the main CLI's `source` family provides source init/index/open/forget/repair, while Installer still exposes direct superworkspace creation and one-source clone. This produces two separate “source” vocabularies: local authoring/indexing and first-party repo acquisition. Neither is the unified selector/ownership lifecycle described by Roadmap 11.

This sequence reveals a recurring boundary reversal: Git was initially treated as player-installable bootstrap, then deliberately removed from Player mode, while later owner-facing planning still assumed a clean machine could use Composer acquisition after role promotion. The unresolved product decision is whether Git becomes a Vapor-managed developer capability, is declared/checked as a prerequisite, or is replaced by an acquisition provider that does not require host Git. Current source establishes the gap; this report does not choose that policy.

Clarification to the July–October source lifecycle trace: Installer documents `--super-workspace PATH` as required for `source clone`, but the shared helper also accepts omitted root by reading `VAPOR_SUPER_WORKSPACE_ROOT` or discovering a `Superworkspace.vapor.toml` above the current directory. This is a distinct fallback from the Client's persisted canonical Superworkspace setting; it does not make Installer source selection use the Client state.

A later source-path check narrows the above chronology: Registry-backed multi-source acquisition is present in the shared Client service and is reachable from Studio's “Vapor source folder” panel. The endpoint comes from the installed ecosystem bootstrap; the service preflights the requested repository set and delegates clone/submodule work to Git. The Installer/RustRover clone workflow is an older parallel path using a hardcoded four-repository preset list. Therefore October did not leave all acquisition Registry-independent; it left two competing source-acquisition paths with different catalog authorities, selector UX and lifecycle completion. The [detailed current-state comparison](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--roadmap-11-spans-multiple-still-disconnected-source-workflows) contains the source anchors and verification limits.

The October 25 first-launch review finds another user-facing consequence of the same split: app-root Player setup receipt, user-data role, and developer-tool readiness are separately computed, but the Installer's continuation button joins them with one gate. It can block a completed Player setup when developer readiness lookup errors, yet fail to require every developer capability for a higher role. The owner-directed first-launch requirement (“setup required before play”) is implemented as an app-root receipt, but “setup complete for selected role” is not represented as one role-specific postcondition. See the [role/setup source trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--installer-role-and-setup-state-do-not-share-one-authority).

The same trace clarifies the scope added by [`Vapor-Installer/2592142`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Installer/commit/259214260b3e1d1f58384638b69ab98cd3b9d136): first-launch setup calls the general `install_installation_for` routine before Player setup and the selected role action. That routine both ensures the canonical `~/Vapor` Superworkspace and writes user command integration, so choosing Player still creates/adopts developer workspace state and changes shell/PATH integration. The commit wires the mandatory setup gate, but does not create a Player-only bootstrap boundary. This is an implementation consequence of the accepted setup path, not evidence that the owner explicitly approved those additional Player-facing side effects.

The gate's state identity also narrows after the Installer closes: the Steam Entrypoint checks only the app-root Player receipt. That receipt is written before any selected higher-role promotion finishes. If promotion fails, direct Play can still pass the EntryPoint gate on a later invocation. This means the historical “required setup before play” decision is enforced as a Player-prerequisite gate, not as successful completion of the selected role. The current-state trace documents the exact route and marks this as source-derived, not runtime-reproduced.

### October 25 — console convergence is still adapter-level

The in-game console has a separate evolutionary line from Vapor's host console. Loo-Cast `7d9af82` on September 27 is the major F2/command rewrite (+730/−133 across three files). `cffbab6` on October 1 adds runtime-variable registration and input-binding commands alongside a much wider game/debug surface (+2,826/−153 across fourteen files). This establishes the game console as a powerful live-world tool whose commands execute against Bevy `World`, not just a generic output pane. `d806e3d` on October 8 then decomposes completion and adjacent engine areas; the F2 facility remains game-owned.

On October 22 Vapor `7ab704b` creates the host-neutral record/history/filter foundation; `8e3d1ba` adds the service command parser and structured operation-output protocol. GUI `ba6fe8c` and `dab912c` reuse the record/view panel in Launcher and authoring modes. Loo-Cast `c070bf3` embeds the shared telemetry record as a payload and aligns Rhai lexical vocabularies. October 23 IDE commits add structured diagnostic context and navigation to this GUI view. This was real cross-product consolidation, but the source shows no transfer of game command registry, ECS dispatch, completion model, tracing transport or transcript history into Vapor Client. The command surfaces remain separate; only selected records, rendering code, and lexical vocabulary overlap. The sequence is deliberately layered: 7ab704b first adds the host-neutral record/filter/history and Rhai token-category core; 8e3d1ba adds quoted-argument tokenization and the service operation-output envelope; 1a5796a adds typed diagnostic context a day later. The final console adapter still turns diagnostic context into string fields, while stripping terminal control sequences and splitting process output into lines. The persisted design asks for consistent semantic records and formatted progress across hosts; that remains a goal rather than a runtime-proven result. See the [source contract review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-shared-console-core-is-semantic-data-not-a-shared-console-runtime).

The October 25 code cross-check adds the concrete limits behind that conclusion: 4,096 queued game records before oldest-entry eviction, a separate unbounded command submission queue, per-update drain/dispatch, 512 game F2 scrollback entries, 4,000 GUI history entries, and GUI visible-row virtualization over a full filtered-index scan. These are source-derived bounds, not profile results. Full rationale and source links are in the [latest console semantic trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#latest-state-console-trace--game-command-runtime-versus-vapor-operation-console).

The design lineage confirms that the incomplete merge is partly a scoped choice and partly unfinished integration. The Oct 22 shared-core spec explicitly preserves host command boundaries and says its first slice does not create one visual widget; its own status leaves live stream comparison open. A second console design specifies one Client-owned extensible typed command catalog, but the implementation is currently a fixed command list with frontend-local parser/dispatch calls, while CLI descriptor reuse is still a stated follow-up. The Oct 23 IDE work adds context-rich diagnostics and navigation, not a shared game/Vapor event feed. The owner's broader request for a reusable egui toolkit and rapid UI preview goes beyond both specs and remains an unplanned workstream. Thus the record layer is delivered, the service command slice is useful, and the full “F2-like console everywhere” ambition remains open. Exact source/doc crosswalk: [design promises versus current implementation](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#design-promises-against-the-october-25-implementation).

#### Roadmap 08 versus the Workshop implementation (October 15–25)

Roadmap 08's “no Workshop implementation” snapshot is older than the current subsystem and was not updated as the implementation landed. On October 15, [`Vapor/379615f`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/379615f37083644551889b3d94f82c7371cc0c67) introduced Steamworks UGC search/subscription operations. October 16 [`aef5d98`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/aef5d98b903f505837dace8fd32c2c4e3b878ac0) added common operation identity/progress and source registration, but the early operation runner did not yet queue behind conflicts. October 19 [`971ab112`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/971ab1126b531a6f79146e652219b54e151c7b2a) added cache staging, identity checks and composition-aware acquisition handling. On October 22, Platform Server [`d02a0c6`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/d02a0c6acf083a00f06d62b35cff49852ed3cab1) recorded the accepted future authority split: Registry owns canonical content/release identity and Steam bindings; Identity authorizes; Steam transports files. By the October 25 snapshot, the first provider/service/client lifecycle exists, but the Registry still has source-topology tables only and content install records remain local Client state. This explains why Roadmap 08's blanket absence claims are stale while its Registry and trust questions remain open. The [current-state reconciliation](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--roadmap-08s-child-statuses-mix-stale-absence-with-still-missing-authority) separates those conclusions.

#### Roadmap 06 versus generated state (June 30–October 25)

The lockfile name has two historical traps. On June 30, [`Vapor/d0fd8773`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/d0fd87730fcfb0f862ceb03c42c422d890b6157b), titled “Add Vapor lockfile,” adds Cargo's dependency `Cargo.lock` for two crates; it is not a Vapor content-selection lock. On July 4, Roadmap 06 asks for generated state and says there is no `Vapor.lock`, no fingerprint, and no durable receipt. By July 10, [`Vapor-CLI/8464f463`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/8464f4632acb5ba38c0d7f9bede5513f1f8a2a0a) adds a 2,193-line content lifecycle containing non-cryptographic tree fingerprints, local installed index/lock/receipt mechanics. The October 18–19 service/domain extraction decomposes much of that into a provider `ContentIndex`, write-only per-content lock copies and operation receipts, while Composition gains a durable exact resolved graph plus an optional graph fingerprint. By October 25, fingerprint/receipt absence is stale, but the general `Vapor.lock` target has not materialized and no unified release/provenance lifecycle replaces it. See the [artifact-by-artifact current-state audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--roadmap-06s-no-fingerprints-or-receipts-claim-is-stale-its-general-lockfile-target-is-still-absent).
### October 23 — semantic visibility becomes guarded Rust authoring

`Vapor-GUI/e30cdac` introduces the semantic-workbench slice: multi-format semantic objects, bounded Rust/TOML/XML/Rhai projections, diagnostics, IDE navigation and a first Rust authoring surface. Subsequent GUI commits `320541c` and `7b8ebf6` add canonical module authoring and a typed module-kind selector. The nested `Vapor/868bbc1` moves module creation behind the shared Client service; it validates the Cargo `src` parent, rejects stale parent fingerprints, writes a conventional module file and updates the parent declaration with rollback of the new file if that second write fails. `Vapor/5743065` centralizes the nine module categories in Client domain. The order matters: semantic visibility preceded UI authoring, which preceded service-owned filesystem mutation.

By the October 25 source snapshot, the IDE also includes tree ordering/display behaviors requested by the owner: ordinary workspace folders before files; alphabetical ordering within detected Cargo crates; `.rs`-less labels; and shortest-unique `mod.rs` labels. The nine-kind scaffold currently applies to discovered Cargo `src` directories rather than a Vapor content/crate role, and some category semantics are explicitly Bevy-specific. Placement rules remain advisory IDE warnings rather than a shared build/service/CI policy. The implementation therefore establishes guarded scaffolding and semantic navigation, but not the broader Vapor-enforced Rust architecture envisioned for managed crate/content types. The owner’s intended scope—every Cargo crate or selected Vapor-managed classes—and framework-specific policy remain open rather than historically settled. See [semantic IDE versus Rust architecture governance](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-semantic-ide-teaches-rust-structure-but-does-not-govern-it-yet) and [latest-state Rust governance cross-check](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#rust-workbench-semantic-visibility-exists-crate-policy-and-authority-do-not).

The accompanying `vapor_gui_core` expansion is also a partial, not terminal, convergence: Launcher and IDE now consume shared console state, editor rendering, panel treatment, severity icons and semantic contracts. The resulting crate is still a small utility/widget layer, while most layout composition remains frontend-local and no preview-gallery workflow was found in the inspected GUI repository. The [current toolkit review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--vapor_gui_core-is-a-useful-seed-not-the-promised-egui-workbench-toolkit) distinguishes delivered reuse from the larger toolkit goal.

Correction to the October 25 snapshot: those product surfaces are not modes of one deployed executable. Cargo declares five binary targets in `vapor_gui`; the Steam Entrypoint resolves Launcher, Studio, IDE, Installer-GUI and chooser as sibling executables, and the Steam provider's staging manifest requires each for Linux and Windows. The stronger coupling is that the five targets share one package, host library and permissive `--mode` router, with product UI crates linked at build time. This is a distinction between executable/process separation and code/service separation; the source establishes the former contract, not successful depot publication or runtime behavior. See [the corrected binary/host analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--gui-products-have-distinct-binaries-but-share-one-host-package-and-overridable-mode-router).

The service lifecycle is shared in runtime intent but has more than one bootstrap owner. Steam Entrypoint pre-starts the service for direct Play, Launcher, Studio, IDE and Shell; Installer is omitted from that pre-start so recovery can open, then its UI connects-or-starts the same local service. Chooser does not need it. The service process stays while a client is connected or an operation is active, then exits after 15 idle seconds; this is not tied to Steam closing. This matters against the owner’s “close when Steam closes” idea and prior reports of lingering processes: source now defines a short idle policy, but only a process trace on Linux/Windows can establish actual shutdown behavior. See [the current launch/service trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--product-launch-images-converge-on-one-short-lived-local-client-service).

Operation output now carries a typed frontend origin, but the service infers it from the executable filename. The current vocabulary has Launcher/Studio/IDE/Installer/CLI/Unknown, no launched Game/Composition identity, and `vapor-gui` defaults to Launcher provenance even though `--mode` is overrideable. That provides useful attribution for ordinary product binaries while leaving the requested game-origin trace outside this protocol. The detailed source path is in the [origin-provenance review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--operation-origin-is-typed-but-inferred-from-the-frontend-executable-name).

### October 25 — the local Client protocol becomes the shared product-state boundary

The latest Client protocol combines domain actions, durable and live snapshots, operation output, semantic IDE data, LSP traffic and telemetry over one local IPC connection. It is strongly typed and versioned, but directly re-exports Client Domain models rather than translating them into independently versioned wire records. Exact version equality is required, and each action receives a complete snapshot followed by a broadcast snapshot. The service caps serialized outbound queues at 40 MiB per client and accepts eight clients; that permits a 320 MiB aggregate queue ceiling, a configured limit rather than measured usage. The extraction began at version 13 on October 18 and reached version 33 by October 23 as SDK/workspace, authoring, console, LSP and diagnostics surfaces converged. This is a significant unification step with an important condition: it serves lockstep product binaries, not independently compatible frontend and service versions. The [source-pinned protocol review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-client-protocol-is-the-product-state-surface-not-a-thin-transport-dto-layer) records the exact boundary and evidence limits.

### October 25 — latest-state cross-check: the common service and Library still expose split ownership

The October 18–23 extraction did create one serialized `ClientSession` shared across connected frontends, with typed background-completion messages and a resource-conflict registry. Re-reading the latest implementation against the owner's later requests exposes two boundaries that the extraction did not finish. Workspace roots remain mutable session-global state while each IDE client can display a local root; actions still carry relative paths without workspace identity. Operation resources are typed only after a string-labelled `domain`/`action` classifier, conflicts are rejected by the service, and Studio alone retries them through a bounded in-memory queue that is cleared on disconnect. This is not a contradiction that invalidates the service extraction: it narrows the claim. The shared state owner is real; multi-workspace identity and service-owned queue semantics are not. See the [latest service cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#the-shared-service-has-one-serialized-owner-but-not-yet-one-operation-contract).

The same distinction appears in content lifecycle. The latest provider gives Steam download staging, acquired cache, installed/disabled content, quarantine, app-owned indexes, selected Packagepack, locks, receipts, source workspaces and subscription projection separate paths and records. The UI-facing local catalog merges cached and installed locations by content ID, while source discovery remains outside that Library view. More consequentially, Composition stores exact version nodes but cache/install indexes, directories and locks use the stable content ID alone. Thus the code remembers an exact resolution without retaining multiple versions of the same dependency in parallel. Current source does not establish whether one global version per identity is the intended user contract or whether each playable Packagepack must retain a separately reproducible dependency closure. This is an owner-level composition/install invariant still to settle, not a conclusion supplied by the old resolver vocabulary. See the [latest Library/content-store cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#library-crosses-several-stores-while-the-durable-records-are-keyed-to-one-version-per-identity).

The compatibility story has a narrow exception: commit `25aeced` adds structured dependency facts while retaining the older string labels, marks the new field serde-defaulted and omits it when empty, and does not increment protocol version 30. That is an intentional additive bridge for already-running peers on the same protocol version. Later operation identity and diagnostics/origin additions advance the version to 31 and 33, respectively, and exact mismatch is rejected. The protocol crate has 16 focused round-trip/defaulting tests, the IDE crate has 65 tests for semantic helpers/diagnostics/edit safety/stale-result handling, and the Service has 13 child-process integration tests for selected lifecycle and persistence paths; none of these suites was run in this documentation pass. The process tests use the real local transport but run only on the test host, while the IDE/protocol suites primarily exercise local deterministic contracts. They do not establish the deployed cross-platform process/UI path. The source therefore shows both additive evolution and explicit lockstep breaks, not a universal “versioned means compatible” guarantee. The [latest protocol/test cross-check](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#client-protocol-v33-centralizes-typed-actions-but-its-transport-remains-one-json-line-envelope) records that boundary.

### October 25 — the player camera contract supports modes but not one cohesive selection surface

The detached freecam has its own earlier lineage inside this same camera story: October 1 `cffbab6a` adds the v2 observer policy, exclusive/passthrough input and projection/view-demand controls. October 2 `1f6d356` adds the live `debug/freecam_speed.rhai` scalar host hook; it composes with, rather than replaces, the Rust-owned speed, boost, input and transform policy. October 6 `ab65b8e` extracts the freecam into movement, observer and policy modules during a much broader cleanup. The split makes the separation of gameplay authority, camera motion and presentation demand explicit, but does not turn the freecam into a camera registry or persisted user setting. Current code's default is a 20 m/s linear movement speed with an 8× modifier; projection follows while view demand remains frozen. This helps explain why the camera can be detached from gameplay movement yet still fail to reveal newly visited world detail by default. Source confirms the policy and defaults, not the resulting visual coverage or runtime travel feel.

The current camera system also contains meaningful subject profiles, Cockpit/Chase/Orbit selection, portal-aware third-person boom collision, telemetry-backed flight HUD, and semantic action bindings. This answers part of the older request for camera modes, but only as an F5 cycle and console command; spacecraft cockpit head-look and an obvious visual mode chooser are not present in the inspected source. Camera policy is split between the global primary `PlayerCamera`, target-owned `ViewCameraProfile`, freecam settings resource and console commands. HUD dimensions are fixed in pixels, the velocity marker uses a fixed clamp instead of viewport/FOV projection, and key bindings are runtime-only. The October 9 `46e1eac` player/control/HUD patch is the relevant historical implementation boundary; current source still contains its core choices. These are structural source findings; no current screenshot or cross-resolution test was performed. See the [camera/HUD review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--camera-choices-exist-but-control-and-presentation-are-still-split-across-paths).

### October 25 — Installer evolves from a compiled bootstrap into a partly service-backed product

The Installer's first durable path appears July 18 as bootstrap tooling. On July 27, `af43868` collapses setup into shared app-root tools and `6603574` moves workflow launching into a compiled control surface; this solves a real distribution constraint because the setup tool must work before Rust, Cargo, Git or SteamCMD exist on a player's machine. October 14's `0a49cee` adds an eframe Installer module hosted by Vapor-GUI. Over October 20–23, the UI gains explicit app-root binding (`85d3ecf`), role controls (`c11a791`), target-subdirectory service discovery (`ccd5ecb`), a mandatory first-launch role/setup path (`2592142`), operation identity tracking (`0a84194`, `d1b38d4`) and promotion choices that remain available when readiness probes fail (`b3ddcf9`). Each step responds to a concrete integration failure, but they do not converge all lifecycle operations onto the service: role changes use the service, while repair/install/uninstall and first-run player setup still execute in the GUI or embedded CLI process. Core does provide opt-in user-data and Superworkspace purge paths, but the Installer does not surface them; the Superworkspace preflight itself performs network fetches and its expected-origin check is only a URL-suffix comparison. The source-pinned current ownership analysis is the [Installer review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--installer-is-a-partial-service-facade-with-a-second-bootstrap-owner).
