### October 25 — the Platform Server's operational surface outgrows its inventories

The current deploy script installs and restarts five app services, including Registry, but the deploy and systemd operator inventories still enumerate four and omit Registry. The local post-deploy health script probes only the first four services; the GitHub workflow checks Registry publicly only when an optional base URL is configured. Thus source can perform a successful local deploy without demonstrating Registry readiness. Separately, hourly root-state backups retain 48 default-named files (about two days at the configured cadence), while the recovery scripts still omit Registry from their stop lists despite its SQLite state living under the archived root. The validator accepts a regular file where restore assumes a directory, and restore has no automatic rollback once the live state root has been moved aside. The dated deployment report records a successful July 25 four-service host at the pre-rename root/env paths; the undated manifest `status = deployed` does not prove the current five-service source was subsequently deployed. These current-state findings are linked in the [deployment/recovery cross-check](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#current-root-deployment-bootstrap-and-recovery-cross-check); they are not evidence of a live outage or restore failure.

### October 25 — project-local audits are reconciled as dated evidence, not current authority

The project artifact corpus includes an Engine architectural audit pinned to Loo-Cast `ad479d5` (October 4), a handoff that authorizes a later refactor but explicitly requires refreshing the source first, an October 13 Studio/Launcher implementation plan, and the Loo-Cast developer startup prompt. These documents capture real design pressure and process intent, but their instructions and ownership maps do not automatically survive later repository and owner decisions. In particular, the Studio plan names the former Vapor-Launcher/Shell/SDK ownership split, while the October 25 source has distinct GUI binaries routed through a shared GUI package and a service-backed Client architecture; the Engine audit is 21 days older than the current Loo-Cast snapshot and cannot stand in for reviewing it. This corrects the research-corpus boundary: the timeline must account for project-local plans and audits alongside repository docs, while preserving their revision/date and authority limits. See the [evidence atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#intent-and-documentation-corpus-inventory).


### October 25 — a September rebase reproduction is compared with the current chart implementation

An auxiliary diagnostic bundle pins a headless reproduction to Loo-Cast `e14e928` on September 26. Its production run records both stale-child-coordinate interpretation after an origin rebase and a static-floor collider AABB left at its old chart position; an explicit collider refresh fixes the immediate query in the counterfactual, while a smaller 100-unit threshold reproduces the failures. The separate Earth surface-switching report was not tested. Later history adds `93b1a2a` (September 29) and `0e48843` (October 6), and the current implementation directly transforms chart-tagged physics/collider state and refits the affected trees. That is a plausible structural response to the recorded pair of defects, not proof of runtime closure: no October 25 replay was performed, and the Earth and Moon reports remain open. Detailed evidence: [semantic review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--historical-rebase-runtime-evidence-versus-the-current-chart-boundary).


### October 25 — Cargo diagnostics stream through the operation console, while progress remains step-granular

The current managed-build path requests Cargo JSON for compiler diagnostics, summarizes artifact events, streams child output through bounded readers, and emits a notice when the service’s retained operation-output queue evicts older records. This connects the managed Rust toolchain to the shared operation console more deeply than raw terminal forwarding. Its progress callback still fires only after each complete Cargo command returns, so a long compile can produce changing output without finer-grained completion progress. Source inspection only; no build/runtime replay. See [the current-state trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--cargo-output-is-structured-but-build-progress-is-only-step-granular).


### October 25 — RustRover setup survives as two incompatible repair implementations

The shared Core maintenance path reconciles modern JetBrains workspace/VCS settings and deletes old generated files. The CLI facade rename on October 18 (`c5b7025`) adds a separate `ide repair` that writes two of those files (`cargoProjects.xml`, `rust.xml`) as its expected output. Both target the discovered Superworkspace root, so their status/repair commands disagree about the canonical project state; CLI mutation also bypasses the Client service. The underlying intent—make Vapor's managed toolchain and repositories work cleanly in RustRover—survives, but the current implementations embody different generations. Source-level only; no IDE files were edited or commands run. See [current-state review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--two-public-ide-repairs-disagree-about-which-rustrover-files-are-canonical).

### October 18–25 — root Steam distribution gains a new service path without retiring the old Core API

The October 18–19 Client extraction adds an Application/Provider route for staging the current app source-root policy, with an explicit review fingerprint and a `dry_run` that stops before SteamCMD. In parallel, Core's older ecosystem deployment function remains public and re-exported; its file lineage begins September 6 and includes October 14 and October 21 changes, but no in-workspace invocation was found at the current snapshot. It loads `Vapor-Client.vapor.toml`, stages an ecosystem payload and calls SteamCMD even with `preview = true` (the generated VDF asks SteamPipe to preview). The newer path instead loads `[root.steam]` from `App-Source.vapor.toml` and returns from dry-run before launching SteamCMD. This is a parallel-contract finding, not proof the payloads should be merged or the old API can be deleted: their intended distribution roots differ, and external API consumers were not inspected. See [the current source comparison](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#a-second-public-steam-deployment-path-remains-in-core-with-different-manifest-and-preview-semantics).

### October 16–21 — Studio's Share screen grows from Workshop authoring to root-app publishing

Studio commit [`5ffb2a8`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/5ffb2a8e6eb6ae8c3283b8d4be646b94fbb27758) created a dedicated Publish screen for reviewing authored Workshop content. The next day, [`3e8ec88`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/3e8ec880fa0203620c4849ff9209298ab6c0e583) added guarded Steam root-app/depot publishing as a second tab on that screen. The distinction was operational—Workshop uploads package an authored content item; root publishing uploads the Vapor application/depot—but both became one Studio navigation destination. October 18–19 moved Studio and then its workflows behind the shared Client service (`ef6e6b1`, `d169e48`); October 20's `708bbf8` focused the visible fields on user actions without splitting the audience. The current source still presents both under Creator-area “Share”: typed actions centralize execution, but the interface does not distinguish routine community publishing from first-party release work. That is a product-boundary inference from code placement and visibility, not proof of an authorization bypass; root release still requires Steamworks access. See [the latest-state analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--studios-share-page-combines-community-publishing-and-first-party-release-controls).

### October 25 — the Composer’s acquired-content bridge is present only inside an authored workspace

The October 16–19 Studio sequence adds composition editing, then moves the workflow through the shared Client service. At the current snapshot, its primary Compose page still draws candidate content from registered source projects. A separate Catalog action can hand a workspace-located runtime item with a registered source counterpart into a Packagepack draft, but both target and item must resolve through the same open workspace; the action then returns to the source manifest editor. This preserves an editable authoring path, but it does not yet realize the owner’s broader rule that Composer combines already existing content and packs into new packs, with compilation/reusable-library production owned elsewhere. The older Cargo roadmap itself calls generic realization narrow, and the current Core reconciliation remains Crate-only and has no Client-service caller. This is partial integration, not zero functionality. See [current Composer/Cargo boundary](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--studios-composer-edits-authored-source-graphs-not-the-broader-acquired-content-graph).

### October 25 — IDE Problems gains a scale caveat beside its correctness coverage

The semantic IDE has 65 focused tests including source/build diagnostic merging, filtering and semantic-range lookup. Current Problems storage nevertheless bounds only build history (2,000 plus an omission record); source diagnostics are retained per file without a matching aggregate cap, and filtered virtual ranges still rescan retained rows. This is an unmeasured scaling risk, not an observed performance regression. The key distinction is that semantic correctness coverage exists while large-workspace behavior remains unproven. See [the current diagnostics review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--ide-problems-caps-build-output-but-source-diagnostics-have-no-comparable-aggregate-bound).

### October 25 — installed role depth and per-action tool requirements remain different models

The latest Core makes `Player → Composer → Content Developer → Ecosystem Developer` an ordered local role, but all three non-Player values cross the same `requires_developer_environment` threshold and reconcile the same Rust/Analyzer, Windows GNU target/linker and Tracy bundle. The current Developer Environment guide explicitly codifies that broad “Composer and higher” policy. Per-action `WorkflowTier` has only Player/Composer/Developer and is expressly not an installation or authorization model; its capability list names generic Rust, Rust Analyzer and Tracy, not target-specific build tooling. This follows a distinct consequence of the October convergence: one install bundle is shared, but the role ladder's increasing authoring scope has no corresponding local capability delta. The owner's later clarification that Composer may perform Cargo-backed composition without writing constituent Rust source identifies a missing middle operation between manifest-only authoring and Developer-tier content packaging. Demotion is deliberately non-destructive, so lowering a role does not reclaim these tools. Exact current-state cross-check: [role/toolchain analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--role-tiers-collapse-to-one-developer-bundle-while-action-profiles-describe-only-three-capabilities). This records a policy seam, not a decision to split or remove the broad bundle.

### October 22–25 — concurrent service work is real; queued retries remain Studio-specific

`3b692e7` adds explicit resource reservations and permits independent Client operations to overlap, while rejecting conflicting reservations at the service boundary. The approved workflow design speaks more broadly about conflicting operations serializing. Studio then adds a local retry path (`142a0f4`, expanded in `b7d457d`): it catches the service's conflict response and stores up to 64 actions in a process-local FIFO, retrying after terminal events. The queue is cleared on Studio disconnect. The Launcher consumes the same `queueable` availability flag as “enabled” but has no matching request retention/retry handler; a conflict becomes a logged rejection. Thus the architecture has concurrent service operations and one frontend-local queue adapter, not a shared all-frontends operation queue. The plan still leaves the concurrent-client/conflict-serialization verification item open. Detailed source trace: [operation queue ownership](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--operation-queuing-is-studio-local-even-though-readiness-is-advertised-across-frontends).

The October 23 Launcher snapshot makes that ownership mismatch concrete in the player surface. Play maps the selected composition’s install/readiness state to its primary action; Library excludes source projects; Workshop merges Steam search, subscription, and local catalog projections by PublishedFileId and suppresses Crate rows. Yet the screen’s single `busy` flag is derived from any active service operation, while its only deferred request is one replaceable search boolean; search and paging use a fixed 50-item Steam page and then paginate the returned items locally at 10/20/50. This is a meaningful player-first projection, but not the accepted common queue or canonical type-filter contract. The exact current-state code analysis is in the [Launcher cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#launcher-a-player-facing-projection-with-partial-shared-service-semantics); this observation is source-derived and was not runtime-tested.

### October 25 — operation identity outlives neither the service process nor Studio's history

The shared service gives operations a process-local monotone number, then shuts itself down after 15 seconds with no clients or active work. Studio separately persists up to 20 completed events and treats an incoming event with a matching number as already seen. These decisions compose badly across restart: a new service can reuse an old number, causing Studio to discard that new `OperationChanged` event before its terminal history/status path runs. Snapshot reconciliation still updates active-operation state, so the finding is event/history loss rather than task failure. This is a new source-derived lifecycle seam, not a reproduced user report. See [operation identity trace](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--persisted-operation-history-can-suppress-a-new-operation-after-service-restart).

### October 25 — the current Pack model is narrower than the owner's branch semantics

The October 15 Studio lifecycle plan marked composition from “compatible content identities” complete, and the current Create cards still teach Packagepack as one Engine plus one Game and Modpack as compatible add-ons. The owner’s later clarification and the local October 24 graph design note describe a richer contract: Packs are manifests, can contain mutually exclusive paths, and need resolution to choose a branch rather than install every member together. The current candidate resolver carries dependencies but not authored conflict declarations or a selected-branch record; optional edges are skipped, while fixed shape validation demands one Engine/Game closure. Installation does honor authored conflict records against enabled installed artifacts, so the history does not support “conflicts are wholly unimplemented.” It supports a more specific boundary: install-time exclusion exists, but pack-branch composition is still not represented by the shared resolver. The same latest-state comparison finds the generic generator maps Engine to a placeholder binary and Packagepack to metadata-only, opposite the flagship Loo-Cast library→Packagepack executable graph. The [latest-state comparison](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--studio-teaches-one-compatible-selection-the-content-graph-cannot-express-pack-branches) distinguishes these layers and preserves the unresolved design questions.

### October 25 — spatial demand is split into scopes, residency and capability realization

The current spatial runtime has a more explicit decomposition than the early legacy chunk managers: `SpatialDemandSource` describes an interest cuboid; `SpatialRefinementDemand` is a separate capability-specific detail request; `UsfContextResidency` stores a sparse ancestor-closed graph of canonical 1000-unit contexts; voxel realization turns generic/view/interaction/refinement inputs into scale-local realization intents; and a separate materialization pipeline owns dense voxel caches and readiness gates. This is a substantive separation of concern, not just a rename of “loaded chunk.” The schedule deliberately collects generic scopes before resetting and repopulating the shared residency request buffer, then reconciles USF contexts before voxel materialization residency.

The same latest-state pass finds two seams worth carrying into future implementation work. First, demand-to-context conversion validates each integer coordinate but does not bound the total three-dimensional range before iterating it; very large finite authored extents can be coordinate-representable yet computationally explosive. This is a source-derived risk, not a reproduced hang. Second, failed USF residency reconciliation retains its prior graph, while failed voxel demand-plan reconciliation retires stale desired materializations and retries. They may be valid subsystem-specific recovery policies, but no larger transaction was found that states their combined safety meaning. Neither generic residency nor voxel-role readiness by itself proves collision coverage for a high-speed sweep or accounts for the owner’s proposed accumulated scale-local epsilon. The detailed current cross-reference is in [demand, residency and realization](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#demand-residency-and-realization-bounded-later-work-no-end-to-end-planning-bound); no build, tests or runtime replay were performed.

This split formed through short-lived redesigns, not one clean implementation pass. On October 6, [`ab65b8e`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/ab65b8e2190a42e81f1bbae6b22a090297d8d987) first adds the separate `COLLISION_QUERY` role beside local `COLLISION` and creates a voxel-intent collector. On October 8, [`f588206`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/f5882067b0bcfc2ef206e1b888f91c616ab516c6) removes unconditional whole-body voxel demand and unused shell planning; later that day [`eb6814f`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/eb6814f24572aad8ad7406b0978f3315ac267b3a) adds a substantially expanded intent and contact-aware region planner. The `COLLISION_QUERY` bit survived that architectural churn without a Rust producer/consumer by the October 22 snapshot. This sequence supports “planned vocabulary outlived its integration,” not “a functioning query-role system was removed.” The October 8 commit messages and sizes establish selection/pruning pressure; explaining every deleted resolution path requires its own diff review and is not inferred from the summary alone.

### October 25 — the desired set is capped after uncapped region enumeration

The planner's nominal 65,536 desired-chunk limit applies before collection only to the moving non-view predictive tube. Stationary and view-backed demands instead enumerate full cuboid leaves or recursively cull a region, then sort and truncate afterward. Region spans limit each axis to the integer representation but do not check total volume. The entire operation is one non-preemptible Planning unit; a cooperative frame pacer cannot stop an unusually broad finite synchronous walk. This identifies a missing practical work bound in the current source, not a confirmed runtime freeze. The design sequence matters: [`cb094c1`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/cb094c12d9459ff105fab2de8b692da6c6bc5f85) introduced cooperative frame pacing on October 2; [`f588206`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/f5882067b0bcfc2ef206e1b888f91c616ab516c6) removed unconditional whole-body demand on October 8; [`eb6814f`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/eb6814f24572aad8ad7406b0978f3315ac267b3a) added intent and contact-aware region/tube selection later that day. The retreat narrowed what was requested, but neither it nor the later result truncation established a traversal budget for every request shape. See [the current plan-cost analysis](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#demand-residency-and-realization-bounded-later-work-no-end-to-end-planning-bound) and [the source review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-voxel-plan-cap-truncates-results-after-some-demand-paths-finish-enumerating).

The newer work-budget cross-check adds a narrower chronological result: `cb094c1` introduced cooperative frame pacing on October 2; `f588206` pruned unconditional whole-body demand on October 8; `eb6814f` then added intent and contact-aware region/tube selection. The current moving predictive tube honors its desired-set limit, but stationary and view-backed region traversal collect candidates before final truncation. Thus the historical direction reduced unnecessary broad demand without establishing a hard bound on every later planning path. This is not evidence that the October redesign caused a runtime stall; the current risk is source-derived and unprofiled. See [the current plan-cost cross-check](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#demand-residency-and-realization-bounded-later-work-no-end-to-end-planning-bound) and [the focused review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-voxel-plan-cap-truncates-results-after-some-demand-paths-finish-enumerating).

The October 25 collision cross-check sharpens a separate boundary: the direct semantic sweep provider is real even though the query-role publication path is not. It returns `Unknown` on any incomplete query, which is safer than treating uncertainty as free space, but its completeness flag is shared across all authorities: failure to project one authority or one edit’s bounds can make unrelated proposed motion unknown. The same provider calls candidate collection twice per request (once to publish candidate intervals and again while resolving), converts all geometric edits into each authority’s local edit list, and caps each narrow trace at 256 steps. The spacecraft’s `UsfCollisionQueryDemand` also stores a two-second lookahead that has no source reader; only the current step’s radius/error are submitted, so that field itself does not drive future residency. These are source-level coupling/workload findings, not reproduced latency or a proven cause of a reported braking failure. The provider modules contain no focused tests; policy tests elsewhere cannot substitute for semantic-query and flight-commit cases. See [the latest collision analysis](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#spatial-scale-and-collision-authority-scaffolding-exists-coverage-is-not-proven).

### October 25 — the collision provider agrees with the sphere that replaced terrain

The current swept query is semantically aligned with the current dense voxel base: both evaluate `CelestialFieldRealization`, whose distance is radial `length - radius`, with Add/Remove edits applied by the query path. That is a useful single-field property, but the shared field is now a sphere, not the planned Rocky/Lunar relief-and-cave model. The Oct 7 [`69780e1`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/69780e125ca9149548a408e9a55447eb0e6bc451) deletes 2,701 lines across 21 files in a change titled “removed unoptimized af terrain shit”; removed components include scale-introduced relief bands, rocky morphology, lunar/stellar profiles, cave SDFs and much of the GPU terrain path. Oct 8 [`f19d73f`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/f19d73f93867b04e8119a2fdcc93bbc508e2d113) removes remaining presentation-sampler/cave-support adapters while consolidating sampling. Current fixture construction explicitly calls `CelestialVoxelField::sphere` for authored bodies. Some current comments and scenario descriptions still speak of procedural terrain, caves and noisy gradients, so the repository contains vocabulary from the pre-retreat model beside the sphere-only implementation. The old algorithm’s removal is concrete; whether the removed design should be restored, replaced, or selectively redesigned is a future owner decision. The semantic collision query is therefore a real high-speed sphere-plus-edit query, not evidence that rough terrain collision works or that the reported Moon braking defect is fixed. See [the terrain/query comparison](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#the-collision-query-is-authoritative-for-a-sphere-not-for-the-terrain-that-was-planned).


## October 25, 2026 — source selection remains split after the App-root correction

A latest-state cross-check following the September source registry, October service extraction, and October 22 App-root fix finds that the root concepts are now named correctly but their selection lifecycle has not converged. Core's September `source.rs` registry owns a remembered active source and a known-root-aware current-directory fallback. The October 18 shared Client extraction added a separate durable `authoring_workspace_root` for all frontends. The October 22 correction clears one stale value when it points at an App root marked by `App.vapor.toml` without `Workspace.vapor.toml`; it does not reconcile Core's active-source record or validate every Workspace Open path. The CLI adds `VAPOR_WORKSPACE` as an override before it queries Core, while the IDE has its own opened-root projection; the provider's older `EnvironmentPaths::discover` documents yet another order but has no production call site in this checkout. Thus a single product action can enter distinct selection paths even though the Steam App/Workspace marker distinction itself is now explicit.

The present API asymmetry is concrete: `remember_source` parses a valid Vapor Workspace, while direct Core `open_source` persists any canonical directory outside the Installation. Service `Workspace Open` also accepts any canonical directory. The ordinary CLI `source open` narrows its path by provider validation before it invokes Core, so the arbitrary-directory behavior is exposed by the direct service/Core contract, not established for the normal CLI path. `AuthoringAction::OpenSource` writes Core source state; `Workspace Open` writes Client durable state. Each can therefore select a root invisible to the other's active-context mechanism. This is the latest source-level explanation of why “current working directory,” “active source,” “open workspace,” “Superworkspace,” and “installed App” have repeatedly become entangled in user-facing workflows. It does not establish that the Windows Installer report itself was caused by this path; current Windows behavior remains untested. See the [full source/selection contract review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--workspace-selection-has-two-persisted-authorities-and-unequal-validation) and [latest-state cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#source-roots-and-installed-app-roots-are-distinct-workspace-selection-is-split).

## October 25, 2026 — SDK absorption and CLI service routing leave a second workspace generator

The historical SDK became shared source on October 14: `0e5789bfe8d7590d401f33f7617ae75a6a2f023c` added `vapor_sdk_core` to Vapor (3,278 insertions, 29 deletions across 49 files), carrying workspace Cargo workflows, a pinned toolchain, Steam helpers and first-party root-package/SteamPipe code. That consolidated ownership of code, but not its runtime route. October 19's `5e8474f946970550658ff7bdf653a116799fe777` sent the primary `vapor` command workflows through the shared Client service and left `vapor sdk` as a direct in-process adapter.

The distinction persists at the latest checkout. The service reuses SDK Core for first-party root publishing, while `vapor sdk workspace sync/build/check/fmt/test/deploy` runs the SDK implementation directly from the terminal process. `workspace sync` uses its own upward CWD/`--workspace` discovery and generates Cargo manifests/source from listed project paths; it does not share the newer Client provider's lexical relative-path/parent-component guard. That guard is not canonical symlink containment. The workspace generator can create files outside the declared workspace when an explicitly invoked manifest supplies an absolute or parent-relative path. This is source-level conditional behavior, not a reproduced incident. It shows that the repository absorption and service centralization were different milestones: shared code can still be invoked outside service-owned scheduling, identity and operation reporting. The detailed contract and limits are in the [latest SDK/workspace review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--sdk-absorption-centralized-code-not-every-workspace-operation) and [current-state cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#the-embedded-sdk-command-keeps-a-second-workspace-engine).

## October 25, 2026 — Workshop payloads co-stage source and binaries while Pack and Cargo graphs remain separate

The current packaging path copies each authored artifact's source tree into an installable staged package, excluding `.git`, Cargo `target`, and the prior `output` directory; it then adds the selected target's declared binaries/libraries and rewrites the deployed manifest. Workshop publication packages through this same path before upload. Current source therefore distributes source files and runtime outputs together, without recording a source Git revision or proving that those outputs were built from the copied revision. That is a concrete implementation fact; whether source should instead be separately obtained from GitHub was raised as a design option, not settled owner policy.

The user-facing Pack graph and the actual Cargo linker graph are likewise distinct. The public Wheel Salvage example names Engine, Game and GameMod references in its Packagepack manifest, while its Cargo binary directly depends on the corresponding Rust crates; the flagship Loo-Cast Packagepack similarly links its Engine and Game through Cargo. The examples manually align those declarations. The current book says Packagepack is metadata rather than a Rust crate, while the registered Packagepack projects in both examples and Loo-Cast are Cargo executable crates. The sequence matters: Loo-Cast adopted the executable root on October 17 (`4551c53`), the book promoted “metadata, not a Rust crate” from an outline on October 20 (`a194167`), and the example created its Cargo binary root October 21 (`c157496`). The SDK's `quick-start`, `content-authoring` and `packs-and-packagepacks` pages show the same two-stage editorial history: all three were target-outline stubs in the July 4 book-seeding commit `9134d3f`, then gained concrete template/validate/deploy guidance in `a194167`. That rewrite also normalized a generic **Mod** role in authoring prose, although the implemented closed vocabulary has separate EngineMod, GameMod and ExtensionMod kinds. The new quick start accurately scopes `--host-only` to local smoke deployment, but none of these guides explains how an arbitrary resolved Pack graph becomes Cargo linker dependencies; authors still manually align both graphs. The statement may be coherent if the manifest kind and registered realization project are distinguished, but that contract is not documented or reflected in generic templates. This illustrates why Packagepack-as-root semantics, prebuilt constituent libraries and composition-time linking remain distinct from today's source-workspace build. See the [SDK pages](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/sdk/src/quick-start.md#L1-L34>), [latest release and graph cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#the-current-vapor-book-is-not-yet-aligned-to-the-latest-packagepack-model), and [detailed implementation review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--authored-content-and-runtime-artifacts-are-co-staged-pack-edges-do-not-generate-cargo-links).

The current-source review distinguishes the Playground's “Creative Menu” from Vapor's Composer/Creator workflows. Its immediate structural ancestry is the September 19 cleanup commit `f43573f`: a large creative-menu module was split into catalog, cursor, hotbar, and layout modules. The behavior stayed gameplay-oriented: it pages the registered item catalog, edits runtime hotbar slots, and consumes the held cursor item when the menu closes. ### October 25, 2026 — the spacecraft loop is integrated, but remains a single reference fixture

The latest source connects semantic ship identity, one authority partition, a scale-local realization, shared flight/navigation, collision-gated landing, boarding and a physically validated disembark pose. This is the clearest current player-facing proof that constituency, control, physical realization and presentation are separate concepts with real callers. It is still one Rust-authored starter craft: the spawn path refuses a second manifestation and the landing action expects one controlled ship. The design history moved from person→ship constituency and local-control vocabulary on September 22, to collision-query wiring on September 29, to hull-based landing/disembark on September 30, and semantic-constituency visibility on October 7. The last direct spacecraft-file edit (`46e1eac`, October 9) changed two lines; later shared control/spatial changes affect the surrounding handoff without adding a vehicle catalog, fleet, save lifecycle or authored craft API. The current review therefore treats this as a substantial gameplay integration loop and a deliberately narrow content boundary, not as general vehicle infrastructure. The user's earlier high-speed Moon braking/collision report is not verified as fixed by this source review; no current runtime session was performed. See [spacecraft current contract and lineage](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--the-spacecraft-is-a-complete-reference-loop-not-a-vehicle-lifecycle) and [the player-facing current-state map](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#gameplay-horizon-the-latest-product-ambition-exceeds-the-current-feature-set).

### October 25, 2026 — authored Earth arrival uses a bounded terrain search, but the fixture remains spherical

The current Earth bootstrap does more than place a player at a fixed coordinate. A bounded deterministic resolver searches outward from the authored arrival direction, samples a hull-sized neighborhood, scores slope and roughness, and chooses the best acceptable candidate. The selected point is offset by the physical hull's support radius plus a character or spacecraft clearance, written canonically, and then followed by a coverage-gated spatial transition. Yet the fixture's active `CelestialVoxelField` is a sphere, so this algorithm's rocky-terrain/cave safeguards have no varied terrain to discriminate. The first semantic position is written before transition admission; the later coverage gate is not evidence that collision was ready before that write. This source review did not reproduce a collision failure. It clarifies the gap between a thoughtful placement algorithm and the field/readiness guarantees that its comments can imply. The [worldgen evidence atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7a-worldgen-means-deterministic-construction-inputs-today-not-procedural-worlds) records search bounds, hull clearance, coarse provenance and the absence of active generated terrain.

### October 25, 2026 — Play crosses the service, application and provider, but release identity remains unbound

The October 19 service migration (`d7e21dc3`) already moved real composition actions out of the frontend and into a typed session/worker path. The current Play path confirms that this was more than a common snapshot API: Studio submits a `CompositionAction::Launch`; the Client service captures the selected composition and owns the asynchronous operation/output; application code checks or acquires the installed composition graph; provider code validates typed dependency closure and resolves the host-specific executable. October 21's `a10ca0e6` adds cross-target tooling and launch/content updates, and `92ab2b9b` further stabilizes the process/service path and adds managed Rust Analyzer. These commits establish successive boundary work, not proof that the shipped Steam experience works on each OS.

The latest implementation still checks graph and executable separately. The provider selects the first binary declared for the current host target and confirms it is a file; packaging stages existing build outputs and the source tree into one release directory. No current step binds that binary to the exact resolved Cargo link graph/source revision. Service fixture tests exercise launch readiness and operation conflicts, but the inspected provider path has no direct executable-resolution tests, and the process integration file has no real Packagepack Launch action. This is a concrete remaining gap between “shared service owns Play” and “every published Packagepack is a verified realization of its declared content graph.” It also explains why service architecture and full-stack Steam launch assurance must be tracked separately. See [current service-to-binary path and evidence limits](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7c-play-is-service-routed-but-the-executablecontent-binding-remains-a-separate-contract) and [the release identity cross-check](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#what-looks-like-one-release-but-is-not-yet-one-contract).


### October 25, 2026 — role setup remains a monolithic provisioning step

The current code has a persisted four-value role ladder but one provisioning threshold: every role above Player installs the same developer environment. That environment includes Rust/Cargo, Analyzer, Windows GNU cross-target/linker, Tracy Profiler and Tracy analysis. Operation profiles, by comparison, declare narrower local capabilities. The Installer makes the broad contract visible by promising all of these tools to Composer; it is not merely misleading copy. The architecture is internally inconsistent: role setup bundles by user level, action admission gates by concrete capability, and host support is a third dimension. Promotion may consequently require tools irrelevant to the immediate workflow; demotion intentionally preserves all installed tooling. This source review did not test a Windows promotion. See [the implementation analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--role-setup-is-one-all-tools-transaction-not-a-progressive-capability-plan).

### October 25, 2026 — Workshop type filtering is tag-backed; subscriptions remain eagerly rendered

The chronology separates the feature into distinct layers. The October 16 [`9ee075a`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/9ee075a645d9dfce6a71df95a127e71cd92fee2f) split the browser into acquisition, search and subscription panels. On October 21, [`30037ea`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/30037eadd18a7f6c5c5d419dd48d3f5dd9aa8349) introduced the Vapor content-kind dropdown as a string-tag filter. October 22's [`7ab704b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/7ab704bf7978a9e387e29236b750f9002135b64a) moved the search request and result snapshot to typed `ContentKind` across domain, protocol, service and Steam provider, while the actual query still translated the type into a Steam-required tag; it did not use the accepted Registry catalog. Studio's [`b47056c`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/b47056cf269510a3420591058f85739281d06247) preserved that typed value and added configurable 10/20/50 local slicing plus selection across search pages. Vapor's same-day [`b32fec7`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/b32fec76eaa5d49e9fadad31b5557764a29bd8e4) preserved raw Steam tags in subscription records, but the current subscription UI still only searches ID/title/Steam status, does not expose kind filtering, and eagerly renders all matches. Current Browse therefore has a real tag-backed filter; Subscriptions does not have a kind filter at all. ### October 25, 2026 — Rust Analyzer refactors are revision-safe previews, not full workspace edits

The current IDE validates Rust Analyzer's returned edits against open-buffer versions and the active workspace, limits one proposal to 64 files/4 MiB, and requires review before changing buffers; disk writes remain explicit saves. It refuses edits to closed files and LSP file operations, including file create/delete/rename operations. This is a defensible guard against stale or out-of-workspace edits, but multi-file refactors can require users to open every affected file, and module move/create actions are outside this edit route. The distinction sharpens the implementation status: Rust Analyzer is integrated for intelligence and bounded in-buffer changes, not yet a general workspace refactor engine. No editor interaction or refactor was run. ### October 25, 2026 — shared Workshop results can redirect every Studio client

The local Client service stores one latest acquisition batch in its shared session snapshot and broadcasts that snapshot to all connected frontends. This means a Workshop acquisition initiated in one Studio can trigger the same navigation in another connected Studio. The source path is confirmed, but no multi-client runtime reproduction was performed. The application's acquisition result was also checked while tracing this path: requested root items and required dependencies are intentionally separate counts, so a suspected mismatch in that count comparison was rejected. ### October 25, 2026 — game debug traversal has a control path, but no bounded command-level pace contract

The F2 command surface does include the requested characteristic-speed debug traversal: `debugfly` suppresses collision and gravity through the override and derives flight speed from the existing TravelPace multiplier. The controls remain split across Shift-wheel log2 steps, throttle wheel input, debugfly's plain-wheel pace behavior, and a numeric `speed` command. The latter writes any finite nonnegative `f32` directly, bypassing the log2 range enforced by wheel-step changes; the character movement multiplication can overflow for a sufficiently large accepted value. The command metadata also has no permission/scope field, though this pass did not establish who can invoke the F2 console at runtime. These are source-contract findings and an arithmetic boundary, not a reproduced gameplay failure. See [the detailed travel-command audit](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#latest-state-console-trace--game-command-runtime-versus-vapor-operation-console).

### October 25, 2026 — Docs publication stages a tree but concurrent upload ownership is undefined

The Docs Server protects upload with its own configured bearer token and validates archive paths, entry kinds, total bytes and file count before promoting a staged tree. Promotion first moves the current tree to one fixed `.previous-current` path and then moves the staged directory into place. This is recoverable on a single failed promotion, but it is neither an atomic reader-visible swap nor serialized across concurrent upload requests; overlapping installers can remove or replace the same previous-tree path. The source supplies no publication ordering guarantee and has no multi-upload test. This is a source-derived race risk, not evidence that an upload corrupted the live docs. It also sharpens the shift in July from immutable versioned releases to one mutable `current/` tree: less product machinery, but no per-release rollback authority in Docs. See [the current Docs endpoint analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-20-docs-publication-becomes-a-local-build--vps-authorized-workflow).

### October 25, 2026 — Studio's player lifecycle inherits a global authoring dirty-state gate

The composition panel derives launch/install/update/repair affordances from service-projected availability, but overlays a local unsaved-editor guard. That guard spans every open workspace document and authoring draft; install, update, repair and preview handlers call it even when the selected playable composition has no source-workspace association. The service itself accepts the workspace as optional for those operations. This makes the intended Player-versus-Developer cordon porous in one direction: unrelated unsaved source edits can block an independent Player install/update, although retaining a save guard for a composition actually built from that source remains justified. The code path was traced across the UI and service layers; no interaction or runtime reproduction was performed. This finding sharpens the previously identified workflow-tier mismatch rather than proving the entire panel is wrongly designed. See [the source review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-25--studios-composition-panel-lets-unrelated-authoring-dirt-block-player-operations) and [current-state boundary comparison](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#player-composer-developer-one-intended-ladder-several-current-authorities).

### October 26, 2026 — the basic-content starter is documented as playable but emits no Packagepack executable

The generic starter's stated local loop and the actual authoring/launcher contract diverge at two stages. `source init basic-content` creates an Engine Cargo binary, a Game library, and a metadata-only Packagepack manifest; the generated Packagepack declares no executable or target runtime. The guides tell authors to deploy/select this root as playable, but the launch resolver requires a target-specific runtime entry and binary under the Packagepack. Separately, `content deploy` does not compile Cargo projects: its CLI branch sends a service Library Install action, and packaging reads existing build outputs. The Cookbook falsely says deployment builds the registered projects; the generated README and SDK quick start omit the separate `content build` step. Therefore the scaffold lacks both compiled Engine/Game outputs on a clean path and the Packagepack-owned executable needed to launch. This source-level mismatch echoes the earlier end-user error reported in this thread (“no ready-to-run build”), but does not prove that the user's old report had this exact cause; no current deployment or launch was run. The Cookbook also uses generic “Mod” terminology for its extension workflow, compounding the gap between starter language and the closed ten-kind taxonomy. ### October 26, 2026 — F2 record history is bounded, but command ingress and dispatch are not

The September 27 console refactor (`7d9af82`) established a game-owned command/diagnostic path; October 22's shared telemetry-record adapter (`c070bf3`) aligned the record payload with Vapor's console vocabulary without moving command authority into the Client service. The current source makes the resulting distinction concrete: pending diagnostic records are limited to 4,096, and visible F2 history to 512, but command submissions are held in a separate unbounded queue. Every Bevy Update drains that entire queue and executes each handler synchronously against the mutable World. Native stdin reads and submits whole lines without an explicit size cap, while parsing allocates token strings from the input. This does not prove a real frame hitch or memory failure; it shows that record-count limits do not bound ingress bytes or per-frame command work. This finding sharpens the shared-console history: record reuse progressed, while command scheduling and resource policy remain game-local and distinct from Vapor's bounded service-operation path. ### October 26, 2026 — the CLI's standard root lifecycle is service-backed; SDK commands remain a parallel path

The October 19 CLI split (`5e8474f`) and October 20 root deploy/package migration (`61ee983`) reduced the old CLI-owned workflow implementation and moved normal operations toward Client actions. Current source confirms that `root build` also goes through `WorkspaceAction::RunTool`, while `root deploy`, `root package`, and `root publish` use typed Workspace/Publishing actions and service operation output. This corrects any reading that all Cargo/root work still runs directly inside the CLI. The local `client deploy local` path calls Core to bootstrap/update the app itself, and `client launch` starts the installed Entrypoint; both are local host/deployment edges rather than ordinary content-domain operations. The remaining substantive overlap is the `vapor sdk` subcommand, which dispatches into SDK Core directly and carries overlapping build/test/package/publish command concepts outside Client operation identity and scheduling. October 23's latest CLI commit (`a09c49c`) adds origin/composition provenance to printed operation records but does not remove that second command authority. The user-approved direction favors one local service API, but the accessible decision record does not settle whether these SDK actions are a deliberate low-level escape hatch or should become service operations. No CLI command was run. See the [command-level routing review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26-follow-up--root-operations-are-service-routed-bootstrap-and-sdk-paths-remain-distinct) and [shared-service cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#the-central-contract-under-examination).

### October 26, 2026 — Identity's role administrator is implemented, but the accepted cross-service authorization path is not

The July 23–24 Identity burst produced an operational account model rather than only a role enum: Steam-anchored profiles, linked GitHub identities, short-lived root dashboard sessions, role grant/revoke routes and audit records. Role administration remains limited to `root` and `content-developer`, requires both external identities to resolve to one enabled profile, and records role mutations with audit events. A sequential sole-root revoke is rejected, although the current aggregate-count guard runs before its write transaction and therefore leaves a concurrent-revocation race window that has not been reproduced. The key boundary change came later: the July 25 cross-service contract proposed audience-bound session introspection; the September Registry implementation created provider topology; the October 22 decision moved canonical content/workshop/release authority to Registry while keeping people/role authority in Identity. By October 26, this still has not become a consumer path: no Identity introspection route, Registry catalog, or Client/Docs/Diagnostics consumer exists in the inspected source. The current result is real account/role administration plus an accepted-but-unintegrated authorization architecture. See the [Identity code/design cross-check](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--identity-manages-local-account-roles-ecosystem-authorization-is-not-integrated) and the [historical authority decision](#identity-implementation-and-its-later-authority-contract).

### October 26, 2026 — SDK toolchain repair remains a declared stub

The current SDK command specification describes `vapor sdk toolchain repair`, but its dispatcher handles only status and install; repair falls through to a generic `not_implemented` result. Install refuses an existing toolchain root, so it cannot repair a damaged partial installation, and status checks only the root plus Cargo/rustc file existence. This is a source-level mismatch, not an observed failed command. It also clarifies that the SDK toolchain route and shared Developer-role provisioning are separate: the latter handles the Windows GNU-LLVM target/linker, while the SDK install plan lists Rustup-host targets. See the [toolchain route review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--sdk-toolchain-repair-is-advertised-but-unimplemented).

### October 26, 2026 — the shared Client makes composition state durable but keeps install state observational

The October 18 extraction (`f9e8b13`) added the first service-owned Client state store and Composition model in the same large change that split the shared service/domain from frontends. The current store migrates legacy eframe profile values only when `studio-state.json` does not yet exist; otherwise that file is authoritative. It persists the active Composition ID, exact resolved graph and launch settings, while clearing runtime installation status to `Unknown` on both load and save. The legacy migration keeps an old selected content ID but cannot recover its exact version or resolved dependency graph. This is the technical history behind the current product-model seam: the record model began as part of service consolidation, whereas later owner direction says Packagepack itself is the playable selection and “composition” is informal shorthand. The migration is source-backed, but no historical user-state file was available and no migration was run. See the [current persistence review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--composition-state-persists-selection-and-resolution-not-installation-status).

The October 19 follow-ups did not replace that storage design. `971ab11` adjusted the legacy-import fixture to the renamed `workspace_root` field; `c3b0a78` added regression cases for schema-1 profile-shaped state migrating to schema 2, preserving its active record, root selection and launch arguments, and for runtime installation state being discarded from disk. The migration code itself was already present in the October 18 extraction. This distinction matters: the later commit adds evidence for the intended migration contract, not a new runtime experiment, and the tests remain unrun in this audit.

The same October 18 extraction also made installed Packagepack launch self-healing: its launch helper installs a missing dependency closure, repairs when a persisted resolved graph is available, and downloads/imports missing Workshop root seeds before installation. October 23's [`4fe3ab2`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/4fe3ab2121b81c4eaeb62effaf16ac298607d6da) adds operation-context output forwarding for the launched process, but the original install/repair branch remains in place and still has no corresponding staged operation context. The service snapshot exposes Play while install state is `Unknown`, and its operation phase remains `Running` throughout acquisition/install/launch. This behavior predates the later explicit player journey and install lifecycle discussions; code history confirms the mechanism, while the owner's intended consent boundary between Play and install remains unresolved. No launch or Workshop call was run. See the [current Play analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--play-can-acquireinstallrepair-before-launching-while-reporting-running).
### October 26, 2026 — source-derived IDs narrow an older generic identity type

The identity contract entered the tracked Vapor code in the September 4 vertical-slice work (`fedee52`): `VaporId` was a version-independent string that rejected only emptiness and whitespace. The September 5 follow-up (`c65f1e7`) renamed the exact pair from `ResolvedContentId` to `ContentVersionId` and clarified that exact identity exists independently of resolution. On October 18 (`f9e8b13`), the shared Client extraction moved that vocabulary into `vapor_content`; the same extraction added a source-manifest parser that rejects authored `id` fields and synthesizes content IDs from a root/workspace prefix plus constrained names. At the October 26 snapshot, therefore, the system has a permissive API/persistence ID type beside a stricter source-discovery naming rule. The implementation could intend the latter as a subset, but it does not name that distinction in the type system or state the canonicalization/alias policy. This finding is source- and commit-history-backed; rename/move effects and runtime behavior were not exercised. See [the focused identity analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--content-identity-has-two-lexical-contracts).

### October 26, 2026 — Workshop staging grows a review gate, not a durable release record

The July 10 content lifecycle (`8464f463`) put manifest discovery, build-output staging, cache/install state, fingerprints and SteamCMD VDF publication into one 2,193-line provider-shaped module. The October 18 extraction moved that content provider into the shared Client architecture; the October 19 `d7e21dc` follow-up moved operation execution into the service. The present Stage action explicitly builds the selected authored workspace for target triples before producing a review, while the Publish action re-stages and compares the reviewed fingerprint before invoking SteamCMD. This is a meaningful correction to a simple “publish whatever is in the output directory” interpretation. The remaining gap is provenance: local receipts do not bind source revision, build configuration, exact target set and remote Steam item revision into a common release identity; the generic receipt filename also has only second-level precision. The chronology therefore shows the system becoming more guarded and service-owned without becoming an authoritative release ledger. Source comparison confirms the path; no build or publication was run. See [the current release-path analysis](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--workshop-review-protects-a-local-stage-but-receipts-do-not-identify-a-release).

### September 20–October 6, 2026 — canonical spatial transition becomes an explicit admission/commit path

The current transition event is present in the September 20 `c9f1c84` spatial lineage. On October 5, `e987230` changed the transition applier to use `UsfRuntimeChartState` in place of the older `UsfSpatialFrame`; it did not split the implementation into new modules. October 6's `0e48843` made smaller transition refinements, and the later October 6 cleanup (`ab65b8e`) performed the substantial extraction into separate `intent`, `admission`, and `apply` modules, keeping one-shot relocation, continuous interaction requirement and motion-reanchor intents together in the new facility. The `f32` native-velocity conversion preflight moved with the apply implementation: the parent version already used the same exponentiation and early return, so the extraction did not introduce the full-range failure now identified in the source audit. The resulting contract admits destination capability coverage before canonical recharting and allows a physics provider to veto continuous coarsening when the destination hull would overlap. History and current source support a real architecture evolution from chart recentering toward a typed transition transaction. They also show that “safe transition” remains scoped: physics veto is not applied to every relocation, finer-scale contact transfer is explicitly deferred, and the focused current test checks destination demand rather than end-to-end commit/liveness. This chronology describes source evolution; it does not validate the Moon-approach behavior reported by the owner.


### September 10–October 6, 2026 — combat and health gain modules without crossing the Engine/Game package boundary

The September 10 `68717b4` “Schtuff” commit added the first 293-line combat implementation and documented a generic chain: projectile → hit → damage → health → death. The initial interaction used a hand-written axis-aligned Hitbox. September 19's `356aa47` (“cleanup part 18”) extracted Health, presentation and thermal injury from the combat file, and separated hit conversion from damage application through `HealthSet`; `d523d73` later renamed `Hitbox` to `DamageableBounds`. Current source preserves the staged request/effect boundary, but projectile checks remain endpoint-only. More significantly for the owner's package model, Combat and Health remain in `spacetime-engine/src/game`, while the separate `loo-cast-game` crate installs a Game plugin from the Engine crate. This is a chronological example of internal decomposition improving without a matching artifact ownership migration. These commit summaries and current source do not establish why the original placement was chosen, prove the generic subsystem is genuinely reusable, or reproduce collision tunneling.

### July 7 – October 17, 2026 — a Game content crate is created, but implementation stays inside the Engine

On July 7, `afe1d77` created `loo-cast-game` as a member of the unified Loo-Cast workspace. Its own module comment was unusually explicit: the game implementation was temporarily housed under `spacetime_engine::game` while the runtime/composition boundary was proven; physical relocation could follow without changing the host contract. This means the intended seam preceded the actual code move. July 17 `fc58aa7` reset first-party content to product placeholders and July 28 `146fe37` changed the Engine placeholder handoff, but neither completes the Game-source migration. September 19 `4abb207` refactors the wrapper; September 24 `32b05dc` changes it from the earlier `TestGamePlugin`/`LooCastPlugin` names to `LooCastGamePlugin`, still implemented inside Engine. October 17 `4551c53` moves launch to an explicit Packagepack-owned binary, which calls `spacetime_engine::run(loo_cast_game::install)`. The final executable boundary therefore advances while the code ownership boundary remains where the July note called it temporary. This sequence is evidence that artifact/build integration and semantic source relocation progressed independently, not evidence that the owner consciously abandoned the migration. The current Game plugin also contains generic-claiming domains whose schedule sets are defined by the Game aggregate, so deciding placement requires disentangling both implementation ownership and dependency direction.

### September 22 – October 9, 2026 — reference spacecraft and authored worlds grow inside the Game facade

The current reference spacecraft lineage begins on September 22 with the USF experimentation sequence (`71867eb` and adjacent commits). It grows into a real semantic ship manifestation with its own locomotion/flight/navigation state, hull-based landing checks, boarding/disembarking transactions and player-control transfer. The September 25 `e14e928` unifies celestial fixture geometry and canonical-coordinate ownership. October 6's `0e48843` performs a broad integration/reorganization across Player, Spacecraft and World; October 9's `46e1eac` continues control/visibility behavior. The resulting current contract distinguishes human Player identity from controlled subject and vehicle manifestation, and treats the celestial fixture as authored scenario policy over shared Engine facilities. But both the reference ship and scenario selector remain compiled under `spacetime-engine::game`; the world choices are a hard-coded enum and the active gameplay plugin set is not selected from resolved content. These changes strengthen a first-party game's use of generic primitives, not an independent content plugin or a resolved world/mod graph. Commit lineage does not prove a deliberate decision to keep the scenario permanently built-in.

On September 23, `b5b6d6f` introduced a dedicated `SurfaceContext` between canonical body geometry and flight telemetry. The intent was to stop treating a measured distance as proof that collision support existed: it split nominal/procedural surface reference, radial altitude and hull-adjusted clearance from a separate collision-coverage readiness fact. The current implementation preserves that distinction, but the latter fact remains a local coverage probe rather than proof that a predicted approach corridor is collision-resolved. The current selector also chooses by absolute center altitude before subtracting hull support, so the type's “nearest” interpretation is narrower than nearest hull clearance. This marks real conceptual progress in the collision story while preserving the gap between readiness telemetry and safe arrival; neither the commit nor current source verifies an actual landing approach. [Current surface projection](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#flight-safety-is-layered-across-travel-policy-directional-supervision-and-collision-response).

### October 7, 2026 — performance pruning removes authored planetary relief and caves

Commit `69780e1` replaces the authored celestial constructor's profile/detail/noise-key field with `CelestialVoxelField::sphere(radius, detail_root)`. It deletes 2,701 lines across 21 files, including rocky/lunar profiles, semantic terrain bands, cave SDF generation, noise-backed morphology and most GPU density code; the commit message explicitly calls the removed terrain “unoptimized.” The resulting current source samples a radial sphere and assigns ROCK/VOID only. October 8 restructuring builds a clearer deterministic construction/provenance and canonical-field boundary, but does not restore that morphology. The meaningful historical distinction is: earlier terrain complexity existed in source but was deliberately removed, while today's newly explicit WorldSeed and PhenomenonGeneration machinery is mostly construction-fact infrastructure and Earth/Moon currently use exact constraints. This establishes why terrain authoring and generation need a fresh owner-designed contract. It does not establish that the removed algorithm was accurate, usable, or adequately benchmarked; no visual/performance comparison was run. [Commit `69780e1`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/69780e125ca9149548a408e9a55447eb0e6bc451), [October 8 field work](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/f19d73f).

### October 19–21, 2026 — create-from-content remains split at the Studio workspace boundary

On October 19, `9501276` replaced Studio's recent-Workshop-acquisition shortcut with a catalog-based flow, but the newly added helper creates and activates a blank composition before assigning its exact Packagepack and optional workspace in a second service request. October 21's `8765f62` added a validated atomic `CreateFromContent` action to Vapor's shared service/domain; it validates exact catalog identity, Packagepack kind, availability and conflict state, but has no workspace field, so Studio did not adopt it. The resulting history is a concrete example of cross-repository API growth without end-to-end integration: the backend's atomic option cannot carry a piece of Studio's current composition meaning, and Studio's two-step alternative can leave an empty active record after the second request fails. The intended repair is one shared mutation that includes the workspace association, not merely swapping one enum variant. Source evidence is recorded in the [current-state review](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#studio-composition-creation-is-split-across-service-mutations) and [semantic diff review](loo-cast-vapor-semantic-diff-review.md#october-26--studio-creates-a-playable-selection-through-two-durable-mutations); this chronology establishes code history, not an observed user failure.

### September 12, 2026 — portal orientation settling introduces a third character frame

Commit [`67160378`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/67160378248ebe0f26dd3f311f4c9e3250a038da) introduced `CharacterControlFrame` after the earlier player path used physical body rotation directly for view-relative movement. The patch routed movement and noclip orientation through this control basis, left `CharacterLocomotionFrame` responsible for stable up, and began a smooth settle after both conventional portal traversal and the split-character crossing. This explicitly separated three ideas: gameplay/gravity orientation, physical pose, and the orientation from which the player looks and steers. Current code preserves that distinction after later file/module restructuring, and adds `snap_to` for explicit pose transactions. It now also eases new movement input and gates jump input during settling. The timer advances in render `PreUpdate`, while gravity/frame synchronization and intent sampling are pre-fixed-loop operations; this cadence is established by source but has not been measured under catch-up, pause or low-frame-rate conditions. The commit explains intent and implementation shape, not verified player feel. The September 11 portal decomposition (`54fc79a9`) moves a monolithic gameplay portal toward `domain`, `topology`, `simulation` and `rendering` modules and introduces recursive render-tree/camera code alongside the first crossing/mapping tests. On September 19, `eaf0454e` moves the portal subtree from `game/portal` to `spacetime-engine/src/portal` while adding the first rigid split solver adapter. October 5 `e987230f` removes the split-visual triangle-count test and the crossing/mapping tests during the portal-simulation restructuring; no local portal tests remain in the current source tree. The concrete display path survives and becomes easier to navigate, but current audit finds two implementation-level limits that the historical chronology alone did not show: configured recursion depths 3–4 exceed Bevy's 0–63 layer constructor because node IDs grow in radix four, and split visuals regenerate meshes every Update pass. Current code is source evidence; the accepted depth failure was not executed, and the repeated mesh cost was not profiled.
